### Stage 2b — the spanning (triple) header — BUILT 2026-09-25

**As built, on branch `smearforn-stage-2b`, in eleven commits, then a round of code-review fixes (2026-09-26).** No `PROJECT_FILE_VERSION` bump. (An earlier draft of this line said "eight commits" and the branch had eleven — a small thing, recorded because a count nobody checks is exactly the kind of claim that gets believed.)

**The model, exactly as confirmed.** A spanning header is a **wall-level record over a slot-index range**, per wall per story: `SpanningHeader { id, heightIn, headerHeightIn?, startSlotIndex, endSlotIndex }`. Its **width is derived, never stored** — the sum of the covered slots' widths — so it follows those panels rather than being a second copy of the same number that can drift. The arithmetic is a pure module, `packages/geometry/src/spanningHeader.ts` (+ its test file), the same shape Stages 1 and 2 took; the app-level record, the catalog-aware height resolution and the naming walk are `apps/web/app/spanningHeader.ts` (+ its test file), mirroring how `midWallBeam.ts` splits from `wallVerticalBands.ts`.

**The reuse is total and it is the point.** `SpanningHeaderGeometry` is *structurally* `MidWallBeamGeometry`, so `computeWallVerticalBandsForSlot` shortens the panels beneath a header **with no change to that function at all**, and a header stacks with a Mid-Wall Bond Beam on the same slot instead of fighting it (asserted). One helper, `wallBandGeometry(beams, headers)`, is the single place those two lists are joined, and **every** band consumer takes it: `allPanelInstances`, the wall elevation, the 3D split, the 3D naming pass, and the zone reconciliation. Passing only the beams to any one of them is how the elevation and the cut list would come to disagree about how tall a panel is; `reconcileWallZonesForBeamChange` is accordingly now `reconcileWallZonesForBandChange` and takes the full geometry either side of a change.

**The span adds no width to the wall.** Nothing in the geometry module returns slots, the slot array is asserted untouched, and the browser harness measures the wall's own total in eighths before and after a header lands: unchanged.

**Naming, as decided.** One global counter over stories → `footprint.walls` order → each wall's headers by start slot, so `H1` may be on the north wall and `H2` on the east. A test puts one header on each of two walls and asserts `H1`/`H2`, because **a per-wall counter is the natural thing to write by mistake**; another asserts the name matches `/^H\d+$/` and carries no direction letter. The browser harness asserts the same thing through the real UI.

**The cross-reference is built, both ways, and it is on paper.** `H1`'s sheet: *"East wall — spans E4, E5."* `E4`'s and `E5`'s sheets: *"Header above: H1."* `PanelFabricationInstanceRef` gained an optional `note` for exactly this. `panelFabricationGroups` had to gain `spanningHeaderCrossReference` as a dependency — a memo one dep short of its real inputs is precisely the stale-sheet defect Stage 3's review found, and it would have left every panel sheet claiming there was no header above it.

**What it is, as a fabricated part.** `buildBigHeaderMembers` at the derived span — the geometry the Big Header panel type already has (chords, repeating W-truss webs on both wythes, two jack studs). **No new member geometry and no new building number.** Its own Shop Fab page is grouped by span + height (the "exact copies together" rule), walking the records directly the way the Mid-Wall Bond Beam pages already do, since a wall-level record has no `PanelSlot` for the instance pipeline to walk. Weight = wood + fasteners off the real member set, added to the project total so a panel on a cut list is not weightless.

**⚠ Two things stated rather than buried, because both are judgement calls a reviewer should see:**

- **Price: it is charged at the header/sill (`opening`) rate — TOMMY'S DECISION, 2026-09-25**, asked directly what rate a spanning header carries. It shipped as a declared assumption and stopped being one on that date. **Two things this does NOT mean, both stated in the code as well:** it does not promote any catalog value's status — what he settled is *which existing rate applies*, not that the rate is a confirmed number — and it is deliberately **not** consistent with its nearest neighbour, since the mid-wall **Big Header BEAM is priced at the `roof` rate**. Two spanning things, two rates, by decision. **The Review Log entry says the disagreement out loud**, because that is what reaches the engineer and silence there would read as consistency.
- **Project wood weight gains spanning headers and is still wrong in two pre-existing ways, both now named in the code beside the new line.** `totalWoodWeightKg` walks standard/braced *slots*, so (1) Mid-Wall Bond Beams have always been absent from it, and (2) every slot is charged at **full story height**, so a panel shortened under a header keeps full-height wood while the header's own weight is added on top — a small over-count, in the opposite direction to (1). **Documented rather than fixed**, deliberately: the fabrication sheets are already right (they build at `heightOverrideIn`, the real band height), so nothing reaching a shop is wrong, and correcting the total means running the band pipeline inside that sum, which changes the displayed weight of every existing project that has a beam in it. That is its own change with its own Review Log line, the same call this branch made about the beam's 3D anchor drift.

**The refusals, all at the point of edit and never at load.** A one-slot span (a header above ONE panel is already expressible as a zone *within* that column, so duplicating the concept is refused and the message says what to use instead); a range off the end of the wall or inverted; two headers over the same panel; a span outside `bigHeaderWidthInRange`; a header taller than its story or outside `bigHeaderHeightInRange`. Every refusal writes nothing at all and quotes the real number. **The span refusal names the range as unconfirmed in the same sentence** — see the flags check.

**⚠ Stage 2 and Stage 3, the two interactions that just landed:**

- **Stage 2's insert/replace/delete: the header's range rides the existing machinery, with no second copy of it.** `shiftSlotCoverageRecords` now moves header ranges through the same `shiftSlotCoverage` and the same every-move-not-the-net-one list the beams and the Box Beam already use. A header the edit leaves standing on fewer than two panels is removed, and `placementCommitNotice` says so (`EmptiedCoverage` gained `spanningHeaders`) — a header's own width IS the panels it spans, so one that has lost them is not a header. Harness-verified: deleting a panel to the LEFT of a header moves its range by one so it still covers the same two panels.

  **⚠ And moving the range correctly is NOT the same as leaving the part unchanged — the harness recorded that too, and the first version shipped silent about it.** The same delete moved the header's own cut width **80" → 85¾"** (the range was right; the panels under it were different widths), and the notice said only *"15 panels → 14, 12 still automatic"*.

  **⚠ That second number is NOT REPRODUCIBLE, which is worth more than the number was — established 2026-09-26 by re-running it.** The narrative said 85.75in while the committed `evidence.json` said 84¾", so the figure was re-measured rather than picked. Four clean runs of the same harness, on the same checkout, at the same window size, against the same 549in wall (4392 eighths every time) produced three different answers — **82⅜"**, **84¾"**, **85¾"**, then **84¾"** again: the harness draws its footprint in PIXELS, so the baseline free-run tiling lands slightly differently from run to run (`[…, 40, 40, 34.125, 34.125, 0.75, 40]` one run, `[…, 40, 37.125, 37, 34.125, 0.75, 40]` the next), and the post-delete redistribution follows it. **So the durable claim is "the derived width moved and the notice names both numbers", never a particular pair** — which is what the harness step actually asserts. The committed evidence now reads 85¾" and every narrative copy quotes that, with the variability stated beside it. Same standard this pass set when it corrected "eight commits" to "eleven", one step further: a measured number nobody re-checks gets believed, and this one could not have survived being re-checked. (The fixture in `placementNotice.test.ts` reads 85.75 and stays — it is a fixture, and the file says so.) A header already on a shop sheet, quietly re-cut. **Fixed 2026-09-26:** `placementCommitNotice` now carries a per-header clause naming **both** widths, and flags one that has landed outside the span range a *placement* would have refused — reported, not refused, because the panel edit has already been decided and unwinding it would leave a user unable to delete a panel because of a header three panels away.
- **Stage 3's wall run stop: REFUSED BY NAME.** A stop re-tiles a wall wholesale — the run is re-derived, not shifted — so a header's slot range would come out over different panels of different widths. That is a real part, already on a shop sheet, silently re-cut. The refusal fires when a candidate stop would change either the covered slot COUNT or the span WIDTH, it names the affected headers, and **it fires for a neighbour's headers too**, since the orphan-corner rule lengthens whichever wall was butting into a corner a stop removes.

**A real defect the browser harness found, in code written the same day: a 15.5in drift in 3D.** The header was anchored on `wallAxis` plus a slot offset — but a slot offset is measured from the panel RUN's origin while the axis starts at the wall's true corner, and on a wall that butts a longer neighbour the run begins a wall-thickness in. The header floated off the panels carrying it, and no unit test could see it. It is now anchored on **the first panel it spans** (that slot's own `PanelSlotBox3D`), so it inherits the corner inset and the run stops for free; the harness measures the alignment at 0. **The Mid-Wall Bond Beam loop beside it has the same drift and is deliberately left alone** — fixing it would move the rendered beam on every existing project, which is the same call Stage 3 made about the roof-bearing anchor. Noted, not matched.

**No `PROJECT_FILE_VERSION` bump, and the argument is a test rather than a paragraph.** `spanningHeadersByStoryAndWallId` is additive and optional with one shared default, which this file's own v24→v25 note already establishes needs no bump. Asserted: a file **without** the key loads to a state without it (so every file ever saved still round-trips byte-identically), a file **with** it keeps every field of every header, and a half-written record is normalized so no consumer can see an undefined story. It carries a `not-money` classification in `cloud/redaction.ts`, which the exhaustive type required. Nothing else in `supabase/` or `app/cloud/**` is touched.

**Not built, and said plainly:** there are **no drag handles** on a spanning header. Its coverage and its two heights are typed in the left bar, because a span is a set of whole panels rather than a free position, and the numbers it is built from are the ones a shop sheet quotes. The beams' drag machinery would carry it; that is a scope call, not a technical limit.

#### Review fixes — 2026-09-26

**The one with real-world weight: a derived width can change without anybody editing the header, and now something says so.** A spanning header's width is the panels beneath it, and **three separate paths change those panels**: the insert/delete shift (above), any path that RE-TILES the wall, and a file written under different limits. None of them re-validated the span, so a stored header could sit at a width under 48in or **over the 144in maximum the app refuses at placement** with no refusal and no notice — which also made the Review Log's own sentence *"a span outside them is refused rather than accommodated"* **false**, and a false note is worse than the geometry it describes.

- **`spanningHeaderSpanOutOfRange`** (pure, in `packages/geometry/src/spanningHeader.ts`, with its own tests) answers *"is what is stored still a width the shop builds"* — separate from `resolveSpanningHeaderPlacement`, which answers *"may this be placed"* and refuses. It is computed from the **CURRENT slots and the stored range**, never from the edit that caused the change, and that is the design requirement rather than a convenience: **it therefore covers the re-tile routes as well as the shift**, including re-tile routes not written yet. Asserted directly: the same stored range flags or does not flag purely on what is under it now.

  **⚠ Which re-tile route this flag actually catches, corrected 2026-09-26 — an earlier draft of this bullet named the wrong one.** It implied the out-of-range flag is what catches the **51–75in two-corner dead-band re-tile** on branch `fix-corner-dead-band`. It is not, and it cannot be: on that sub-route the wall's whole length goes to its two corner panels, so their TOTAL is bounded by the band itself — at least 2 × 25.5in = **51in**, at most one eighth under 75in = **74.875in** — and that is **always inside 48–144, so no out-of-range flag is reachable there at all.** (Stated as a total rather than as a per-corner figure because splitting 74.875 evenly gives 37.4375in, a SIXTEENTH, which is not a width this app's geometry can hold.) What guards that sub-route is the **stranded** flag (a range clamped below two slots) plus the stated residual below. The half this flag genuinely does catch is `absorbedCornerWalls`, where a wall swallows its neighbour and re-tiles **longer**: a stored range 0..3 over `[40, 40, 40]` produces no flag, and the same range over `[50, 50, 50]` produces `{ spanWidthIn: 150, minIn: 48, maxIn: 144 }`. Both arms are now tests, because as it stood a reader would have trusted the wrong safeguard.
- The **Review Log entry** flags it with the number, names the range as unconfirmed, and says the range is **not widened** to fit it. The stale *"refused rather than accommodated"* sentence now says refused **at placement**, and flagged here afterwards.
- **⚠ A residual, stated rather than implied:** a re-tile that changes a header's width but leaves it INSIDE 48–144in produces no flag, because the part is still buildable — only the insert/delete path announces a width change, since it is the one path with a commit notice to announce it in. The Review Log always shows the header's CURRENT span, so the number on the sheet is never wrong; what a reader cannot see there is that it moved. Giving every re-tile entry point a notice is its own change.

**The opening case Tommy permitted, with its one unvalidated corner closed.** Asked whether a header may bear on a corner panel and span a window/door, he answered **"allow both"** (2026-09-25, the same exchange in which he settled what rate this panel carries) — so the combination is permitted and neither is refused. Corner panels need nothing (geometry, derived span and return-leg pricing are all already right). The window/door case had a hole: a header shortens the panel beneath it, but the window keeps the sill height it already had, so a header placed low enough leaves a **zero-height window header inside a shortened panel** — an opening filling its own panel, with nothing said. Nothing crashes (`computeHeaderHeightIn` clamps at 0); the vertical refusal only checks the header against the story and `bigHeaderHeightInRange`, and the sill-height clamp clamps against the **wall** height, not against a band a header may later put beneath it. **`spanningHeaderOpeningConflicts`** (pure, tested) reports every covered slot whose own opening no longer fits in the band it sits in, and the Review Log entry names those panels and both numbers. **Reported, not refused** — he permitted it. **⚠ Its first version only read the slot's BOTTOM-most zone and said in a comment that this was sufficient; it was not — see the final review fixes below.**

**The nits, each one a real edge:**

- **The "Spans panels" fields commit on blur/Enter now** (`SlotIndexInput` + `resolveSlotIndexEntry`, both new and tested), the way `LengthInput` already does. As raw `<input type="number" onChange>` they committed every keystroke, so **clearing a field sent `Number("") === 0`** and moved the header to slot 0 — a legal index, so nothing refused it — and re-aiming a range could dead-end on an intermediate state (inverted, or over 144in) that the user never meant to commit. It is the same `Number("")` lesson `LengthInput`'s own header already records.
- **The harness could not exit 0 on a passing run**, and the reason previously written down was wrong. It never closed its CDP WebSocket and never called `process.exit(0)`, so the open socket held the event loop: a clean run printed `14 of 14` and then sat there until the browser was killed, exiting **1**. The claim that "the shell swallowed the exit code" was therefore a claim about the shell that belonged to the script. Two lines at the foot of `run.mjs`; the README and this section are corrected too.
- **The harness README now carries the window size** (`--window-size=1578,902`, the size of the checked-in screenshots). At a default headless window the viewer dial never reaches "3D Framed" and the run dies looking like a broken locator — the Stage 0/1 README already carries its own size note for the same reason.
- **Step 1 polls for the canvas instead of sleeping 12s.** A cold `next dev` compile outlasted the sleep and the run then failed with *"no canvas — are you on localhost rather than 127.0.0.1?"*, naming the wrong cause entirely.
- **The OBJ export branches on a real `kind` field**, not on `beamId.startsWith("spanningheader_")`. A string prefix of a synthetic id was the one place this stage kept a discriminant in a string — inside a feature whose own doc comments cite both the `combinedPanelLabel` hyphen parse and the placement notice's verb parse.
- **The 3D header anchor reads the RAW box list for BOTH stories.** It read `rawSlotBoxes` for the ground floor but the already-split `secondStorySlotBoxes` for the second; harmless until a beam consumes a slot's whole height, at which point no box exists for that slot, the `.find` misses and the header is **silently not drawn**. ⚠ **And this fix immediately produced its own defect, caught by the lint delta:** moving the lookup to a new memo left `midWallBeamRenderData`'s dependency array watching the OLD list — a memo that reads one value and watches another, i.e. the second story's headers drawn at stale anchors. It surfaced as a single `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` **WARNING**, which is the entire reason this app's notes insist a lint delta counts warnings and not just errors. Fixed, and the array now names the list it reads.

#### Final review fixes — 2026-09-26 (second review: SHIP WITH FIXES, nothing unsafe to deploy, no wrong number reaching a shop)

**The one that was a real hole in a check, not a wording problem: the opening clearance test missed an opening in a non-bottom band, and its comment asserted that it could not.** `spanningHeaderOpeningConflicts` read the slot's top-level `type`/`sillHeightIn`/`heightIn`, which `applyZonesToSlot` mirrors from `zones[0]`, and justified that with *"and the bottom-most zone is exactly the one a header shortens from above."* **That clause is false for any column a Mid-Wall Bond Beam has split.** `wallBandGeometry` hands the beams and the headers to `computeWallVerticalBandsForSlotWithMaxHeight` as ONE list, bottom-up, so a beam at 48in beneath a header whose bottom face is 96in yields bands `[0–48]` and `[60–96]`: the band the header caps is the **upper** one, and a window in it was invisible to the check. The same is true with no beam at all once `maxPanelHeightIn` sits below the header's bottom face and subdivides the band beneath it. The prior state was no check at all, so nothing regressed — but **a comment that reads as a proof of completeness and is not** is the exact shape an earlier commit on `main` exists to stop.

**Fixed rather than documented**, which was the option worth taking: the function now takes the wall's band-producing GEOMETRY (not a band list, so it cannot be handed one that disagrees with the elevation), reproduces the band split with the same pipeline every renderer uses, pairs each band with its own zone through `effectiveZonesForSlot` exactly as `allPanelInstances` does, and compares each opening against **its own band's height**. The comparison is band-LOCAL on both sides — a zone's sill height is measured from that band's bottom, which is how `WallElevationDiagram` and `membersForPanelTypeId` both read it, so a floor-relative band top would be the wrong number and there is a test for that. The conflict record gained a `zoneIndex`, and the Review Log entry uses it to name the stacked panel that actually has the problem instead of whichever instance at that slot index came first. Four new tests, one of them the reviewer's own repro that returned `[]`.

**`totalWoodWeightKg`'s two gaps now have a Review Log entry of their own, which they did not before.** Still document-not-fix — the fabrication sheets build at `heightOverrideIn`, so no shop-bound figure is wrong, and correcting the sum means running the band pipeline inside it and changing the displayed weight of every saved project with a beam in it. But the approximate number was on screen with nothing beside it: the summary note says *"Wood (N standard/braced panels)"*, which hints at gap 1 only if read carefully and says nothing about gap 2, the full-story-height over-count. One `pending-BI-confirmation` entry now names both, says the two errors point in opposite directions and do not cancel, and says plainly that nothing reaching the shop is affected.

**Two mechanisms, two slot arrays — named rather than "made consistent", on purpose.** `shiftSlotCoverageRecords` measures a header's before/after width from the BASE slots, while placement validation, the Review Log flag, the sheets, the 3D anchor and the price all measure from `overlayWallSlots`; under `square-bale-panels` or `timber-frame-curtain` those differ in both widths and slot COUNT. It keeps reading the base slots because a header's stored range **is** a base slot-index range, so summing it over a re-counted overlay array would produce a confident wrong number rather than a better one — prior and next are both base arrays, so "did the panels under this range change width" is answered correctly on its own terms. **⚠ And the mismatch underneath it is real, pre-existing and bigger than this notice — CONFIRMED by reading the code, not inferred:** the elevation renders `overlayWallSlots` while `handleInsertPanel`/`handleDeletePanel` index into `baseWallSlots` via `wallSlotsForStory`, `applyUniformPanelization` re-tiles each infill run so the two arrays do not share indices, nothing gates the placement tool on panelization type, and the Mid-Wall Bond Beam's own coverage range has had the same base-vs-overlay split since long before Stage 2b. **Not fixed here** — it is a Stage 2 defect with its own blast radius; recorded in Open Items.

**One comment narrowed because it claimed more than it proves.** The add-notice comment said the sentence and the drawing "cannot disagree". True of the header's NAME (recomputed from the same global walk with the new header included); not of the PANEL names beside it, which come from this render's `allInstances`, i.e. pre-commit. In the default configuration they are identical either way — a fresh header is born flush against the top plate, so the column it shortens still yields one band and one instance, and panel numbering is positional — and they can differ only where `maxPanelHeightIn` sits below the header's bottom face. Behaviour left alone (the notice is a transient toast; sheets, cross-reference and Review Log recompute from committed state); the claim no longer overruns the code.

**And the residual bullet above named the wrong safeguard for the 51–75in corner absorb, now corrected with tests.** See that bullet: the out-of-range flag cannot fire on that sub-route at all, and what does guard it is the stranded flag plus the stated residual.

**"Allow both" is now dated 2026-09-25** everywhere it is quoted — the Review Log entry, the geometry doc comment and this document. It had sat undated beside *"Tommy's decision, 2026-09-25"* in the same Review Log note, which invites a reader to take it as older or softer; he answered the header-bearing question and the pricing question in one exchange.

### Stage 3 — Incomplete walls: a wall that simply ends — BUILT 2026-09-25

**As built, on branch `smearforn-stage-3`, in fifteen commits** (eight for the stage, then seven for two rounds of code review, Tommy's three answers, and the browser harness). No `PROJECT_FILE_VERSION` bump — Stage 0's v25 keys were already there and already classified; this pass only taught things to read them.

**The arithmetic is a pure module,** `packages/geometry/src/wallRunStop.ts` (+ its test file): `normalizeWallRunStop`, `applyWallRunStop`, `hasWallRunStop`, `builtWallLengthsIn`, `totalBuiltWallPerimeterIn`. `wallRunFor` in `retile.ts` is now the ONE place a wall's run length and per-end corner flags are derived, shared by `retile`, `retilePreservingOpenings`, `wallGeometryFor` and `panelSlotBoxes3D`.

**⚠ The invariant is NOT the form this plan states above**, and the difference cost a real defect. The plan's `Σ slot widths + startStop + endStop === wallFabricationLengthIn` holds only while no wall's length depends on another wall's stop. The **orphan-corner rule breaks exactly that**: a wall whose neighbour stops at their shared corner grows by a wall thickness, so the left side exceeds the right by that much (measured: 344.5 vs 329 on a 30×20 rectangle). **The true invariant, and the one every test here is written against:**

> `Σ slot widths === wallGeometryFor(wall, currentStops).lengthIn`

— this wall's current tiling length under the current stop map, unconditionally, in integer eighths. It is asserted directly, plus a sweep over every whole inch of stop on a 30ft wall. The plan's original form survives only as a special case, asserted separately on a wall that owns both its corners and has no stopped neighbour.

**The trap the plan names, and where it actually was.** Panel-instance-derived totals are correct for free, as predicted. The wall-length-derived ones were not — see the audit table below. The one the plan did not predict is in 3D: `panelSlotBoxes3D` carries a defensive rescale (`lengthIn / totalWidthIn`) that exists to absorb float slop, and a stopped wall's slots deliberately sum to less than the wall. Left alone it reads that shortfall as slop and **stretches every panel on the wall to fill the unbuilt span** — drawing a solid wall exactly where the plan says to draw nothing. Pinned with a test.

**The too-short remaining run: REFUSED, at the point of edit.** Zero is legal (build it all) and a stop covering the whole wall is legal (an edge with no wall of ours on it — the plan's one-concept model). The band in between is refused. Rather than re-deriving what "legal" means, the refusal **tiles the candidate run for real** and asks the same `findSubMinimumPanelWidths` the Review Log uses whether the result holds a panel the shop cannot build, plus a sum check so an edit is refused whole rather than partly applied. **A stored file is never checked this way** — limits are enforced at EDIT, never at LOAD.

**Two things the plan did not say, found while building it:**

- **A stop at an end and a corner OWNED at that end are different facts, and the drawing needs both.** `WallGeometry` grew `ownsCorner*` beside `hasCorner*`; passing the tiler's `hasCorner*` to the elevation drew a phantom neighbour at a stopped end. **(Superseded in part by the orphan-corner decision below — the elevation now keys off the ADJUSTED inset, not off ownership at all.)**
- **A stop is keyed by wall id, and two operations renumber wall ids.** `insertBumpOut` and the near-zero-wall collapse behind a drag both rebuild every id. A stale key does not fail loudly — it **stops a different wall than the one the user stopped.** Both paths now remap stops through the same point-pair correlation they already use for slots. A fresh footprint draw clears them outright, as it already does openings.

**A stop is measured from the wall's own TILING length**, i.e. after corner ownership has taken its inset out. On a wall that owns its corner — the common case and the ADU's — that is exactly "inches from the corner point on the plan". On a butting end the run already starts a wall-thickness in and the stop is measured from there. Written into the module's own doc comment rather than left to be discovered.

#### After the code review — SHIP WITH FIXES, all applied 2026-09-25

**The MUST-FIX was a stale memo, and it is worth stating plainly because it is this stage's own failure relocated one layer up.** `roofBearingRenderData` in `Building3DView` read `wallRunStopsByWallId` and did not list it as a dependency. On a single-story building the panels moved when a stop was set (`rawSlotBoxes` does list it) and **the truss plate stayed drawn at full length across the unbuilt span**; clearing a stop went stale the same way. The reviewer hand-checked every dep array in `page.tsx` and found them complete, including three justified `eslint-disable`s — so this reads as a single oversight in the one file that did not get that attention.

Four smaller fixes alongside it: the multi-story roof-bearing **position** (`computeRoofBearingSegments` returns `startXIn` relative to the SLOT RUN's origin while the 3D anchor measures from the wall's true corner — "shrinks for free" was true of length and false of position; both branches are now run-relative and the stop is added once at the anchor); a **zero-length truss plate** on a fully-stopped wall, which emitted a real shop sheet for a 0in part with its own Timber HP weight line; the refusal checking **only the ground story**; and two different **clamp bases** (`applyWallRunStop` clamps against the tiling length, `builtWallLengthsIn` clamped against the raw length, so a clamped stop on a butting wall could make the tiler build nothing while plaster and membrane still counted up to ~15¾in as built — fixed rather than commented, with a test asserting the old wrong number so the regression is named).

#### Tommy's two answers, 2026-09-25

- **Gable + stop: CLAMP THE GABLE ROW TO THE BUILT RUN.** This was the one place the audit's "no panels means no instances" premise did not hold by itself, and the distinction is worth keeping: `computeGableTiledRow` is not a total that reads a wall length, it is a **panel generator** that reads one, and its output becomes real `"gable"` instances that are fabricated, priced, weighed, BOM'd and cut-listed. Unclamped, a stopped Gable End wall built gable panels above a span that same wall declares carries no panels — parts cut wrong, not a number read wrong. **The ridge and roof profile still span the full wall**; `resolveGableProfilePoints` and `ridgeLine` stay in the "deliberately left" column and a test reads the roofline height at the stop off the full-wall profile to prove it. A fully stopped gable end returns `[]` rather than one zero-width tile. Two things found wiring it: a clamped run can squeeze a segment to zero width, and segment tiles feed BOTH the panel loop and the `naturalCounts` pass, so one shared helper now serves both; and the structural-column block indexes `segments[0]`/`segments[1]` directly, which is safe because clamping collapses a segment rather than removing it.

  **⚠ A claim made here in the first draft was overstated and is corrected rather than edited away.** It said the shared helper stopped gable windows being renumbered by a clamp. It does not: the helper keeps the two passes consistent about *collapsed segments*, but `beforeTileCount` is positional and a start clamp removes leading tiles, so windows slid along the wall — measured, with one crossing the peak. See the next item for what was actually done about it.

- **Gable windows STAY PUT ON THE BUILDING — Tommy, 2026-09-25.** *"A window is dimensioned from the building, not from wherever the panel run happens to begin."* Stopping the near end of a wall must not move a window at the far end. So window positions are now derived from the **unclamped** row and the clamped row places the survivors at exactly those x values; the ordinal path still owns the unclamped case, which is why every existing project tiles byte-identically.

  **The byte-identity claim, stated exactly.** Proven by output over **1440 configurations** (5 wall widths × 3 profiles × 3 window sets × column on/off × safety-gap on/off × 2 insets × 2 anchor modes × 2 heel heights) against the pre-clamp commit: **zero differences**, so the positional tiler is provably unreachable on an unclamped wall — established from outputs, not by reading `isClamped`. Against **`main`** there are 24 differences, all on a 144in wall with a flat-top profile whose second anchor (160) sits beyond the wall: main emitted a gable tile at **`[144,174]` on a 144in wall — past the wall's own end** — and the branch drops it. That is **a real bug part 10's zero-width segment guard closed by accident**, found only because the sweep compared against two baselines instead of one. So the accurate form of the claim is *"identical except where `main` emitted a gable tile beyond the wall's end on a degenerate flat-top profile."* Recorded because the shorter sentence was true of the delta and false of the release.

  Two consequences he was **not** asked about, stated rather than buried:
  - **A window entirely inside the unbuilt span is not built** — no panel, no cut-list part. **INFERENCE**, consistent with the rest of the stage, but not confirmed.
  - **A window the stop cuts through is REFUSED by name**, not resolved. Half a window is a fabricated part that does not exist, and silently swallowing a whole one is worse. `classifyGableWindowsAgainstRunStop` is the seam; if Tommy later wants a cut window to simply disappear, that is one branch.
- **Orphan corner: THE CORNER SIMPLY DOES NOT EXIST**, over transferring ownership. A wall butting a corner its neighbour owns was inset a wall-thickness to make room for a panel the neighbour never builds — butting into air, with a phantom filler sliver on its elevation. `cornerOwnershipWithRunStops` clears that inset so the neighbour runs out to its own true end, and the elevation keys the sliver off the **adjusted inset** (`startInsetIn`/`endInsetIn` replace the `hasCorner*` booleans, because "does not own the corner" and "the neighbour's panel is really there" have stopped being the same fact).

  **This is the first thing in Stage 3 where a stop on one wall changes another wall's tiling**, so the safety argument is written into the function and asserted: only a CONVEX loser carries an inset, so reflex corners are untouched by construction (tested on a bumped-out shape with every wall stopped at both ends); the adjustment only ever makes a wall LONGER, so no wall's own "is my corner built" answer can change as a result and one pass reaches a fixed point; and a stopped wall can never take the merged-corner branch, since merging needs corners at both ends. Consequently a stop now re-tiles **every** wall through the house's own lossless `retilePreservingOpenings` path, and the refusal checks every wall on both stories.

#### The truss plate LAPS THE CORNER — SETTLED by Tommy, 2026-09-25

The question came out of the Stage 3 audit and is now answered, so it is recorded as a decision rather than left as inherited behaviour.

**What the code does:** on a butting wall with no stop, `builtWallLengthInByWallId` is the **raw** wall length, so the fabrication sheet cuts a truss plate to the full wall line — up to two wall-thicknesses (~31in) longer than the panel run beneath it.

**Tommy: that is correct, and it is standard top-plate framing — plates lap at the corners.** A plate that stopped where each panel run stops would leave every corner unplated. So the cut length stands, unchanged, and the reason is on the record instead of being a coincidence of which length the code happened to read.

**⚠ Do not conflate this with the 3D roof-bearing ANCHOR offset.** They were conflated once and they are different things:

| | Truss-plate cut length | 3D roof-bearing anchor |
|---|---|---|
| Where | `roofBearingFabricationGroups` → a real shop sheet | `roofBearingRenderData` → `widthFt` from `seg.lengthIn` |
| Cuts a part? | **Yes** | **No** — render-only, never reaches the fabrication path |
| Status | **Settled: laps the corner, correct as-is** | **Still open**, and only a render question |

The anchor still measures from the wall's true corner and ignores the butt-joint inset, so a two-story wall's beam can sit up to a wall thickness off where its panels are. That is pre-existing, render-only, and deliberately untouched by Stage 3 — fixing it would move the roof-bearing render on every existing two-story project. The harness pins it as a **bounded** discrepancy (plate length ≥ panel run, and no more than two wall-thicknesses over) so it cannot grow unnoticed. It stays open on its own terms.

#### The browser harness — `apps/web/harness/smearforn-stage-3/`

14 asserted checks, all passing. **The trick that makes the 3D assertions exact:** the 3D view is WebGL, so a pixel diff cannot tell "the plate is stale" from "the panels moved" — but `Export as OBJ` builds its geometry from the same memos the scene renders, so intercepting that blob gives a precise textual model of the scene. The memo pin sets a stop, then forces a recompute by touching a dependency the memo DOES list; a scene that changes as a result was stale.

**It found two defects in code written the same day**, both in the refusal: it compared each wall's tiled total against its *unstopped* length plus the stops, which — once the orphan-corner rule deliberately lengthened a neighbour — **refused every legitimate stop that reached a corner**, i.e. the main case the feature exists for; and it reported a downstream symptom ("the panels do not add back up") instead of saying the run was too short. Both fixed, both with a harness step pinning them.

**It can fail, measured rather than assumed:** exit 0 on a clean run, exit 1 with a single expectation deliberately inverted.

Run as an acceptance criterion, against the code rather than assumed. **Four totals over-counted and are fixed; a fifth was found on a second pass.**

Tommy: *"We need an addition tool setting or stop wall tool so that it is possible to make incomplete walls."*

**Reference walls have dropped out of scope — Tommy, 2026-09-24:** *"For new construction the bare walls meet the other bare walls. This project being all new construction is just a simple end to our wall, no need to have the rest of the plan drawn."*

That answers the corner/junction Open Item and deletes a whole feature at once. The ADU does **not** need the garage drawn, labelled or dimensioned; it needs the ADU's own wall to **stop**. No junction detail, no inset question, no "REFERENCE ONLY" print treatment. The earlier plan's reference wall was solving a problem the job does not have.

**Recorded for later, not built:** the addition case, which is the one that *would* need a junction detail. Tommy: *"For additions, a toe up made of 2x4s and insulation is installed vertically over a vapor closed membrane."* That is a real assembly and it belongs with the Detail Guide pages (it is a close cousin of detail 4, the toe-up/foundation load path, rotated vertical). Nobody should invent it from this one sentence — see Open Items.

- **Hard decision, unchanged: the footprint polygon stays CLOSED.** An open polygon would break `computeFootprintAreaSqFt`, `perimeterRing`, `pointInPolygon`, `computeRoofBearingSegments`, the floor framing and the 3D pipeline simultaneously — every one assumes a closed ring, and `cornerOwnership` walks it by `walls.find(w => w.startCorner === wall.endCorner)`. **"Incomplete" is a property of the panel run, never of the shape.** This survives Tommy's answer intact and matters more because of it: the ADU's floor and roof still extend to the line where the wall stops, so that edge must still exist geometrically even though nothing is built along it.
- **Data (added in Stage 0's v25 bump, inert until this stage):** one record keyed by wall id — `{ startStopIn: number; endStopIn: number }`. Absent entry = fully panelized, today's behaviour, byte-identical. Stops are inches on the eighth grid, measured from each wall end. **An edge with no wall at all is just `startStopIn` covering the whole length** — no separate mode, now that the "reference" mode is gone. One concept, one field pair.
- **Geometry:** `wallGeometryFor` subtracts the stops from `lengthIn` before tiling. The invariant becomes **`Σ slot widths + startStop + endStop === wallFabricationLengthIn`** — still exact, still integer eighths.
- **Drawing:** the unbuilt span draws as a **dashed boundary line**, not a hatched wall — it is where the building ends, not a wall of unknown type. It carries its own dimension in plan and elevation. **In 3D, nothing is drawn there.** A ghost solid would read as a wall that exists, which is exactly backwards.
- **Printing:** the span's dimension prints, labelled **NO PANELS**.
- **Totals and the cut list — still the real trap.** No panels means no instances, so anything derived *from panel instances* (price, weight, carbon, BOM, cut list, shipping) is correct for free. **Anything derived from `wall.lengthFt` is not**, and will silently over-count — plaster and wall-assembly areas are the first suspects. **An explicit audit of every total that reads a wall length rather than a panel set is an acceptance criterion of this stage.**
- **A stop that reaches a corner takes the corner panel with it** (the corner is simply not built; the neighbour is unaffected, since it already butts or owns by its own rule). Inference; stated so it is not discovered mid-build.
- **Review Log:** one entry per wall carrying an unbuilt span. A wall that stops short is by definition an incomplete design and the engineer must see it. Mechanism: the existing `reviewLog` useMemo (`page.tsx:5023`), which already takes `{ label, status, note }` entries.

**ADU reach after Stage 3:** the wall that stops where the garage begins. **The full 60-panel schedule, minus the A/B/C naming.**

#### Stage 3, second pass — an opening in the unbuilt span: DROPPED, and REMEMBERED — BUILT 2026-09-29

**Why this is in the spec at all, and the process gap it closes.** Tommy's decision below, the 174in diagnosis and this pass's flags check existed **only in code comments and a harness README** for most of a day. Every other stage records its decision and its flags check here, and this project's rule is that subagents read the spec and never the memory files — so a decision that lives only in a doc comment is a decision the next agent will not find. Written up here on the review-fix pass, where it should have been on the build pass.

**Tommy, building the Rogers-Sehorn ADU:** *"i am having trouble building the seahorn project using the stop wall tool. whenever i stop wall over a certain amount, for one wall this boundary was 174", it says that the panel wall doesnt add up and will not let me edit the layout how i need to"*

**The diagnosis, and the meaning of his 174.** `retileWithOpenings` reserves EVERY opening on a wall at its full width, because an `OpeningAnchor` carries `beforeStandardCount` — an **ordinal** in the slot sequence — and nothing in it says where along the wall the opening sits. Shorten the run with a stop and the openings come along whole. Once the shortened run is narrower than `Σ openings + Σ corner panels`, `plainBudgetIn` goes negative, `Math.max(0, …)` clamps it, and the slots then sum to MORE than the wall — so Stage 3's own sum-invariant backstop refused, correctly, and reported the downstream symptom.

**174in is that wall's own openings-plus-corners total:** two 61.5in windows plus two 25.5in corner panels. Measured against the tiler: the **last** eighth at which the sum breaks is **173.875in**, and every eighth from **174in** upward is correct. ⚠ **It does NOT break at every eighth below the boundary** — counted, 793 of the 984 eighths from 51in to 173.875in break — and the first draft of the code comment said "every", which is the kind of over-claim this log exists to catch. The boundary is the sharp fact; the density below it is not. Same law at other widths: three openings of 47.625/41.5/37.5in with 14in corners last break at 154.5in and are correct from 154.625in = 126.625 + 28.

**Tommy's decision, 2026-09-29, given three options — "Drop them, and remember":**

> *"Openings in the stopped-off part are removed from the built run, but stored so they come straight back if you un-stop the wall. Physically honest — an unbuilt section has no windows — and non-destructive."*

So an opening inside an unbuilt span leaves the slot list, and with it the cut list, the fabrication groups, the shop drawings, the price and the weight — an unbuilt section of wall has no window in it — and it is **not deleted**: it is held per story per wall and comes back, every field intact, the moment the stop no longer covers it.

**As built.** `packages/geometry/src/runStopOpenings.ts` (+ its test file) derives each opening's real position by tiling the wall's **basis** run — the run it would have with its own stops removed but every other wall's applied, the same basis `wallRunStopBasisIn` measures a stop against — and walking the slot widths. An opening is built only if it lies wholly inside `[startStopIn, basis − endStopIn]`; both ends and both-ends-at-once fall out of that one test with no end-specific branches. `runStopOpeningFit` lets the refusal name the real constraint (*"the 2 openings and 2 corner panels still on it need 174\""*) instead of the arithmetic symptom. `unbuiltOpeningsByStoryAndWallId` is an **additive optional** `ProjectState` key with one shared default, so `PROJECT_FILE_VERSION` stays **25** and it is not in `REQUIRED_STATE_KEYS`; classified `not-money` in `cloud/redaction.ts`.

##### After the code review — DO NOT MERGE AS IS, all fixes applied 2026-09-29

**The MUST-FIX: a start stop that dropped an opening could permanently SWAP two openings on the wall.** Not a lost window — a silently wrong drawing, a door where a window was, which on a shop drawing is worse than a refusal.

The build pass claimed survivors were deliberately not re-anchored and that this made the merged list "byte-for-byte the list the wall had before the stop". **That is true of `partitionOpeningsByRunStop` in isolation and false through `tileOneWallPreservingOpenings`,** because a survivor's ordinal does not survive the round trip: the next re-tile reads it back with `getOpeningAnchors(oldSlots)`, and on a stopped wall `oldSlots` is the **shortened** run. The remembered opening kept its long-run ordinal while the survivor was re-derived against a shorter one, so the two halves of the merged list were in different coordinate systems, and a plain sort put them back in the wrong order whenever the survivor's re-derived ordinal fell below the remembered one. Reproduced end to end on a 47ft wall carrying a window and a door, sweeping every whole-inch start stop from 0 to 532in: **116 of those 533 stops came back swapped.** End stops were clean by accident (survivors keep the low ordinals), which is exactly why the first round of tests missed it — and **Tommy's 174in wall is stopped from both ends and carries two openings, the failing shape precisely.**

**The design chosen, of the two the review offered: (b) carry the pre-stop order with the memory.** The memory is no longer a bare anchor list; `RunStopOpeningMemory` is `{ unbuilt, preStop }`, where `preStop` is the wall's opening sequence as it stood immediately before the stop withheld anything — one entry per opening, left to right, each carrying the `beforeStandardCount` it had **then** and whether the stop withheld it. `mergeRunStopOpenings` walks that sequence, rebases survivor *i* onto the *i*-th recorded kept ordinal and interleaves the remembered ones where they sat, so both halves end up in one coordinate system and the merged list is the pre-stop list. Successive stop changes chain correctly, because each new partition records the ordinals of the list the merge just rebased.

**Why (b) rather than (a), re-anchoring survivors onto the shortened run.** (a) improves a stopped wall's own layout by a panel or two and destroys the only information that makes the restore exact — you would then have to reconstruct a remembered opening's ordinal from a position, which is approximate and moves the survivors too. Tommy's decision was "remember", and remembering means the wall comes back as it was. (b) also changes nothing about what a stopped wall looks like today, so the existing harness evidence stays meaningful rather than being re-baselined against a new layout.

**The claim it replaces is written down rather than deleted.** The module doc comment now states the defect, the 116-of-533 measurement, and the one case restore is **ordered but not byte-exact**: if openings are inserted or deleted on the wall while it is stopped, the survivor count no longer corresponds to `preStop`'s kept count, so the merge splices each remembered opening back at its recorded position and clamps the merged ordinals monotonically. ⚠ **This pass then claimed "order is still exact — no two openings can trade places", here and in two pieces of user-facing text, and the THIRD review measured two shapes where that is false.** Corrected in the third-review section below: the memory now carries each opening's payload as well as its ordinal, and no user-facing text promises exactness unless the geometry says it holds.

**The test that covers it,** because nothing did: `retile.test.ts` drives `start stop → clear` with **two openings of different types** through `retilePreservingOpeningsWithRunStopMemory` — the function page.tsx actually calls — at every whole inch of a 564in run, asserting nothing is lost, nothing is swapped, and the restore is byte-exact wherever the stop withheld something. Four unit tests in `runStopOpenings.test.ts` pin the same rule at the merge, including the tie case and the inserted-while-stopped fallback. **All five were run against the old plain-sort merge first and all five failed there**; the restore tests also no longer feed `partition.kept` straight back — they tile the shortened run and read the survivors out with `getOpeningAnchors`, which is what made the defect invisible before.

**The four smaller fixes.**

1. **`runStopOpeningFit` under-counted an octagon's corners.** It tested `slot.type === "corner"` only, and `retile` runs `markSafetyCorner`, which rewrites one corner slot to `"safety-oct-corner"`. Measured: a mitered run reported `cornerCount 1, requiredIn 87, plainBudgetIn 13` where the truth is `2, 112.5, −12.5` — so the new refusal quoted wrong numbers, **and there were stops where `refuses` stayed false** and the user fell through to the old "does not add back up" sentence. One line, plus a mitered case in the test file.
2. **A tautological test replaced.** `retile.test.ts`'s unstopped byte-identity test compared `result.slotsByWallId` to `retilePreservingOpenings(...)` with the same arguments — and that function is now *defined* as `retilePreservingOpeningsWithRunStopMemory(...).slotsByWallId`, so both sides were the same call and it could not fail. The claim matters (every project ever saved is unstopped), so it is pinned instead against a captured ten-slot fixture for the wall with the openings and against `retile`'s own output for every wall without.
3. **Second-story memory is pruned of dead wall ids at write time** — `pruneOpeningMemoryToLiveWalls` in `apps/web/app/runStopOpeningMemory.ts`, with its own test file. This is *not* the same as the pre-existing stale-key cases: those lose **slots**, which the next re-tile rebuilds, whereas wall ids are **reused** (`buildRectangleFootprint` always emits "AB"/"BC"/"CD"/"DA", `buildOctagonFootprint` always "0".."7"), so a memory outliving its wall attaches to the next wall that takes the id and **resurrects a window on an unrelated wall**. A null footprint is left alone: nothing drawn yet is not every wall deleted.
4. **Two comments corrected to say what is actually true.** The `spans.length !== sorted.length` bail-out said "today's behaviour, unchanged", which holds for an unstopped wall and is false for a stopped one — handing a shortened run every opening at full width is the exact over-length condition this module exists to prevent. No code change, because every reachable instance is latent (the basis run is the longest this wall is ever tiled at, and the branches that drop reservations there need a run under 51in or corner 39 with `cornerMayWiden`, which the app does not produce) — but the comment now says so, and says what to do if a caller ever makes them reachable. And the 51in–173.875in sentence, above.

**Also on this pass: `ui-reorg-u0/run.mjs`'s minimum wait — and the wait turned out to be bounded on BOTH sides, which nobody knew.** The build pass replaced a flat `sleep(9000)` before a canvas drag with a poll, which changed no assertion but dropped the **minimum** wait from 9s to 3s, so on a fast machine the following drag started about six seconds earlier than the run those coordinates were tuned at. Putting a 9s floor back **on top of** the build pass's new 2s settle — 11s in total — **broke the harness**, reproducibly, two runs out of two: `context-line-names-the-view-as-the-app-labels-it` came back with `plan: null`, meaning the FIRST `openIcon("Report Bug / Request Feature")` after the drag did not leave the note on screen while every later one did. The same run at the build commit was green, which is how the cause was isolated rather than guessed.

**So the fix is the floor REPLACING the settle, not added to it** — exactly 9s again, with the poll as insurance above it — and that is green. The measurement, and the warning not to re-add a settle on top of it, are in the file. **The real fragility is named there and deliberately NOT fixed: `openIcon` toggles and nothing asserts which way it went**, which is what gives the wait an upper bound at all; making it assert the resulting state would remove the bound, and it is left alone because that helper serves about ten steps in that file. Worth doing by whoever is next in it.

##### Third review — DO NOT MERGE AS IS, two more must-fixes, applied 2026-09-29

**MUST-FIX 1: a remembered opening survived a brand-new footprint and landed on the new building.** `handleDraw` deliberately resets everything a new building must not inherit — `setWallRunStopsByWallId({})`, `setSecondStory(null)`, a plain `retile` — and did **not** reset `unbuiltOpeningsByStoryAndWallId`. Wall ids are reused (`buildRectangleFootprint` always emits "AB".."DA"), and **no stop is needed to cash the stale memory in**: `hasStop` in the tiler is true whenever the memory holds anything, so the very next re-tile of any kind — a wall-length edit, a drag, a bump-out, a stop — merges the old building's window in as a **real** opening, with a cut list line, a fabrication group, a shop drawing and a price. Measured: a fresh 22×18 rectangle with a stale `AB` memory and **no stop anywhere** had 0 openings on AB after the draw and **1 after one re-tile**.

**The prune could not catch it, and that is the general lesson rather than a detail.** `pruneOpeningMemoryToLiveWalls` drops ids the footprint LACKS, and "AB" is live in the new building — the prune cannot tell "this wall still exists" from "a different wall took its name". A new building must therefore CLEAR the memory, which `handleDraw` now does beside its run-stop reset. Pinned at the level where it is provable, in `retile.test.ts` ("a leftover memory puts a window on a wall nobody drew one on"), and the blind spot is asserted in `runStopOpeningMemory.test.ts` rather than only described.

**Asked and answered: should the prune run at every write to state, not only in `buildProjectState`?** Not as the fix for this, and not in this diff. It would not have caught this at all (the id is live), and a prune that runs on write has to be handed the NEXT footprint explicitly — the closure's `footprint` is the stale one in exactly the handlers that renumber ids, so a write-time prune keyed off it would delete a live bump-out wall's memory. The honest version is the same discipline the run-stop map already follows (pass the next footprint, as `nextRunStops` is passed), and it is worth doing as its own change.

**MUST-FIX 2: "order is still exact" was false, in three places including user-facing text.** Claimed in `runStopOpenings.ts`, in this spec entry, and — worst — in the Review Log entry and the elevation notice, both of which told the user the openings come back *"exactly as drawn"*. Two reachable shapes, both measured, both needing an edit while the wall is stopped:

1. **Delete a survivor while stopped.** Pre-stop `[door(1), WINDOW(3, withheld), column(5)]`; the user deletes the door; survivors read back as `[column]`. The counts no longer corresponded, the fallback spliced the window in after one survivor, and the result was `[column, window]` — **the remembered window on the wrong side of a survivor.** Two openings traded places, which is the same class of defect as the window/door swap the first review blocked on.
2. **Delete one and insert another, count unchanged.** Same memory, survivors `[column, big-header]`. The counts still corresponded, so the merge took its *exact* path, which assumes survivor *i* is `preStop`'s *i*-th kept entry — one delete plus one insert breaks that without breaking the count. Merged `[column, window, big-header]`, and the code called itself byte-exact.

**Fixed: the memory records each opening's PAYLOAD (type, width, height) beside its ordinal**, and the fallback matches survivors to the kept entries they came from by payload, in order (an LCS walk, not a greedy two-pointer, so one delete does not mis-match everything after it). Shape 1 now restores the window on the correct side of the column, and **a single deletion is no longer approximate at all** — the matched survivors carry their pre-stop ordinals, so the result is the pre-stop list minus the deleted opening. A memory with no payloads (this change's own earlier commits, or a hand-edited file) degrades to the old recorded-position splice rather than matching against nothing.

**NOT fixed, deliberately: shape 2 still takes the index path.** ⚠ **The reason recorded here on the third review was the weaker one, corrected on the fourth:** it is not mainly that a count-preserving change is usually an edit, it is that **payload alignment would MANUFACTURE an order defect in the case the index path gets exactly right.** An unmatched survivor is placed at `lastMatchedIndex + k/(n+1)`, and before the first match `lastMatchedIndex` is `-1` — a NEGATIVE position, which sorts ahead of a remembered opening recorded at `preStop` index 0. So pre-stop `[WINDOW(withheld), door]` with the door's width edited while stopped — no insert, no delete, the commonest edit there is — would stop matching the door to its kept entry and restore `[door, window]`: two openings traded places, the same class of defect that blocked the first review, introduced to fix a rarer one. The index path restores `[window, door]` there. Frequency is the secondary argument and it is **reasoned, not measured** — *we believe* an edit is far commoner than a delete-plus-insert, but nobody uses this in anger before November, so it cannot be more than a prior. Without stable opening ids the two are indistinguishable either way. **The full fix is stable opening ids and is out of scope.** So the promise is now stated in the only form that is true everywhere: *nothing is ever lost* (unconditional), *restore is exact while the wall's opening payloads still match the ones the memory recorded* (`runStopRestoreFidelity`), *otherwise placement is approximate and order can differ*.

**And the user-facing text is conditioned on exactly that.** `runStopNotices.ts` (new, with its own test file) composes both sentences from one answer, so the Review Log entry and the elevation notice cannot drift apart: with an exact restore they still say "back exactly as drawn"; otherwise they say the openings come back **on this wall** and add that openings have changed since the stop was set, so a restored one **may** come back beside a different panel. ⚠ A width edit on a survivor also reports approximate and in fact restores exactly — a caution the user did not strictly need is the cheap side of that trade, and "may" is what keeps the sentence true of it.

**Four smaller fixes on the same pass.**

1. **A malformed memory white-screened the editor rather than degrading.** The tiler reads `…?.[wall.id]?.unbuilt.length`, so a value that is a bare anchor ARRAY — the shape this feature's own first commit wrote, and which still exists on a live branch — gave `undefined.length` and threw straight out of the re-tile: *"Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'length')"*, with no building on screen. `parseProjectFile` normalised the two story keys and never the inner value; it now reads a bare array as the withheld anchors with an empty pre-stop order, drops a value that is not a memory at all, and passes a well-formed one through by reference so a round trip stays an identity. For the record: nothing was ever pushed, `origin/main` is still `ac55a39`, and no harness saves a project file, so no real file of that shape can exist — the guard is two lines and makes the question moot.
2. **Second-story opening memory is remapped by the id-renumbering gestures.** `handleAddBumpOut` and the wall drag's collapse branch built `nextRemembered` from `.ground` only, so the second story's map kept its old keys. Same point-pair correlation now carries both. Lower severity because those gestures already leave the second story's own slots stale — but a stale key here is stale DESIGN data, which is the argument the prune itself rests on.
3. **The refusal sentence has its own tests.** Extracted to `runStopNotices.ts` following this repo's own `placementRefusalNotice` pattern, with the formatters injected, so the numbers can be tested without a browser. Byte-identical wording. It inherits one cosmetic pre-existing quirk, now named in the code rather than discovered later: when the refusal is about a NEIGHBOUR wall, the closing "or stop all N of it" still quotes the edited wall's length, exactly as the sum-invariant message beside it always has.
4. **`ui-reorg-u0/run.mjs`'s two wait comments no longer contradict each other.** One said a flat 9s failed three times in a row; the other said 9s + a 2s settle (11s) fails two runs out of two. Both are true and they are **on different clocks**: the lower bound is "the canvas must exist" (the 9s floor plus the poll, however slow the compile), the upper bound is "do not then sit idle" (what the settle violated). Time spent waiting FOR the mount is not time spent idling after it, and the three slow runs that went past 9s through the poll were green end to end. Reconciled in both places. The underlying fragility — `openIcon` toggles and nothing asserts which way it went — **is to be fixed as its own change** (third review: yes, fix it rather than name it; no, do not grow this diff into it).

##### Fourth review — one must-fix, four should-fixes, applied 2026-09-30

**MUST-FIX: the malformed-shape guard deleted the openings it claimed to rescue, and the predicate called it "exact".** `openingMemoryStory` in `projectFile.ts` normalised a bare legacy anchor array to `{ unbuilt: memory, preStop: [] }` and its doc comment said the openings then *"come back approximately rather than not at all"*. Measured: they did not come back at all. `mergeRunStopOpenings([door], { unbuilt: [window], preStop: [] })` returned `[door]`; with no survivors it returned `[]`. **Both paths of the merge emit a withheld anchor only by walking `memory.preStop`**, so an empty `preStop` emits none, and the payloadless fallback that splices straight out of `unbuilt` is gated on `keptEntries.every(payload !== undefined)` — vacuously true over an empty `keptEntries`, so it was never reached. `retile.ts:646` writes a wall back into `unbuiltOpeningsByWallId` only while `memory.unbuilt.length > 0`, so on the first re-tile after the load the anchors were gone from the slots AND from state, permanently and silently. And `runStopRestoreFidelity({unbuilt:[w], preStop:[]}, [])` answered **`"exact"`** on the same vacuous `every` — a fully stopped wall in that shape told the user "1 opening … back exactly as drawn" and then dropped it, which is precisely the false promise the second review blocked on, surviving in the one branch the third review added.

**The choice was binary — synthesize the order, or drop the value — and this pass took SYNTHESIZE.** `openingMemoryStory` now builds one all-withheld `preStop` entry per anchor, each carrying its own payload: the same shape `withholdEverything` writes for a fully stopped wall, so the legacy memory becomes an ordinary memory rather than a special case anywhere downstream. **The reason for choosing it over dropping:** dropping is honest about the order and deletes the openings, and "never deleted" is Tommy's own decision on this feature, unconditional in every other branch. What synthesis asserts that a bare array cannot actually tell us is that there were no survivors; where there are, they sort ahead of the restored openings and `runStopRestoreFidelity` reports `"approximate"`, so nothing is lost and nothing promises exactness. Pinned three ways: the parser output itself, the parser output driven **through the merge** (`projectFile.test.ts`, "a legacy bare array really does restore its openings through the merge"), and the failing shape itself (`runStopOpenings.test.ts`, "LOSES anchors that its pre-stop order does not account for"), which is written as a pin on the precondition rather than a blessing of the behaviour.

**SHOULD-FIX 1 — the resurrection fix had no test that could fail if it were deleted.** `retile.test.ts`'s "a leftover memory puts a window on a wall nobody drew one on" is a geometry test; it never touches `page.tsx`, so it passes identically with and without `handleDraw`'s `setUnbuiltOpeningsByStoryAndWallId({ ground: {}, second: {} })`. Nothing below `handleDraw` can guard `handleDraw`, and the reviewer confirmed every other building-replacement path (file load, cloud open) goes through `applyProjectState` with no undo and no separate New Project handler — the draw gesture was the only gap. **Stage 3 harness step 16** now stops the wall until it really is withholding an opening, draws a different rectangle over the top, takes an ACCEPTED stop on the reused wall id and clears it, and requires the opening count on that wall not to move and nothing to be withheld on the new building. ⚠ Its first run exposed a second lesson worth keeping: the re-tile has to be an **accepted** stop, because a refused one changes nothing and the assertion would pass for free — the step now walks down through candidate depths, records every attempt with its refusal sentence, and asserts one was taken.

**SHOULD-FIX 2 — the merge trusted a correspondence nothing validated.** `mergeRunStopOpenings` does `merged.push(memory.unbuilt[unbuiltIndex++]!)` per withheld `preStop` entry, so a memory with MORE withheld entries than anchors pushes `undefined` into the anchor list and `retileWithOpenings` dereferences it: the same white screen the guard exists for, one field over, and reachable from the same hand-edited file. **One comparison in the parser closes it** — `preStop.filter(withheld).length === unbuilt.length`, and a memory that fails keeps its anchors and loses its order. The invariant is now stated on `RunStopOpeningMemory.preStop` itself, with `parseProjectFile` named as its one enforcement point, and `mergeRunStopOpenings` is deliberately NOT made defensive about it (hot path; one enforcement point beats two that can disagree).

**SHOULD-FIX 3 — the non-fix decision is right, its stated reason was not the strongest, and one phrase overstated.** Corrected in `runStopOpenings.ts` and in the third-review entry above: the decisive reason to keep the count-preserved case on the index path is that payload alignment would **manufacture** an order defect in the case the index path gets right (an unmatched survivor before the first match takes a NEGATIVE position, `lastMatchedIndex + k/(n+1)` with `lastMatchedIndex = -1`, so it sorts ahead of a remembered opening recorded at `preStop` index 0 — pre-stop `[WINDOW(withheld), door]` with the door's width edited would restore as `[door, window]`). "Far more often" is softened to *we believe*, since it is a prior and cannot be a measurement before November.

**SHOULD-FIX 4 — the hand-edit defect is broader than "hand-placed".** Measured one step past the harness finding: a hand-SET width (`lockedWidthIn`, Stage 1's own feature) is lost to a stop and does not come back when the stop is cleared. Rewritten as its own entry in "Six things left uncoded" with the before/stopped/cleared slot runs and the mechanism, and added to the `## Open Items` bullet about Stage 2's count preservation, where the stop is now named as a fourth member of that family. **Not fixed** — Tommy is being asked whether a stop should refuse rather than silently revert, and that is recorded as a new Open Item with no recommended default.

**SHOULD-FIX 5 — the coverage consequence of step 15's REPLACE choice is written where someone will find it.** Step 15 replaces a standard panel instead of inserting one, deliberately and correctly, which means **no harness drives the INSERT shape any more** — so the hand-placed defect is documented in two comments and asserted nowhere. Named under its own heading in `apps/web/harness/smearforn-stage-3/README.md` and in the "Six things left uncoded" entry.

**Not built, on purpose:** the hand-edit refusal itself. It is Tommy's decision about how much the app should get in his way while he is drawing, and the reviewer's read is recorded with it — likelihood on the Rogers-Sehorn job is high rather than theoretical, because its cut list is irregular widths throughout and Stage 3 exists because he hit the stop tool on that same job.

##### Six things left uncoded, named rather than left silent

- **A wall with no old counterpart loses its memory entirely.** `insertBumpOut` and the wall drag's collapse branch renumber every wall id, and a wall whose run no longer exists as a run gets plain-tiled with no openings — its remembered ones go with them. That is a genuine deletion inside a feature whose promise is "never deleted", and it is deliberate: there is no basis left to measure a remembered opening's position against, and it matches how those same operations already treat the wall's **built** openings. Recorded in `retilePreservingOpeningsWithRunStopMemory`'s doc comment and in `runStopOpeningMemory.ts`'s. **If it is ever revisited, the fix is a real old-to-new wall correlation on the caller's side, not in the geometry.**
- **A stop that withholds NOTHING still moves a survivor by up to one standard panel, and clearing it does not put it back.** Measured on the same 564in sweep: from a 151in start stop the door's ordinal drops from 8 to 7 because the shortened run has fewer standard slots, and clearing the stop re-tiles it at 7. This **predates Stage 3 entirely** — `tileOneWallPreservingOpenings` has always re-derived its anchors out of `oldSlots` — an opening memory cannot fix it (there is nothing withheld to remember), and it never moves an opening past another opening. Asserted in the test as a **known band** rather than silently excluded, so that if it ever grows to include a stop that withheld something, the test fails.
- **The braced-combine residual: a ~6.5% band of stop values still refuses with the old sentence.** On the test fixture, stops from 192.5in to 215.875in. The cause is pre-existing and outside this work: `reconcileBracedPlacement`'s corner-brace combine fixes a safety-gap slot at `standardWidthIn + buffer` and sheds the difference onto the nearest standard panel **clamped at zero**, so when that neighbour is narrower than the swing the shed is partial and the wall comes out over its own length — reproducible with no stop anywhere, and its own doc comment already names the tradeoff. **Being fixed by a separate agent on a branch taken from this one; expected to shrink or vanish once the two merge.** Recorded here so that if it does not, it is a known item rather than a discovery.

- **One opening deleted and another inserted while the wall is stopped restores in the wrong place, and says so rather than claiming otherwise.** Added on the third review. The count is unchanged, so the merge cannot see that the correspondence broke; matching by payload there would break the far commoner case of a survivor whose width was simply edited. Nothing is lost, `runStopRestoreFidelity` reports `"approximate"`, and both pieces of user-facing text drop the words "exactly as drawn" for it. **The full fix is stable opening ids** — every one of these shapes reduces to that — and it is out of scope here rather than half-started.

- **A stop silently reverts HAND EDITS on the wall — both a hand-placed panel and a hand-set width — and nothing warns.** ⚠ **The third review wrote this up as the hand-PLACED case only; the fourth review measured one step further and it is broader than that.**

  *Hand-placed panel* (third review, from the harness): a wall with a hand-placed window inserted at a boundary went into a stop with **17** panels and came back from clearing it with **16**, length still exact to the eighth and both openings restored.

  *Hand-set width* (fourth review, measured on `retile.test.ts`'s own 360in fixture, a 120in start stop): a wall carrying a panel pinned to 35in by the typed width field — **Stage 1's own feature, the stage that had to land** — loses the pin to the stop and does not get it back when the stop is cleared.

  ```
  BEFORE : [corner 25.5][std 40][win 61.5][std 40][std 32.625][win 61.5][std 37.625][gap .75][std 35 LOCKED 35][corner 25.5]
  STOPPED: [std 40][std 36.125][std 36.125][win 61.5][gap .75][std 40][corner 25.5]   <- no lockedWidthIn anywhere
  CLEARED: [corner 25.5][std 40][win 61.5][std 40][std 32.625][win 61.5][braced 32.625][gap .75][braced 40][corner 25.5]
  ```

  **Mechanism, read from the code rather than guessed:** `reconcileBracedPlacement` maps old markers (type, braced pattern, zones **and `lockedWidthIn`**) onto the new run **by standard-family ordinal counted from index 0**. A start stop removes slots from the LEFT, so every marker past the shortened run's count has nowhere to land and is dropped — and once dropped it is not in `oldSlots` when the stop is cleared, so clearing cannot restore it. The width-edit path has a guard for exactly this class of loss (`handPlacedWallRetile.ts`'s `tilerWouldChangeThePanelCount`); **the stop path does not consult it at all.**

  **This is Tommy's call, not an implementer's,** and he is being asked directly: a stop could **refuse** when it would destroy a hand edit (as it already refuses over a spanning header), warn, or keep today's silent revert. Recorded in Open Items — Project Smearforn rather than implemented. **Likelihood on the Rogers-Sehorn job is high rather than theoretical:** its cut list is irregular widths throughout (43", 41½", 37½", 35", 31½", 30", 29½", 28½"), so he hand-sets widths on most walls, and Stage 3 exists because he hit the stop tool on that same job.

  **And it is asserted NOWHERE.** The stage-3 harness step that found the hand-placed half now deliberately REPLACES a standard panel instead of inserting one, so the insert shape is no longer exercised by any harness; the hand-set-width half above was measured in a scratch run, not a committed test. Both are documented in comments and in this entry, and neither would fail if the behaviour got worse. Named in `apps/web/harness/smearforn-stage-3/README.md` under its own heading so the next person finds it where they would look.

- **A legacy or hand-edited opening memory restores its openings, but not their ORDER — and the merge is deliberately not made defensive about it.** Fourth review. `RunStopOpeningMemory` carries an invariant the whole design leans on: `preStop`'s withheld entries correspond one for one with `unbuilt`. `parseProjectFile` now enforces it (a bare legacy anchor array gets an all-withheld order synthesized from the anchors; a memory whose withheld count disagrees with its anchor count keeps the anchors and loses the order), so **nothing is lost on any reachable path**. What is deliberately NOT done is making `mergeRunStopOpenings` itself defensive: it still emits remembered openings only by walking `preStop`, on both paths, and a memory that breaks the invariant would still drop anchors there. That is pinned as a failing-shape test (`runStopOpenings.test.ts`, "LOSES anchors that its pre-stop order does not account for") rather than patched, because the merge is on the hot re-tile path and one enforcement point that runs at load is better than two that can disagree. **The residual cost, stated:** a legacy memory has no record of where its survivors sat, so a wall restoring from one puts the remembered openings after the survivors and `runStopRestoreFidelity` reports `"approximate"` — honest, and no user-facing text promises otherwise.
