#### The corner-brace combine — review-fix pass, BUILT 2026-09-29/30

The build pass is recorded against the struck Open Item above ("`applyBracedPlacement`'s corner-brace combine can still shed a panel out of range"), which now carries the corrected numbers and all three consequences. This section is the flags check and the gates, which the build pass never wrote — an omission the review caught, and the reason points 5 and 6 below failed until now.

##### After the code review — DO NOT MERGE AS IS, all fixes applied

The verdict was that the arithmetic held and every published number reproduced exactly, but three *consequences* were unhandled. All three are in, plus four corrections to numbers I had published wrong. See the Open Item above for what each one is. Two things about **how** they were fixed are worth having here rather than only in the code:

- **The reconcile fix went into the marker walk, as the review directed, not into the swallow candidate set.** `combineSwallowedOrdinals` derives where the hole in `oldMarkers` is from the combined gap's own position, which is a RECONSTRUCTION rather than a record: the combine always eats `swallowCandidates[0]`, the nearest unlocked plain standard walking away from the corner, so the missing ordinal is the count of standard-family slots before the gap. **If the combine ever stops taking the adjacent panel** — a locked panel beside the gap already pushes that choice one slot out — **the reconstruction is off by however far it reached.** The alternative is persisting the swallowed ordinal on the combined slot, which is a `PanelSlot` key, a `PROJECT_FILE_VERSION` bump and a value in every saved file; not worth it while the candidate order makes the adjacent panel the answer in every case today, and pinned by the fixpoint sweep rather than trusted.
- **Alignment alone was not enough, and the extra permission is narrow on purpose.** On a 145in wall the combine's leftover is 1⅜in and the only panel left to take it is the far corner's brace. So `preservedBracedIndices` lets the leftover **RESIZE** a brace that came from the wall's own history — never swallow one. Restricting it to *preserved* braces is what keeps the first pass byte-identical: **7,878 first-pass combines either way with that restriction, 15,727 without it.** Dropping the restriction would have bought back thousands of refusals by firing the combine on walls that are correct today, which is exactly the trade the review ruled out.

##### Two process traps this pass paid for, written down because the next agent will not guess them

- ⚠ **`git stash` IS SHARED ACROSS WORKTREES, and it will hand you another agent's work.** `refs/stash` is one ref per repository, not per worktree. Stashing here and popping here popped the **`elevation-fit`** agent's stash into this worktree — a conflicted merge of their `WallElevationDiagram.tsx`, plus their `elevationViewport.ts` and `elevationZoom.mjs` as untracked strays. Nothing was lost (git keeps the entry when a pop conflicts, and both stash commits stayed reachable by SHA), but it is a genuine way to destroy a colleague's uncommitted work. **Do not use `git stash` in this repo while other agents are live.** Commit to your own branch instead, or measure a baseline by running against the main checkout rather than by emptying your own tree. If you must: record both SHAs first (`git rev-parse "stash@{n}"`), and `git stash apply <sha>` rather than `pop` by index, because the indices move underneath you.
- ⚠ **A baseline you measure by stashing is void the moment you restore.** ESLint and vitest read files as they go, so restoring your work while a "baseline" run is still going produces a number measured against a mixed tree. Two runs were thrown away here for exactly that.

### Stage 4 — Shop drawings, to match Cameron's sheets

New workstream, 2026-09-24. Tommy uploaded shop drawings made by **Cameron** on his team (SketchUp, open-cut extensions) and wants the app's per-panel output to read like them:

> *"bird's eye view of the interior face at and up and clockwise angle, (more) clearly denote what the length of each cut is, and somehwere on the page clearly note what overall size (length, depth, height, AND the diagonal measurement of the exterior face. And I NEED to have total weight at 7lbs/ft3 of straw plus weight of wood and fasteners on each panels' page. I also want a blank table included on the page for the shop to write in actual height, length, and width, moisture content, weight, quality check date, and initials."*

**Most of this sheet already exists, which is the single most useful fact about this workstream.** `PanelFabricationPage.tsx` already renders, per unique panel: a lettered `PanelElevationDiagram`, a **Materials cut list** table (Letter / Part / Qty / Dimensions, from `computePanelCutList(members)`), an "Also used at" instance list, structural values, a **weight breakdown with a modeled total**, and one blank line — `Actual total weight: _______________`. So this is **mostly a print/sheet-content pass, not a modelling pass**, and almost none of it needs new data.

Taking his list item by item, with the print-vs-3D split he asked for:

1. **Weight at 7 lb/ft³ plus wood and fasteners — nearly done, and flags-clean.** `targetDensityKgM3` in `data.ts` **is already 7 lb/ft³**, noted "7 lb/ft3 (Tommy) — supersedes the earlier ~4.7 lb/ft3 literature-derived starting point", and `computePanelWeightBreakdown` already returns components plus a modeled total. **No new building value is introduced by this item at all.** The work is confirming the breakdown on the sheet names straw, wood and fasteners as three visible lines rather than one total, and that the fastener line traces to what the BOM already computes. **⚠ Fastener counts inherit `fastenerTableStatus`, which is `pending-BI-confirmation`** — a printed screw count must carry that provisionality, not appear as a fact because it is printed in a table.
2. **Per-cut lengths "more clearly denoted" — the data exists; the question is where it is shown.** Every cut length is already in the cut list's Dimensions column. **Inference: he means on the drawing**, as dimension leaders against the lettered members, because that is what Cameron's SketchUp sheets do and it is what "denote" reads as beside "bird's eye view". Confirm before building — if he only means a clearer table column, this item is nearly free.
3. **Overall size block: length, depth, height, and the exterior-face diagonal.** Pure geometry off dimensions the panel already has; the diagonal is `hypot` of the exterior face. **It is a squareness check** — that is why it sits beside height and width on his QC sheet — so it must be labelled as the *exterior face* diagonal and never as a generic "diagonal". No building value, nothing flagged.
4. **The bird's-eye interior-face view — a camera preset, not a new projection.** `StandardPanel3DView` already embeds a single-panel 3D view inside a sheet (see the Jack Stud Shop Drawing). **Recommendation: a fixed camera preset on the existing renderer** — up, clockwise, interior face toward the viewer — rather than a hand-drawn axonometric, which would be a second renderer to keep in sync with the member geometry forever. **⚠ One risk to settle before committing: the 3D view is `@react-three/fiber` (WebGL), and a WebGL canvas does not reliably print** without the drawing buffer being preserved. Verify on a real print preview *first*; if it prints blank, the fallback is rendering the preset to a raster at print time, not abandoning the view. **This also finally answers the long-standing Open Item "'Typical architect angle' set for 3D renders"** — Tommy has now described the angle he wants in his own words.
5. **The blank QC table — match his sheet, do not invent one.** The cut list PDF's **"QUALITY CONTROL PROJECT SUMMARY CHECK LIST"** already has the columns: PANEL ID, ACTUAL HEIGHT, ACTUAL WIDTH, ACTUAL DIAGONAL, MOISTURE CONTENT, SCREW COUNT, ACTUAL WEIGHT. He wants **QUALITY CHECK DATE** and **INITIALS** added. **Use his columns verbatim, in his order, plus the two new ones** — a shop that already fills in one layout should not have to learn a second.
   - **⚠ One real difference to settle: his existing table is project-level (one row per panel); he asked for a blank table *on each panel's page*.** Recommendation: the per-panel page carries **his columns with one row per placed instance of that panel** — since a fabrication sheet already covers N identical copies ("Also used at (12)"), one row per copy is what a shop actually fills in, and PANEL ID is then pre-filled per row rather than blank. The project-level checklist stays exactly as it is. Confirm.
   - The existing single `Actual total weight: ____` line is **superseded** by the table's ACTUAL WEIGHT column and should be removed rather than left as a second place to write the same number.
6. **What a panel page shows when a value is not known: a visible gap.** The house convention, already settled twice in this log (`PanelStructuralStatus` carries no invented value; the logo placeholder "claims nothing"). An unknown dimension prints as a dash with a note, never a plausible substitute. A blank cell in a QC table is *correct* — it is the shop's job to fill it.

**Monday relevance: almost none, and that is the honest answer.** The Monday goal is *creating* the project, not printing it. The one item that could ride along is (1), because the number already exists and the breakdown is already computed — but even that is not needed to draw a wall. **Stage 4 goes after the editor stages.**

New workstream, 2026-09-24. Tommy:

> *"I would like to develope and impliment the most user friendly nomenclature system. I think we have a good one. This particular project I think was named that because we broke those panels down into abc because the other ones didn't want to change - not necessarily because that's the best nomenclature to use."*

So: **positional, cardinal-direction letter plus number, renumbering everything downstream on every insert or delete.** Suffixes are out.

#### The corner-brace combine — SECOND review-fix pass, BUILT 2026-09-30

The first review-fix pass (above) was re-verified in full by a second reviewer: every published figure reproduced on their own runs, the gates re-ran identically, and the permission itself was confirmed sound and is not re-opened here. What that pass did not follow all the way through were the **consequences** of its own three fixes. Two must-fix and five should-fix items; all seven are in.

##### The two that were wrong, not merely unexplained

- **⚠ The pin stopped the combine FIRING but not UN-FIRING — the same index slide, backwards.** A wall whose combine has already fired is stored one panel shorter, its safety-gap slot carrying `secondaryType: "braced"`. If the user then places a Mid-Wall Bond Beam, Box Beam coverage or a spanning header on that wall, it becomes pinned — and the first pass's reconcile **un-combined it**, so every stored index at or past the gap pointed one panel EARLIER. Reproduced as `stored len 4 -> pinned reconcile len 5`. That is exactly the `offsetsIn[header.startSlotIndex] ?? 0` silent fallback the pin exists to prevent, and the ordering that triggers it (place a beam on a combined wall, then edit anything) is the ordinary one. **Worse, the build pass's own test asserted the un-combine as correct.**

  **Fixed by making the pin freeze the wall's slot structure in BOTH directions**, which is the smallest correct answer: `reconcileBracedPlacement` now derives `preCombinedGapOrdinals` from the stored run, and a pinned wall may re-combine exactly those gaps — re-combining is what *reproduces* the array the stored indices were drawn against. The pin is not otherwise loosened: a pinned wall whose stored run has no combined gap still refuses, which is asserted separately. The alternative (route the un-combine through `shiftSlotCoverageRecords`-style remapping) was not taken, because on a re-tile path there is no exact remapping to apply — see the rewritten justification below. The product-space no-op sweep now runs a **PINNED** pass as well: **0 of 98,952 walls move.**

  **One case is still a slide and is deliberately not fixed:** a pre-combined gap whose re-combine the re-tiled run can no longer pay for. It is named in `applyBracedPlacement`'s doc comment, it cannot occur on a no-op (the sweep above), and it is not silent — the wall then carries a plain safety gap a corner walk steps over, so `findCornerBraceCombineRefusals` raises its Review Log entry and the note names the pinning.

- **⚠ The Review Log dedupe silently dropped a second identical wall's entry — a direct hit on flags-check point 5.** `page.tsx`'s `deduped` keys on `note` and nothing else. The refusal note interpolated `braceSlotIndex`, `braceOffsetFromCornerIn`, `gapWidthIn`, `bracedPanelCountOnWall` and the seismic spacing — every one of them a function of the wall's TILING — but not `wallId`, `story` or `end`, which lived only in the label. **On a plain rectangle the north and south walls tile identically, so only one of the two ever reached the engineer's list**, and the same collision could drop one of a single wall's own two ends. A symmetric building is the common case.

  **Fixed by putting the wall, the end and the story into the note**, not by keying the dedupe on `label + note`. #### The hyphen is dropped — `E4`, not `E-4` — and the reason is a physical object

Tommy, 2026-09-24: ***"I have spray paint stencils in the shop, and there is no huphen stencil. So let's drop the hyphen."***

**Quoted verbatim and kept permanently, because nobody would ever derive this from first principles.** A software naming format is being decided by which stencils exist on a shelf in Columbia, Missouri. It is also the best kind of requirement — unarguable, verifiable, and invisible to anyone who only ever reads the screen. It has the side benefit of making the app match the drawings he already issues.

**⚠ This breaks a function, and it breaks it silently.** `combinedPanelLabel` (`panelInstances.ts:544-550`) parses the name it is given:

```
const [prefix] = instances[0]!.name.split("-");
const numbers = instances.map((inst) => inst.name.split("-")[1]);
return `${prefix}-${numbers.join("+")}`;
```

With `"N4"`, `split("-")` returns `["N4"]`, so `prefix` becomes `"N4"` and every entry of `numbers` is `undefined` — the on-canvas label renders **`N4-undefined+undefined`** on every multi-instance slot, which is every window slot (header + sills). **It throws nothing and fails no test that does not look at the string.** The prefix/number split has to become a real parse (or, better, the instance should carry its direction and number as fields and stop round-tripping through its own display string).

- **The combined label itself should lose the hyphen too** — `N3+4+5`. It is a screen and drawing label rather than a stencilled panel id, so the stencil constraint does not strictly bind it, but two conventions one character apart is how the wrong one gets stencilled.
- **Check every other consumer of `inst.name` before shipping.** It is used as a `Map` key in ~10 places in `page.tsx`, as a React key, and as the base of the jack-stud id (`page.tsx:3587`, `${inst.name}-JS${i+1}`). Uniqueness survives the change (`N4`/`NE4` stay distinct), but **anything that parses rather than merely keys is a candidate for the same silent breakage.**

#### The cost of always-renumber, and what the app now owes the shop

**This is the option whose cost lands on the shop floor rather than in the code**, and saying so is the point of writing it down. Insert a panel at E-3 and every panel east of it shifts by one: **the E-7 on the sheet in the shop's hand is the E-8 on the sheet in the office.** Nothing in either document says which is which. Someone installs the wrong panel.

**This is now a requirement, not a nicety: a printed sheet must carry its own identity.** Minimum: **project name, revision, and date issued, on every sheet**, so two sheets naming "E-7" can be told apart at a glance. The pieces exist — `SheetTitleBlock` already takes a date (`resolveTitleBlockDate`) and `sheetNumber`/`sheetCount` from `DocumentMetaContext`, and the backend already keeps `project_versions`. What is missing is the revision on the face of the sheet and a line on the panel schedule saying **names are positional and valid only for this revision.**

**Worth building, not this pass: a renumbering diff.** When a project is re-printed after an insert, show what moved — *"E-7 through E-12 shifted to E-8 through E-13."* That single feature is what turns a dangerous scheme into a safe one, because it tells the shop exactly which labels to re-read. Recommended as the first follow-up after the editor stages.

#### Spanning headers get ONE series for the whole building — DECIDED 2026-09-24: `H1`, `H2`, `H3`

The problem this solves: a left-to-right letter-number scheme describes a **one-dimensional** run, and a header spanning two panels below it is **two-dimensional**. No assignment of consecutive left-to-right numbers keeps all three in reading order — which is exactly why the ADU reached for A/B/C.

**Tommy's answer: a single building-wide header series with no direction prefix at all**, chosen over a per-direction series (`EH1`/`NEH1`/`SWH1`), over numbering panels first and spans afterwards, and over keeping A/B/C.

**The reasoning is the stencil rack again:** eight direction prefixes times an `H` is a lot of stencils to own and to keep straight, and **headers are rare enough that finding one does not need the wall encoded in its name.** So a header's name says **what it is, and nothing about where it is.** That is a deliberate trade, and it moves work onto the cross-reference below.

- **Written `H1`, not `H-1`.** The stencil rule is general.
- **No collision is possible.** Every panel name begins with a direction (N/NE/E/SE/S/SW/W/NW); none begins with `H`.
- **One global counter, not one per wall.** Recommended order: the **same wall-order-then-slot-order walk `allPanelInstances` already does**, so header numbering is deterministic and rises in the same direction panel numbering does. Consequence to state plainly: **`H1` may be on the north wall and `H2` on the east** — the series crosses walls by design.
- **⚠ Renumbering is now building-wide.** Inserting a header on the north wall shifts every header after it *anywhere in the building*, not just on that wall. That is a wider blast radius than the panels have, where a north-wall insert only ever moves `N` numbers. Same staleness problem, larger radius — covered by the same sheet revision identity, but worth knowing before someone inserts a header late in a job.
- **⚠ The cross-reference is no longer a nicety — it is the only way to locate a header, and it is REQUIRED.** With the wall stripped out of the name, `H1` alone says nothing about where the panel goes. So:
  - `H1`'s own fabrication sheet carries **its wall and its span in words**: *"East wall — spans E4, E5."*
  - `E4`'s and `E5`'s sheets each carry the reciprocal: *"Header above: H1."*
  - The elevation drawing shows it graphically, but **a shop reading one sheet cannot see the other**, and that is exactly the situation this decision creates. The cross-reference is what makes a two-dimensional relationship survive being printed as a stack of one-dimensional pages.

**Stage 2b is unblocked on naming.**

#### Two smaller questions the answer did not cover

- **Non-cardinal walls are already handled, and the handling is lossy.** `wallCompassDirection` snaps a wall's outward normal to the **nearest of eight** (N/NE/E/SE/S/SW/W/NW), so an octagon's mitered walls already name correctly (`NE3`) and a rectangle always lands on a cardinal. **But the snap means two differently-angled walls can both be "NE"** and share a number run while pointing different ways. The ADU is rectilinear so nothing bites today; a bay window or an angled wall would.
- **Two walls facing the same direction share one number run — DECIDED 2026-09-24, at the third asking.** An L-shaped building gets one `E1…E12` run spanning both east-facing walls. **His reason is the one that matters and it is better than "it is what the code does": every panel name in the building stays unique, which is what a shop needs when it stacks panels by label.** Recorded as a decision rather than as status quo — it happens to match today's behaviour, but it is now chosen. Noted that it took three asks, because a question that has to be asked three times is usually one where the asker has not made the stakes clear.

**Monday relevance: none.** The app already emits the names he asked for. The print-identity requirement is the part that matters, and it belongs with Stage 4.

Order is by **how much of the ADU each stage unblocks per hour of work**, not by elegance. The elegant model (anchors) is carried by Stage 2 because Stage 1 does not need it.

| Stage | What it is | By Monday evening? |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Foundation checkbox, default off; the single v24→v25 bump carrying every Smearforn key | **Yes**, comfortably — the mechanism exists |
| 1 | Typed panel width + eighth-snap the existing drag + per-panel reset | **Yes** — and this is the one that *must* land |

| 2 | Insert / delete / place-a-type; the anchor generalization; the spanning header | **The insert/delete half: plausible.** The **spanning header is the new risk** — it arrived with Tommy's answer, it needs its own confirmation, and it is a new cross-column concept rather than a width edit |
| 3 | Incomplete walls — a wall that simply ends | **Better than before, and still the most likely to slip.** Reference walls dropping out removed a whole feature; what is left is the stop mechanism plus the wall-length-derived-totals audit, which is the part that tends to find two more bugs |
| 4 | Shop drawings | **No, and it does not need to be.** The Monday goal is creating the project, not printing it |
| 5 | Nomenclature consequences (sheet identity) | **No** — but note the scheme itself needs **no work at all**; the app already does what he asked for |

**⚠ Stage 1r (absorb + the minimums + the hyphen) is MONDAY-CRITICAL and lands BEFORE Tommy opens the app to draw — his call, 2026-09-24. BUILT 2026-09-25 on branch `smearforn-stage-1r`; see the Stage 1r as-built section above for what it does and what it deliberately does not.** It is still its own commit (four of them), but it is no longer a follow-up: it is a gate, and "verified, not merely merged" was met — the sweeps, the `max ≥ 2 × min` property test and the browser harness were all green before this was written.

- **The reason it moved: it changes what the tiler produces for the ADU's own walls.** Absorb should make his job easier — fewer narrow panels means panel counts closer to the real schedule — but **a rule that changes tiling must not change while he is mid-job.** Re-tiling a wall he has already hand-fitted, because a rule shifted under him, is the exact experience Smearforn exists to prevent. Landing it first means he draws against final rules from the first wall.
- **"Verified", not just "merged".** Because it is a gate, the property test over swept wall lengths has to be green *before* he starts, not before the branch merges. A tiler change that lands unverified on Monday morning is worse than one that lands Tuesday.
- **Still its own commit, ordered after typed widths.** Absorb touches `computePlainSizing` and `buildEvenMiddle` — the functions every wall goes through. Fusing it into the typed-width commit means a tiler problem takes typed widths down with it. Two commits, same morning.
- **The 24in refusal changes nothing for this job** — every ADU width is ≥24", so it never fires. It rides along because the file is already open.
- **The hyphen drop is the highest-risk-per-character item in the whole plan.** One template string, plus a silent parse failure in `combinedPanelLabel` that renders `N4-undefined+undefined` and throws nothing. Cheap, not free, wants its own eyes.

**What this does to the order:** Stage 0 → Stage 1 → **Stage 1r (gate)** → Tommy draws. Stages 2, 2b and 3 land around and after that, and anything not finished by the time he starts is simply not part of Monday.

**Two things improved since the first draft of this plan, and one got worse.** Better: reference walls are gone (Tommy's *"just a simple end to our wall"*), and the 14in panel-width scare evaporated once it turned out to be a depth. Worse: **the triple header is a real cross-column concept**, not three adjacent panels, so Stage 2 carries more than it did yesterday.

**The fallback if Stage 3 slips, stated now so it isn't improvised Monday night:** draw only the ADU's panelized walls and accept that the footprint is then short on one side — which changes area, floor and roof. That is a **wrong building with a right panel schedule**, the correct trade for a Monday deadline *provided it is written on the sheet*. It must not become a silent compromise.

**What Tommy will not have Monday regardless:** the shop-drawing sheet changes, any nomenclature decision, and — unless Stage 2's spanning header lands — the `E4A`-over-`E4B`/`E4C` relationship, which would then have to be approximated by two full-height panels with the header drawn as a mid-wall beam. **That approximation is a drawing, not a panel:** it would not produce E4A as a fabricated panel with its own weight and its own sheet. Worth knowing before relying on it.

### The 51in–75½in two-corner dead band — CORNER ABSORB, BUILT 2026-09-25

> **⚠ THE BAND'S CEILING MOVED ON 2026-10-01, and this whole section is written against the NEW one.** The two-tier safety gap made every wall run reserve a gap, so a middle must now pay for the gap *before* it can hold a legal panel, and the band's top edge went from **75"** to **75½"** — 195 eighth-steps where it used to be 191. Five statements in this section were still quoting the old band until this was corrected; the headline title, the 75" row of the named-lengths table, the top-of-band arithmetic and the Square Bale figures are all the new numbers now. See "Corner ownership flips, the two-tier safety gap…" for the reasoning and for why the widening is a correction rather than a widening for its own sake. **Where a sentence below needs the old value to make sense, the old value is given beside the new one rather than deleted.**

**The defect.** A wall owning a corner at both ends spends `2 × cornerPanelWidthIn` = **51"** on them, so its middle is `L − 51`, which must now hold the run's own safety gap **plus** a panel over the confirmed 24" `fabricationMinPanelWidthIn` — so there is no legal middle for any `L` below **75½"** (it was `L` below **75"** until the gap became universal on 2026-10-01). Too long for the merged-corner rule (which needs the corners to actually overlap, i.e. `L < 51"`), too short to hold a legal middle panel. `floor(b / 24) = 0`, so **no legal panel count existed at all**. Live, not hypothetical: a 6ft bump-out return sits three inches inside it, and **a regular octagon's side is 0.41421× its bounding box, so every wall of an octagon between 10.26ft and 15.09ft across landed in it** — small octagons were broken outright.

**The rule.** `resolveCorners`' merge condition is extended from *"too short for both corners"* to *"too short for both corners **plus a legal middle**"*, exactly as the residual note predicted. What the corners then do about it is **absorb** — the same answer `computePlainSizing` already gives a leftover too small to stand alone: widen an existing panel rather than emit one the shop cannot build.

**The two corner panels share the wall; it is NOT one merged panel spanning it.** The single-panel reading of "extend the merge" would emit one corner slot up to **74⅞" wide — past `panelWidthInRange.maxIn`, a confirmed 48" ceiling** — trading an unbuildably narrow panel for an unbuildably wide one. Split two ways, each corner runs from exactly 25.5" up to 37½", inside the catalog at both ends with 10½" of headroom. **No catalog number moved to make this fit; the geometry was chosen to fit the catalog.** Physically each panel is still one corner panel with one return face, butt joined to its partner at mid-wall — the same thing the merged corner has always been, not a new product.

**What the four named lengths produce** (two corners, any standard width — the band's answer does not depend on `standardWidthIn`, because there is no standard panel on these walls):

| wall | before | after | why it is buildable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **51"** | `25.5 + 25.5` | **unchanged** | The pair fits at nominal width with a zero middle. The branch is keyed on "the middle is too small to *build*", not on "the wall is short", so it does not fire here. |
| **60"** | `25.5 + 9 + 25.5` — a 9" panel | **`30 + 30`** | Two corner panels, each 4½" over nominal, one butt joint at mid-wall. |
| **72"** | `25.5 + 21 + 25.5` — a 21" panel | **`36 + 36`** | The 6ft bump-out. Each panel is 36", half the 72" wall, well inside [24", 48"]. |
| **75"** | `25.5 + 24 + 25.5` | **`corner 37.5 \| corner 37.5`** | ⚠ **MOVED INTO THE BAND on 2026-10-01, and this row said "unchanged — the ordinary path handles it" until then.** Its 24" middle was exactly one legal panel; now it is a ½" gap plus a 23½" panel the shop cannot build, so the pair takes the whole wall. This is the one length the gap change deliberately moved, so a table row asserting it was untouched was the worst of the five stale statements. |
| **75½"** | — | the first wall OUTSIDE the band | `75.5 − 51 = 24.5"` of middle: a ½" gap and a 24" panel, exactly at the floor. The first two-corner wall with a legal middle, which used to be 75". |

At the top of the band, `75⅜"` gives `37¾ + 37⅝` — the odd eighth goes to the lowest index, `distributeEighths`' own arbitrary-but-fixed rule. **37¾" is the widest panel the band can ever emit**, 10¼" clear of the 48" ceiling. (Until 2026-10-01 the top was `74⅞"` → `37½ + 37⅜`, and this paragraph named 37½" as the widest — a false universal once the ceiling moved. Note the pair's *mean*, 37.6875", is a sixteenth and is therefore never a width this app emits; the widest EMITTED panel is the number that matters.)

**Openings.** `retileWithOpenings` lets the corners absorb only what is left **after** the openings, so a wall shortened into the band **keeps a window that still fits its nominal middle** (a 74" wall with a 20" window → `27 + window 20 + 27`). Openings are dropped only when they no longer fit there at all, which is what the merged branch has always done and the only answer that keeps the sum exact.

**A legality guard, because the margin is a coincidence of two numbers.** Absorb fires only when the absorbed pair is itself inside [24", 48"]. At the 25.5" corner panel the pair always lands in [25.5", 37.5"] and the guard never fires there; it exists so the rule is self-limiting rather than resting on the same zero-margin coincidence the absorb rule's own notes keep warning about.

**⚠ CORRECTED 2026-09-26 — this paragraph used to claim the guard was "reachable only by a caller passing a non-catalog corner width — a 70" corner on a 150" wall". That was false.** It is reachable straight from the **panelization dropdown**. `squareBalePanel.widthIn` is a **confirmed 39"** and the app tiles Square Bale corners at it, which moves the band to **78"–102½"**; the pair hits the 48" ceiling at a 96" wall, so **every wall from 96⅛" to 102⅜" — 51 of that band's 195 eighth-steps — lands in this guard** (re-measured 2026-10-01 by sweeping every eighth at a 39" corner: band 78⅛"–102⅜" = 195 steps, of which 144 absorb legally and 51 hit the guard). Those walls have **no legal tiling at all**, which also means the neighbouring claim that *"every wall length has a legal tiling"* was never true for Square Bale. Both statements are now corrected in `tiling.ts` as well as here. See "Square Bale refuses the band" below for what the app does about it.

⚠ **Those figures were 78"–102", 47 of 191, until 2026-10-01**, and the change is a real widening of a no-legal-tiling set, not a restatement: **the set grew by 4 lengths** (96⅛"–101⅞" → 96⅛"–102⅜"), because the band's own ceiling moved by the narrow gap's ½". All 51 are refused at the panelization control, so nothing ships wrong and no cut list can contain one — but the growth belongs on the "what is honestly WORSE" ledger of the pass that caused it, and it was missing from it.

**Acceptance, measured.** No tiler-generated panel under 24" or over 48", and the sum invariant exact in integer eighths, swept **every ⅛" from 51" to 720"** across `standardWidthIn ∈ {24, 39, 40, 48}`, both gap ends and **all four corner-ownership combinations** — through `tileWall` and again through `retileWithOpenings` with 1–3 openings. **51" is the sweep floor because it is derived, not round:** the max over the three ownership shapes of the shortest wall each can legally tile (24" with no corners, 49.5" with one, 51" with two). **The old sweeps started at 96", which is precisely why this band could sit in the tiler while two sweeps reported clean.**

**Backward compatibility, proved against real outputs rather than a flag.** Every out-of-band configuration was compared case by case against `main`'s own `tiling.ts` at `a3843f1`: **zero differences over 169,768 `tileWall` and 254,652 `retileWithOpenings` configurations.** The committed form is a digest over the same fold, with the expected values measured on the base commit.

**Octagons, measured end to end through `retile` rather than argued from the ratio.** 10.25ft across is exactly 51" per side (two nominal corners); 10.5ft → `26⅛ + 26⅛`; 12ft → `29⅞ + 29⅞`; 15ft → `37¼ + 37¼`; 15.25ft is 75¾" and leaves a real 24¾" middle. **Every wall of every octagon from 10.5ft to 15ft across now tiles legally** — 80 walls swept, every panel in [24", 48"], every wall summing exactly.

**The referenced "Concentric Wall Ring Buildings" section now exists — this note used to say it did not.** When this branch was written the handoff cited that section as the downstream work this unblocks and no such section was in the document; it was live in another worktree at the time and has since been merged (`main`, commit `a192b59`, *"Spec: the Concentric Wall Ring Buildings plan (planned, nothing built)"*). Corrected 2026-09-26 rather than left standing, since "there is no such section" is now false and the document would contradict itself. This branch predates that commit and does not merge it, so the section is not in *this* copy of the file — it is on `main`, which is where it lands when this branch merges. Nothing was invented to fill the gap while it was missing, and this work still does not depend on it.

**Review Log.** A band wall is legal now and no longer trips the sub-minimum-panel entry. It gets its own **`pending-BI-confirmation`** entry instead (`findAbsorbedCornerWalls`), naming both corner widths, the inches absorbed and the decision it rests on — **Tommy confirmed the corner-geometry ROUTE, not the individual widths it produces**, and the shop has to build them. Silence would have looked identical to nominal corners.

4. **Structural figures using `PanelStructuralStatus` with no invented value?** None in scope.
5. **Does the value surface in the Review Log?** **Yes — one new entry**, `pending-BI-confirmation`, per wall whose corner pair absorbed a middle. It names both corner widths and the inches absorbed. The band's old sub-minimum-panel entry stops firing because the defect it reported is gone, and the stale comment that named the band as unfixable is rewritten rather than left to mislead.

The two adjacent defects that would each need a new corner rule (the one-corner 25.5″–49.5″ zone, and the merged corner exceeding 48″ between 48″ and 51″) got **no code at all**, each has a test asserting today's behaviour so "not attempted" stays distinguishable from "still broken", and both are written up above as his call.

**`cornerPanelWidthIn` (25.5″) and `fabricationMinPanelWidthIn` (24″) are byte-for-byte unchanged, and so is `panelWidthInRange` (15.75″–48″).** The design was chosen to fit them; at no point did the geometry require moving one. The `48 = 2 × 24` coupling the absorb rule rests on is untouched and still asserted.

#### A premise that turned out to be false, checked rather than assumed

**A Stage 3 wall run stop cannot move a wall INTO this band**, though the reasoning that it could is natural (a stop shortens a wall's run). It cannot, and the reason is structural: (1) a wall's own stop takes that end's corner with it, so a stopped wall owns **at most one** corner and can never be a two-corner wall; and (2) the cross-wall orphan rule only ever zeroes an `insetAmount`, and `cornerOwnership` already gives an inset of **0** to every end that owns its corner — so a wall owning both corners has nothing for a neighbour's stop to change, and that adjustment only ever makes a wall *longer* in any case. Asserted directly over a bumped-out shape (convex **and** reflex corners) with stops at both ends of every wall at four depths: every two-corner wall has exactly the run it had unstopped, to the eighth.


### Corner review fixes — BUILT 2026-09-26 (branch `fix-corner-dead-band`)

A review of the corner-absorb work above found one decision reversed by Tommy, one live fabrication defect, and four reporting gaps. All measured on the branch before changing anything.

#### 1. Square Bale REFUSES the band — it does not absorb it

`squareBalePanel.widthIn` is a **confirmed 39"** whole-bale unit (two 18" bales + two 1.5" studs) and the app tiles Square Bale corners at it, so **corner absorb moved this band to 78"–102"** — where ordinary buildings live. An **8ft wall** (`MIN_DIMENSION_FT`, the shortest side the rectangle tool will draw) emitted two **48"** "corner panels"; a 7ft wall two **42"** ones. Tommy, asked directly whether a bale corner may be widened the way a plywood-faced corner panel may:

> **"No — refuse instead."**

Bales do not stretch, so widening a bale corner **invents a product**. Two pieces, and both are needed:

- **Geometry: `cornerMayWiden`** (new trailing parameter on `resolveCorners`/`tileWall`/`retileWithOpenings`/`retile`/`retilePreservingOpenings`, **defaulting to true so every other caller is byte-identical**). False under Square Bale. A band wall then tiles exactly as it did before absorb existed: **nominal 39" corners and a VISIBLE sub-minimum middle**, which the Review Log's existing below-minimum entry already reports. A visible gap beats a substituted value.
- **App: the panelization choice is REFUSED by name**, at the point of edit and never at load (the same posture as Stage 3's run-stop refusal and Stage 2's placement refusals). The message quotes the 39" corner, the offending wall's own run, the middle it leaves, the 24" minimum, counts any other affected walls, and states that **nothing was changed** — including the thickness the button would otherwise set. New pure module `apps/web/app/squareBaleCornerRefusal.ts` (+ test), built on the `placementNotice.ts` pattern with an injected `formatLength`. It renders in its own notice element next to the panelization buttons, because `panelWidthNotice` only renders inside the Selected Panel note and would have been invisible there.

**Why both.** The refusal covers the panelization control. It cannot see a user who is *already* in Square Bale and then draws or shortens a wall into the band — that path never touches the control — so the geometry flag is what keeps that wall from being silently widened.

**⚠ CORRECTED 2026-09-26: this paragraph used to end "…keeps the shop from receiving an invented part on any path", and that was an overstatement which is exactly why a real hole sat unnoticed.** `cornerMayWiden` gates the **absorb** branch and nothing else. It never gated the older **merge** branch, which emits one corner slot of the wall's whole length and under Square Bale fires on every two-corner wall below 78in. The honest statement of what the geometry alone guarantees is narrow: **a band wall is not silently widened.** Everything else about Square Bale's corner legality is enforced in the app, and the merged case is now refused there too — see "Corner review fixes, second pass" below. Both `tiling.ts` and `squareBaleCornerRefusal.ts` carry the corrected wording.

**Measured at the 39" corner** (every eighth from 78" to 103", sweeping `standardWidthIn ∈ {24, 39, 48}`): 78" unchanged (`39 + 39`, zero middle); **84" → `42 + 42`** before, `39 | 6 | 39` after; **95⅞" → `48 + 47⅞`**; **96" → `48 + 48`**; and **96⅛"–101⅞" the legality guard already fired and there is still no legal tiling at all** — 47 of the band's 191 eighth-steps. `cornerBandMiddleIn` is now exported from `tiling.ts` so the refusal and the tiler share **one** definition of "in the band". `absorbedCornerWalls.test.ts` finally exercises 39", which its own doc comment had named all along.

**⚠ NEW OPEN ITEM this exposed — an overrun slot sum nothing reports.** Refusing to widen restores today's tiling, and today's tiling **overruns its wall when an opening no longer fits the middle**: a 90" Square Bale wall carrying a 30" window tiles `39 | window 30 | 39` = **108" of slots on a 90" wall**. This is `main`'s own pre-existing behaviour at *any* corner width (at 25.5", a 60" wall with a 30" window sums to 81") and is exactly the *"the pre-fix slot sum was already wrong"* finding the absorb sweep measured over 4,110 cases — absorb hid it on band walls by dropping the opening. **Nothing reports it**, the same blind spot as the missing over-maximum reporter. Not fixed here (a sum reporter is its own piece of work); there is a committed test asserting the 108" so it cannot be lost. The two alternatives were inventing a 45" bale panel or deleting the user's window silently, and both are worse.

#### 2. Corner panels now frame their REAL width — a live fabrication defect

Tommy, asked whether a corner panel can be built off its nominal 25.5", given it is a 24" core plus two ¾" plywood faces built exactly like a Column Panel:

> **"Yes — any width in the 24–48" band."**

That confirms the pair geometry above — **and made a pre-existing defect urgent.** `buildCornerPanelMembers` was `export const buildCornerPanelMembers = buildColumnPanelMembers`, whose signature has no width at all: **width was hard-locked at `COLUMN_TOTAL_WIDTH_IN` (25.5")**, and `buildCornerPanelSchema` reported that as `overallDimensions.widthIn`. So a 36" corner slot was framed with 25.5" of members:

- a band wall was **visibly short by up to 21"** in Framed 3D and **in the OBJ export** (`toWorldPlacedPanel` places members as-is and performs no width fit);
- and **the per-unique-panel shop fabrication page described a 25.5" panel for a 36" part** — while those pages are already *grouped* by the instance's real width, and **pricing was already correct** (slot width plus the return-leg edge). The cut list and the price disagreed with each other.

**A shop sheet describing the wrong width is a part cut wrong** — the same class as the truss-plate length defect treated as a must-fix. This is not a band-only problem: **every octagon 10.5ft–15ft across** is built entirely of such panels, the merge and clamp rules size a corner *down* on a short wall, and the Rogers-Sehorn ADU's `5'-1¾"` (61¾") wall tiles to two 30⅞" corners.

**No new member geometry was invented.** A corner panel is a column panel with a return face, and the widening reuses the helpers a **Standard Panel** has always used at any width from 15.75" to 48" (`buildSkins`/`buildPlates`/`buildCornerStuds`/`buildGirtRows` — there are no intermediate studs in this system, so nothing had to be decided about stud spacing). The core is `totalWidthIn` less the two ¾" faces; blocking length tracks the plate runners exactly as Tommy specified; the faces stay ¾". `buildColumnStyleMembers` is the shared builder, `buildColumnPanelMembers` calls it at the nominal and is byte-identical (asserted), and **a Column Panel remains fixed at 25.5" — only the corner varies.**

**⚠ Structural capacity deliberately NOT changed, and this is an open question.** `computeBuiltUpColumnBearingCapacityLb` derives I and r from the members' real positions, so a widened corner reports **more** bearing — the two plywood faces sit further apart. Nobody has confirmed that a widened corner's cladding braces the built-up section the same way, so both call sites (`estimatedCornerBuiltUpBearingLb` in page.tsx, `structuralByKey` in FootprintCanvas.tsx) **still use the nominal 25.5" section**, which is the conservative direction. **Does a wider corner panel carry more axial load?** Needs Tommy or his engineer; nothing was inferred.

#### 3. A dropped opening is now reported

On the absorb path where the reservations no longer fit, every window, door and column on the wall is deleted (`dropsReservations`). The drop itself is right — swept over **4,110 drop cases and the pre-fix slot sum was already wrong in every one**, so it is never a regression and is the only answer that keeps the sum exact — but the new Review Log entry named only the two corner widths and the absorbed inches, so **shortening a 90" wall carrying a 30" window into the band lost the window with no notice anywhere.** One clause in the same entry now says so, unconditionally: the record describes the wall as it is *now* and cannot know what it used to carry, and a clause that appeared only when a loss could be proved would be absent in exactly the case that matters.

Measured: a 60" wall was `corner | braced 9" | corner` and is now `corner 30 | corner 30`, so a **12ft octagon has 0 braced panels in the whole building** (16 slots, all corners), `estimatedTotalShearLb` is 0, and the structural line reads *"~0 lb across 0 braced panels"* — which reads like a rounding artefact rather than "nothing in this building resists racking". It disqualified any wall containing a `column` slot while correctly *not* disqualifying `window`/`door`/`big-header` — and a column is a reservation exactly like those. ### Corner review fixes, second pass — BUILT 2026-09-26 (branch `corner-band-final`)

A review of the pass above found one live defect in the Square Bale refusal, three code comments pointing at spec sections that do not contain what they cite, and one piece of prose that overstated what the geometry guarantees. Tommy then answered the question that pass had left open, which turned the largest item from "documented" into "built".

#### 1. The Square Bale refusal was evaluated at the WRONG WALL THICKNESS

`squareBalePanelizationRefusal` built its per-wall facts from page.tsx's own per-render `wallGeometryFor`, which closes over the **current** `thicknessIn` — 15.5in by default. The button that runs the refusal then calls `setThicknessIn(squareBalePanel.thicknessIn)` = **14in**. A wall's tiling run is thickness-dependent whenever it owns a **reflex** corner (`cornerOwnership` gives that end `extraLengthIn = thicknessIn`), so **the refusal was decided against a run length the wall would not have once Square Bale was applied** — validating on one basis and applying on another, the same class of defect as the validate/apply basis split that was a must-fix on Smearforn Stage 3, and against the convention `applyWallRunStopChange`'s own note already states (*"The SAME basis the refusal validated against"*).

**Measured on the branch, both directions.** Sweeping a 6ft bump-out's span start in ⅛in steps along the 30ft wall of a 30×20 rectangle — `insertBumpOut(buildRectangleFootprint(30, 20), "AB", s, s + 6, 5, primary)`, 1,249 positions, **2,498 two-corner walls of which 2,306 change run length** between 15.5in and 14in:

- **12 positions were FALSE REFUSALS.** At span start 62⅝in, wall `01` runs **78⅛in at 15.5in** — inside the 78in–102in bale band, ⅛in middle, **refused by name** — but **76⅝in at 14in**, which is not in the band at all. The app refused Square Bale quoting inches the building would not have had.
- **12 positions were the mirror** (out of band at 15.5in, in band at 14in; span start 86½in gives 102in against 100½in, a 22½in middle). Not a shop-safety hole — `cornerMayWiden: false` still applies and the sub-minimum middle still reports — but the refuse posture was silently incomplete on the one-click path.

*(The reviewer's own figures for this were 482 changed lengths and 36 flips on a different sweep, attributed to the bump-out **depth** and to walls `12`/`34`. The mechanism is identical and the named example reproduces to the eighth — 78.125in against 76.625in — but on this reproduction the driver is the **span start** and the wall is `01`, the segment of `AB` left of the bump-out. With the primary-corner set `insertBumpOut` actually returns, the return walls `12`/`34` own only one corner and cannot be in the band at all. Recorded because the numbers differ and the difference is the fixture, not the defect.)*

**The fix is one call site**, and the fact-gathering moved out of untested page.tsx glue into `squareBaleRefusalWallFacts` in `squareBaleCornerRefusal.ts`, which takes the thickness as an argument — so both measured cases are now pinned by that module's own tests instead of being reachable only through a component.

#### 2. The merged bale corner — Tommy answered, and it is now REFUSED (Case A)

The pass above recorded, and deliberately did not fix, that `cornerMayWiden: false` gates **absorb** and not **merge**. The merge branch — the older *"too short for two corners at all"* rule — emits **one** `corner` slot of the wall's **whole length** at any corner width, flag or no flag. Asked whether *"No — refuse instead"* extends to it, on the grounds that both produce a bale part that cannot be built:

> **"Yes — refuse both cases too."**

**Measured before anything changed.** `tileWall(72, 39, 39, "end", true, true, true, false)` → a single `corner 72in`; at the widest, `tileWall(77.875, …)` → `corner 77⅞in`, **29⅞in over the confirmed 48in `panelWidthInRange.maxIn`**. And it is reached by drawing, not by an exotic edit: under Square Bale (39in corner, 14in thickness) **every wall of every octagon from 8ft to 15.625ft across is one merged slot as wide as the wall** — 8ft → 39¾in, 9ft → 44¾in, 12ft → 59¾in, 15.5ft → 77in; at 15.75ft the side reaches 78¼in and the walls fall into the 78in–102in **band** instead (which is refused in full). **⚠ CORRECTED 2026-09-27: this sentence used to say "from about 9.7ft to 15.7ft across", which understated it.** That range is only the subset whose merged slot breaches the 48in ceiling; the merge branch itself fires from **8ft**, the smallest octagon the draw tool offers, and 8ft–9.64ft produce merged bale corners that are *inside* the ceiling and still not whole-bale units. The distinction did not matter when every merged bale corner was refused; it matters now that only those over 48in are — see the ⚠ below. On a mitered shape the slot comes out typed `safety-oct-corner`, which changes nothing about its width. *(A short bump-out return does **not** reach this case, contrary to how it was first reported: it owns a corner at one end only, so it tiles `braced 21in | corner 39in` — a sub-minimum panel the Review Log already reports.)*

**What was built:**

- **`mergedCornerWidthIn` is exported from `tiling.ts`**, beside `cornerBandMiddleIn`, for exactly the same reason: the refusal and the tiler share **one** definition of "this wall merges its corners". Its test asserts it against `tileWall`'s real output at both corner widths rather than against the formula it shares with it.
- **The panelization control refuses both cases**, through one entry point (`squareBalePanelizationRefusalMessage`) so a caller cannot wire up one and miss the other — which is how the merged case went unrefused in the first place. A building with one of each says both, merged first, each naming its own wall. *(Since 2026-09-27 the merged half of that fires only above the 48in ceiling, per Tommy; the entry point and the one-message shape are unchanged.)*
- **NO GEOMETRY CHANGED.** The merge is Tommy's own rule, the absorb work was instructed to leave it alone, and the plywood path depends on it. Both committed digests re-run **unchanged**: `tileWall` 169,768 configurations → `4137668243`, `retileWithOpenings` 254,652 → `512805668`.

**⚠ SUPERSEDED 2026-09-27 — TOMMY ANSWERED, and the refusal is now the NARROW reading. See "Corner band scope pass" below.** This paragraph used to read *"Every merged bale corner is refused, not only the ones over 48in — and this is a reading, stated rather than buried"*, and it left the alternative priced at one condition. It was a reading, it was offered as one, and he chose the other. Kept here rather than deleted because it is the argument *against* his choice and it should stay visible: the case put to him was the whole merge branch (*"any two-corner wall shorter than 78in still gets a single merged bale corner of the wall's whole length"*), the 48in breach is the severity of its worst end rather than its definition, and a **44¾in** merged bale corner — a 9ft octagon's side — is inside the ceiling and **still is not a 39in whole-bale unit**, which is the thing he said cannot be built. **He was told plainly that the broad reading was the technically safer one and chose *"only refuse over 48 inches"* anyway**, which is his call to make about his own product. The one condition (`mergedWidthIn > maxPanelWidthIn`) is now in `findSquareBaleMergedCornerWalls`; **the Review Log walk was deliberately NOT narrowed with it**, so the permitted sizes are permitted *and reported* rather than silent.

#### 3. …and REPORTED on the one path a refusal cannot see

The refusal covers the panelization control, and this app refuses at the point of **edit** and never at load. That leaves someone already in Square Bale who *draws* a small octagon or shortens a wall under 78in — a path that never touches the control. The band case at least leaves a **visible** sub-minimum middle that `findSubMinimumPanelWidths` reports. A merged corner is over the **maximum**, and this app has **no over-maximum reporter at all**, so that path was completely silent.

So refusing at the control **without** a report would have made the app *quieter* than it was before, on exactly the path the refusal cannot reach — silence that reads as "legal". `findSquareBaleMergedCorners` + `squareBaleMergedCornerNote` add a Review Log entry, second only to the zero-bracing flag, naming the merged width, saying it is not a whole-bale unit, quoting the 48in ceiling **only when it is really breached**, and saying that nothing was rewritten. It is gated on Square Bale: the plywood merged corner between 48in and 51in stays the separate open question it already was.

**⚠ Refusing the drawing gestures themselves is NOT built**, and that is a deliberate stop rather than an oversight. See `## Open Items` — seven candidate write points across six gesture handlers, detection already shared and tested, and **three product decisions that need Tommy** (where a canvas-gesture refusal renders, what refusing a continuous drag looks like, and whether drawing a 10ft octagon under Square Bale should be refused outright and so made undrawable). A refusal covering four of seven write points is worse than an honest report.

#### 4. Three comments cited an Open Items list that did not contain their item

`estimatedCornerBuiltUpBearingLb` (page.tsx), `cornerBearingLb` (FootprintCanvas.tsx) and `buildColumnStyleMembers` (columnPanelMembers.ts) all said the widened-corner **bearing** question was *"recorded in the spec's Open Items"*. It was in the band narrative above and in **neither** `## Open Items` nor `### Open Items — Project Smearforn`. The same was true of the **overrun slot sum**, cited the same way from `tiling.test.ts`. Same class of error as the referenced-section-that-does-not-exist corrected in the pass above.

**Both items were added to `## Open Items`** rather than the pointers softened — they are real and both need Tommy — and each pointer now names its item by title so the claim is checkable.

#### 5. The 108in overrun test asserted a defect and only its body said so

`expect(gated.reduce(…)).toBe(108)` sat under a title about a band wall keeping its window. The ⚠ in the body is unmissable once inside, but a future "fix the overrun" pass reading **test names** would have seen a green 108. **The title now carries it.**

**Its severity is recorded in `## Open Items`** and it is worse than a wrong number in a test: an overrun wall's slots **are** the panel instances, so it reaches **the price, the cut list and the per-unique-panel shop sheets** — 108in of panels drawn, priced and cut for a 90in wall — while being **invisible in 3D and in the OBJ**, because `panelSlotBoxes3D` defensively rescales every slot by `lengthIn / totalWidthIn` (0.8333 here). **The render looks right while the parts are 17% wider than the wall can take.**

#### 6. The zero-bracing entry still counts `panelType === "braced"` only — and now says why

A **combined** safety-gap+brace slot (`secondaryType === "braced"`, which `bracedPlacement.ts` itself calls *"a real brace, not just a safety panel"*) is not counted. **Decision: keep the count and explain it, rather than widen it** — and the stated reason is not "it matches the shear line below it", which would be circular. The real reason is that **`PanelInstance` does not carry `secondaryType` at all** (`panelInstances.ts` pushes `zone.type`, so a combined slot arrives as a plain `safety-gap` with no `bracedPattern` either), so `summarizeBearingAndShear` **already gives a combined slot zero shear** and `estimatedTotalShearLb` really is 0 for a building whose only braces are combined ones. The entry is therefore a **true statement about what the app models**, not a false alarm — the model is what is wrong, not the count.

Counting `secondaryType` here alone would be strictly worse: the entry would go quiet while the displayed shear stayed 0 lb. Fixing it properly means carrying the flag onto the instance and **raising a displayed structural total**, which is not a thing to do by inference. `FootprintCanvas`'s per-panel tooltip *does* count `secondaryType`, so the two genuinely disagree today; that divergence is recorded at both sites.

#### 7. Two things recorded and deliberately not fixed

- **A pre-existing bearing divergence under Square Bale.** `estimatedCornerBuiltUpBearingLb` reads `cornerPanelMembers3D`, which under Square Bale is the **bale** corner body, while `structuralByKey` in FootprintCanvas.tsx always builds the **plywood** corner at nominal. So "bearing is consistent at both sites" holds for Loose Packed Braced and Timber Frame Curtain and **not** for Square Bale. Not introduced by the corner work; noted at both sites and in `## Open Items` beside the widened-corner bearing question, since both are about which section a corner's bearing is taken from.
- **`buildCornerPanelSchema` has no callers today**, so the pass above's schema-width fix is correct but currently dead code. It exists for the future SketchUp exporter. No action, recorded so nobody "cleans it up".

## Corner ownership flips, the two-tier safety gap, and plywood totals that tell the truth (2026-10-01) — ALL THREE BUILT, branch `corner-ownership`

Three changes shipped as one piece because each of them changes how **every wall of every shape** tiles, so the regression net is re-measured once instead of three times. All three are Tommy's decisions of 2026-09-30/10-01, and he cleared the consequence for existing work up front: *"Totally fine changing any current drawings/projects."*

### His sentences, verbatim, because they are the provenance

> *"Can we make it so that once below the threshold (of 12'? If it's somewhere around 10-12' rn that's fine) the safety gap is 1/2"."*

> *"1/2" CDX plywood should be a material that we calculate with all the totals and summary pages next to 3/4" stats."*

And the sentence that settles whether the reserved gap and the plywood are one thing or two:

> *"Safety gaps should be .75" of plywood"*

### CHANGE 1 — the LONGER wall runs through and owns both its corner panels

Until this pass the **locally shorter** wall owned the corner panel at a convex 90deg corner and the longer one was inset by one wall thickness. That is the inverse of the conventional framing through-wall/butt-wall convention — the through wall is the long, continuous one — **and the code comment claimed that convention for the inverse rule.** It is what Tommy reported as a visual defect: on his 241 x 155in rectangle the two 12'11" walls ran vertex-to-vertex while both 20'1" walls were inset 15½in at each end, so *"the short sides seem to protrude a little past where it should."*

**The arithmetic was never wrong.** Every run summed exactly, and the 62in of perimeter difference is precisely 4 x 15½in — one wall thickness per corner. It was the wrong wall. The rule is `cornerOwnership`'s convex branch in `packages/geometry/src/retile.ts`, and the comment that justified the old rule is replaced rather than left standing.

**The tiebreak: equal-length walls give the corner to the SUCCESSOR, which pinwheels.** Ties are now the common case, not an exception — a square has four of them. A tie goes to `nextWall`, the next wall round the ring, which is exactly what the strict `>` in `toEighths(...) > toEighths(...)` encodes. On an equal-sided shape every wall then owns its START corner and butts at its end: all four runs come out the same length and every wall is the same part. An id- or index-based tiebreak instead hands one wall both of its corners and leaves another with none, which is precisely what the old `wall.id < nextWall.id` rule did to a square (AB owned two, DA owned none). The successor rule is a function of the ring's own succession — `walls.find(w => w.startCorner === wall.endCorner)` — so it depends on no object iteration order, no id spelling and no array index.

**The comparison is on the eighth grid, exactly, with no tolerance**, against `wallFabricationLengthIn` — the same integer the tiler sizes the run from, never `lengthFt` as a float. Right-angle corners are the only place ownership is asked, and `quantizeFootprint` makes every wall of a rectilinear shape an exact eighth, so the comparison is an integer identity. **The near-tie worry about the octagon does not arise:** snapping an octagon's clip corners moves them by up to 1/16in and its eight nominally-equal sides really do differ — **measured post-snap on a 30ft regular octagon: 149in and 149.25in, so the spread is exactly 1/4in, two eighths** (⚠ this said *"just under 1/5in"* until 2026-10-01, which is not a number the eighth grid can produce; the spread is 2 eighths at 30ft and 1 eighth at 20ft and 24ft, and 0 at 16ft) — but every octagon corner is MITERED, `isRightAngleCorner` is false there, and the loop returns before any length is compared. A tolerance would only paper over a case that cannot happen while silently ignoring a deliberately hand-set 1/8in difference between two real walls.

**Mitered shapes: ownership does not apply there and nothing about them changed.** `cornerOwnership` skips every non-right-angle corner, so all eight octagon walls keep both of their corner panels, `computeSafetyEnd`'s "left corner seen from outside" gap rule and `markSafetyCorner`'s `safety-oct-corner` slot are reached exactly as before, and an octagon's eight runs are the lengths they always were. Asserted directly rather than argued.

**Reflex corners compose with the flip, and the reflex FALLBACK was deliberately not flipped.** The reflex branch is unchanged: the *original* wall (one with a primary endpoint) still wins and is extended by one wall thickness, and the loser still takes `insetAmount: 0`. Its tiebreak — used only when neither or both walls are original, a reflex corner between two different bump-outs — is still shorter-wins-then-id, for two structural reasons. (1) Tommy's decision is about the through-wall/butt-wall convention at a CONVEX corner; a reflex winner extends instead of insetting, so "the longer wall runs through" is not a statement about it and he has not been asked. (2) **That expression exists in three places that must stay bit-identical** — `cornerOwnership`, `wallBoxes3D` and `computeInsetPerimeterRing` — because a disagreement puts a 3D wall box or a foundation ring segment a wall thickness away from the panel run it carries. Changing it means changing all three in lockstep. See the Open Items.

**One consequence worth stating on its own: a run stop on a long wall now reaches its short neighbours.** The orphan-corner rule (2026-09-25: a stopped corner simply does not exist, and the butting neighbour stops insetting into air) used to fire when a SHORT wall was stopped. It now fires when a LONG one is, because the long wall is the one that owns corners. Measured end to end in the real app: a 30in start stop on the 580in wall grows its neighbour `DA` by exactly 15½in. Two harness steps were aimed at the old shape and had to be re-aimed — see "What the harnesses had to change" below.

### CHANGE 2 — a two-tier safety gap, replacing an all-or-nothing threshold

`SAFETY_PANEL_MIN_WALL_LENGTH_IN = 144` used to decide whether a gap slot existed **at all**; a run of 144in or less got none and was tiled by an even split instead. It now decides only how **thick** the gap is:

| run | gap |
|---|---|
| over 144in | **3/4in**, 5-ply CDX |
| 144in or under | **1/2in**, 3-ply CDX |

**Every run gets a gap**, and that is what makes Change 1 safe: flipping ownership drops Tommy's short walls to a 124in run, which under the old rule would have left his rectangle with gaps on two walls instead of four — against his own *"on each wall"*.

**The reserved wall-run width and the sheet thickness are ONE physical fact, not two.** Verified against `buildSafetyGapMembers` and the catalog description rather than assumed: the gap IS the plywood (*"instead of a safety panel being a standard panel slightly altered, its actually just a 3/4in piece of plywood that is the panel thickness and panel height"*), so a run reserving 3/4in is reserving room for a 3/4in board and nothing else. They are two constants only because `packages/geometry` deliberately imports nothing — and `apps/web/app/tilerFabricationLimits.test.ts`, the one place both packages are visible, now asserts all three numbers agree. The catalog's own description used to say the sheet was 3/4in *"regardless of how much wall-run width the tiling reserves"*; that sentence was true only in the sense that the sheet never GREW to fill an over-wide slot, and it is corrected.

**Two slots are legitimately not their own thickness, and both are documented where they happen:** a corner-brace COMBINED slot (a standard width plus the plywood buffer) and the degenerate CLAMPED slot a wall whose openings ate its middle can produce. `safetyGapSheetThicknessIn` maps a reserved width onto one of the two real sheets as a floor rather than an equality, so a combined slot takes the 3/4in sheet and a clamped sub-1/2in slot takes the 1/2in sheet — a real spec in both cases, never an invented one.

**The plySpec follows the thickness, using the two specs that already existed.** `SKIN_PLY_SPEC` (3/4in **5-ply** CDX, the standard panel's skins) and `GIRT_WEB_PLY_SPEC` (1/2in **3-ply** CDX, its girt webs). ⚠ **They differ in ply count as well as thickness**, which matters to whoever orders sheets. No new sheet, no new catalog entry and no new `status` was introduced for this.

**The misnamed threshold is CLOSED by renaming, not by a comment.** `SAFETY_PANEL_MIN_WALL_LENGTH_IN` said WALL and was compared against the RUN. Those are different lengths the moment a wall butts into a neighbour, and the flip makes the difference ordinary: a 12'11" (155in) wall that loses both corners is a **124in run**, i.e. a short run. It is now `SAFETY_GAP_NARROW_MAX_RUN_LENGTH_IN`, with `safetyGapWidthForRunIn(runLengthIn)` as the one place the tier is decided. **The number itself did not move: 144in before, 144in after.**

**Two things the two-tier gap forced, both arithmetic rather than policy:**

1. **`buildEvenMiddle` is GONE.** The no-gap tiling path had no callers left, and a second tiling path nothing calls is a trap. Its even-split arithmetic survives in `computeSillRunWidths`, which is now the only even split in the file.
2. **The corner-absorb band's ceiling moved from `TILER_MIN_PANEL_WIDTH_IN` to `TILER_MIN_PANEL_WIDTH_IN + gapWidthIn`, so the band is 51in–75½in rather than 51in–75in** (and 78in–102½in at the 39in Square Bale corner). The middle now has to pay for the gap *before* it can hold a legal panel: a 75in two-corner wall has a 24in middle, which was exactly one legal panel and is now a 1/2in gap plus a 23½in panel the shop cannot build. Four eighth-steps wider — **195 eighth-steps (51⅛in to 75⅜in inclusive) where it was 191**, swept and counted rather than inferred — and every one of them gets a legal corner pair instead of an unbuildable panel. **No building value moved to make this fit** — 24in, 48in and the 25.5in corner are untouched, and `resolveCorners` still checks the absorbed pair for legality before absorbing. ⚠ **The band widening is not interchangeable with the alternative of changing what happens INSIDE the band:** membership is decided by `middleEighths < toEighths(TILER_MIN + gapWidthIn)`, so revert the ceiling and a 75in wall still comes out `gap 0.5 | standard 23.5` whatever the in-band rule does. The two are orthogonal.

**What is honestly WORSE, measured rather than argued.** A run too short to hold a gap AND a buildable panel has no legal tiling at all, and the band of such runs **shifted up by exactly the narrow gap's 1/2in**. Measured at the 40in standard, every eighth from 0 to 200in:

| corners owned | sub-minimum run lengths | count | before 2026-10-01 |
|---|---|---|---|
| neither | 5/8in – 24⅜in | 191 | 1/8in – 23⅞in, 191 |
| one | 26⅛in – 49⅞in | 191 | 25⅝in – 49⅜in, 191 |
| both | none | 0 | none, 0 |
| **Square Bale (39in corner), no legal tiling at all** | **96⅛in – 102⅜in** | **51** | 96⅛in – 101⅞in, **47** |

⚠ **That last row was MISSING from this table and is the one honestly-worse item this pass did not disclose.** At the 39in Square Bale corner the absorbed pair hits the confirmed 48in ceiling, so those walls have no legal tiling at all — and because the band's ceiling moved by the narrow gap's ½in, **that set grew by 4 lengths, 47 → 51** (of a band that is itself now 195 eighth-steps rather than 191). **All 51 are refused at the panelization control**, so nothing ships wrong and no cut list can contain one; the omission was a reporting gap, not a safety one. Corrected in the band section too.

The first three rows' band is the same SIZE; **four lengths at the top are newly unbuildable and four at the bottom stop producing a panel at all** (the whole run becomes the gap). The two-corner case has none either side, and that is only still true because of the band widening above.

**The four-moved-each-way shape, named length by length, because "report-only is right" is Tommy's call and the next reader should not have to re-derive it.** Measured at the 40in standard, and the two configurations do NOT move in the same way — stated separately rather than averaged into one sentence:

| configuration | four that became sub-minimum (top) | four that left the band (bottom) | what the bottom four do now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **neither corner** | 24in, 24⅛in, 24¼in, 24⅜in | ⅛in, ¼in, ⅜in, ½in | **no panel at all** — the whole run becomes the gap. Not "buildable": a different unbuildable shape. |
| **one corner** | 49½in, 49⅝in, 49¾in, 49⅞in | 25⅝in, 25¾in, 25⅞in, 26in | **genuinely buildable** — the lone corner absorbs the sliver and the wall is one legal corner panel. |

So "four moved each way" is right about the counts and would be wrong as a statement about direction: on a no-corner run the four at the bottom trade one unbuildable result for another, and only the one-corner run gains four real lengths. **Nothing is silent about any of them** — the Review Log's sub-minimum entry **names each case by wall and slot when a user actually draws it**, which is what makes report-only defensible rather than lazy: the set is small, bounded, measured, and announced per instance rather than per theory. **There is no legal answer for the four lengths that moved in** — a 24in run holding a 1/2in gap leaves 23½in, under the shop's confirmed 24in minimum — and the only ways out are to drop the gap on short runs (reversing Tommy's decision) or to move the 24in minimum (off limits). So they are reported in the Review Log exactly as the rest of that band already was. **Tommy's call, not the code's.** Pinned by a sweep in `tiling.test.ts` so the band cannot move again unnoticed.

**Deliberately NOT changed, and flagged in the code at the point of decision:**

- **`SAFETY_PLYWOOD_BUFFER_IN` (the corner-brace combine's glued-on 3/4in) is still single-tier.** A combined slot on a short run is a standard width plus 3/4in while the gap it replaced was 1/2in, and the extra 1/4in settles against the panels further along the run. The combine's own contract is unaffected — the wall still sums exactly in whole eighths, no zero-width panel, nothing pushed outside [24in, 48in]. What is open is whether that buffer is physically the same board as the gap. It cannot simply read the gap slot's width, because a legacy stored file can carry a 2-to-4ft gap slot and that would glue on two feet of plywood.
- **The GABLE row keeps the old all-or-nothing gate and the single 3/4in width.** `GABLE_SAFETY_GAP_MIN_RUN_LENGTH_IN` used to mirror the wall tiler exactly; the mirror is now only partial, deliberately. A gable row is not a wall run — it is the triangle above the eave, tiled per rise/flat/fall segment — and Tommy's words were about walls.

### CHANGE 3 — the plywood totals say what is actually in them, and name the real spec

`apps/web/app/page.tsx` already tallied both thicknesses by thickness (`computePlywoodAreaSqFt(allRealMembers, 0.5)`), so a 1/2in safety-gap sheet flows into the 1/2in row **for free** the moment the member carries that thickness. Two things were wrong and both are fixed:

1. The row read **"1/2in plywood (girt webs)"**, which stops being true the moment safety gaps contribute to it.
2. **Neither row said CDX**, though the catalog knew the full spec all along.

Both rows now read from one shared module, `apps/web/app/plywoodRowLabels.ts`, whose text is **derived from the catalog's own `plySpec` strings** through a new `formatPlySpecLabel`, so the row says "3/4in 5-ply CDX" and "1/2in 3-ply CDX" because that is what the parts are rather than because somebody typed it:

- `3/4in 5-ply CDX plywood (skins, side plies, header caps, roof-bearing caps, long-run safety gaps)`
- `1/2in 3-ply CDX plywood (girt webs, short-run safety gaps)`

**Both places that render the pair now use it** — the Material Totals detail page and the **Project Summary** page's Materials table, which carried the identical stale label. Those are the only two renderers of these rows in the repo (grepped, not assumed); `plywoodThreeQuarterSheetCount` / `plywoodHalfSheetCount` are consumed only by those two. The Material Totals notes now also say which run length puts a gap on which row, quote Tommy's sentence, and carry a standalone warning that the two sheets differ in ply count.

**Three app-side consequences of the sheet becoming two sheets, each a real defect avoided:**

- `safetyGapMembers3D`, a single memoized member list built on "the sheet is always 3/4in", is **gone**. Every instance is now built from its own slot's reserved width. A shared memo would have reported 3/4in plywood for every 1/2in gap in the building.
- The **Shop Fabrication grouping** keyed every safety gap onto ONE page (`return panelTypeId`). A 1/2in sheet and a 3/4in sheet are different fabricated parts — the same reason two braced panels of one width but different patterns do not merge — so the key now carries the sheet thickness.
- `buildSafetyGapSchema`'s `overallDimensions.widthIn` follows the tier too, so the component schema cannot describe a part the member list does not.

The one new building value is the **1/2in narrow tier**, in `safetyGapTwoTierRule` in `packages/panel-catalog/src/data.ts` beside the existing 3/4in tier, with Tommy's sentence quoted verbatim as its note.    ⚠ **`safetyGapTwoTierRule` originally gave ONE status to THREE fields, and `narrowMaxRunLengthIn: 144` is not the same kind of fact as the two thicknesses.** Tommy's single sentence states the thickness flatly ("the safety gap is 1/2\"") and **hedges the threshold three ways at once**: *"(of 12'? **If it's somewhere around 10-12' rn that's fine**)"* — a question mark, a range, and explicit deference to whatever the code already had. One `confirmed` over both made 144in read as a number he specified. He did not specify it; he accepted the one that was there.

   **SPLIT on 2026-10-01.** `safetyGapTwoTierRule` now carries only the two thicknesses and stays `confirmed`. The threshold is its own entry, **`safetyGapNarrowMaxRunLengthIn`, status `pending-BI-confirmation`**, whose note opens by saying that **144in is one choice inside a 120in–144in band he was indifferent to — "do not read this flag as 'he said 144'"** — and records that what IS confirmed is the band and the acceptability of the existing value within it.
