6. **Where the spec marks something open, does the code treat it as provisional?** **Yes for the code; and the CLAIM about it was false when first written, which is corrected here rather than quietly rewritten.** Three things this pass deliberately did not decide got a named flag at the point of decision rather than a quiet default: the combine's 3/4in buffer, the gable row's single-tier gap, and the reflex-corner fallback's duplication. Each is argued in the code comment where a future reader will stand — that half was true.

   ⚠ **What this point originally said was *"Each is an Open Item below"*, and it was not.** All three lived only in this section's own `### Open Items — this pass`; the spec's top-level `## Open Items` had **zero** hits for any of them, and **none of the four code pointers named its item by title** — `bracedPlacement.ts` and `gableTiledRow.ts` said "see the spec's Open Items", `retile.ts` said "see the Open Items", and the Safety/Gap description in `data.ts` said "see the Open Items". **This is the FOURTH consecutive pass to reintroduce the exact defect class written up at "the third consecutive pass to reintroduce this exact defect class" below**, and in the same shape it describes: a pass fixes the pointers it was sent to fix, then writes a fresh one into the section describing the fix. **Fixed 2026-10-01 both ways the remedy allows**: all three are now real `## Open Items` entries, and all four code pointers name their item by its title there so the reader can search for the sentence instead of hunting a list. The titles are `"Does the corner-brace combine's glued-on plywood buffer follow the gap tier?"`, `"Does a GABLE row's short segment want a 1/2in gap?"` and `"Should the REFLEX corner fallback flip to longer-wins too?"`.

   **The lesson this keeps not teaching, stated as a rule for the next pass:** a pointer is not finished when it tells the reader *where* to look. It is finished when the thing it points at **exists at that address under the name the pointer uses**. Writing "see the Open Items" costs nothing and verifies nothing; grep for the title you just wrote, in the file you just wrote it about, before claiming the item is recorded.

Three notes on that table that are the point of it rather than footnotes:

- **The 684,360 case count fell by 228** because the corner-absorb band is four eighths wider, and a wall whose corners absorb its whole run has no free panel to pin, so the grid skips it. The honoured/refused split moved because the tiler's free-run widths moved. **Zero violations either side.**
- **The census roughly tripled for exactly one reason**, and the histogram proves it: that sweep passes `hasCornerStart`/`hasCornerEnd` to `retileWithOpenings` explicitly, so the ownership flip cannot touch it. Every WIDE-gap offset comes back **bit-identical** (6,559 at 62¼in, 4,064 at 36¾in, 1,100 at 80¾in, 95 at 30¾in) and every new entry is its NARROW-gap twin a quarter inch nearer the corner (2,098 at 62in, 5,490 at 36½in, 1,212 at 80½in, 3,091 at 30½in). Short runs joined the census wholesale because they now have a gap for the corner walk to reach.
- **The "byte-identically to before corner absorb" digest pair no longer means what its title says**, and saying so was better than leaving a constant that fails loudly. It was a proof that corner absorb moved nothing outside its band; the two-tier gap moves every configuration in that sweep by design. It is kept as an unintended-change detector, re-baselined with the old values recorded. ⚠ **And the `describe` has now been RENAMED, which saying so was not a substitute for** — it read "walls outside the band tile byte-identically to before corner absorb" while both digests were baselined on this branch, and **a test whose name is false is the same defect class as an Open Items pointer that names no item.** It is now "walls outside the band: a digest pair that catches an UNINTENDED change (baselined on this branch, 2026-10-01)", with the old name and the reason it went recorded above the block.

**One test's claim had to be narrowed rather than re-baselined. The narrower version is better TARGETED, and it is genuinely WEAKER — an earlier draft of this paragraph called it "the stronger one", which was an over-claim.** `cornerBraceCombineRefusals.test.ts` asserted "every reported brace is still a real fabricable panel" via `slot.widthIn >= TILER_MIN_PANEL_WIDTH_IN`, which **forbade a sub-minimum reported brace outright**. That is no longer true — on 382 of 3,202 swept cases the reported brace is sub-minimum — so it was replaced by an assertion that **permits** one and forbids only this entry being what made it narrow. Permitting what you used to forbid is a weakening, however well aimed, and calling it a strengthening is exactly the kind of claim this log exists to catch.

**And it establishes ATTRIBUTION WITHIN THIS BRANCH, not PRE-EXISTENCE** — which the original wording got wrong too. `tilerAlreadySubMinimum` is computed from **this branch's** tiler, so what the test proves is that the brace walk did not invent the narrow panel: the tiler handed it over already narrow. **"Those 382 are all residual case 2 … which was emitting a sub-minimum panel there before this pass" is false for 8 of them.** Re-measured on both trees over the identical grid: **branch 382 cases, wall lengths 113⅛in–136⅞in; `main` 382 cases, 112⅝in–136⅜in** — the same count, with the set **shifted up by exactly the narrow gap's ½in**. So **8 cases are newly sub-minimum** (136½, 136⅝, 136¾, 136⅞ at each of the two standard widths, 39in and 48in) and 8 left at the bottom. It is the same honest finding the band table above already owns, and it was simply stated inaccurately here; the correct claim is that 374 of the 382 were sub-minimum before this pass and 8 became so because of it.

**The assertion was also tightened, because the version shipped did not assert what its own comment claimed.** `tilerAlreadySubMinimum` was a wall-level `some()`, so a brace newly made sub-minimum at index *j* would have passed on any wall that happened to carry a sub-minimum panel at index *i*. It now asserts **slot identity** — `tiled[entry.braceSlotIndex].widthIn < TILER_MIN_PANEL_WIDTH_IN` — with the index-alignment precondition (`braced.length === tiled.length`) asserted rather than assumed, since `applyBracedPlacement` does change the array's length on 314 of the 3,202 cases whenever a combine fires and swallows a slot. Measured: all 382 pass under the tighter form, and the 382 are a contiguous run of 191 wall lengths at each of the two standard widths.

### Fixtures that had to be re-dimensioned, and why that is not re-baselining

A fixture that says "AB owns both its corners" is a statement about which wall is longer. Six of them were written against the old rule and would have gone **vacuously green** rather than red if left alone, which is the worse failure. Each was moved, not weakened, and each carries the reason inline:

- `retile.test.ts`'s 360in two-corner wall: a 30 x 35ft rectangle becomes 30 x 20ft, so AB is the longer wall and still owns both corners at 360in. Its 564in sibling: 47 x 55ft becomes 47 x 40ft.
- `panelSlotBoxes3D.test.ts`: the wall under test swaps between AB and BC in four tests, and the reflex-extension test moves to a 30 x 10ft rectangle with the bump-out span at 15–20ft so wall "01" is longer than DA and still wins its convex corner.
- `wallRunStop.test.ts`: the orphan-corner block swaps AB and BC throughout — the owner is now the long wall and the butting neighbour the short one.
- `squareBaleCornerRefusal.test.ts`'s thickness-dependence fixture becomes an inward **notch** instead of an outward bump-out. Wall "01" can no longer own both ends (it loses the convex corner to the 240in side), and a wall that does not own both ends is never in the bale band — the three tests would have been green and measuring nothing. The notch's inner face wins both of its REFLEX corners and is therefore extended twice, which **reproduces the two runs that carry the tests' meaning: 78.125in and 100.5in with its 22.5in middle, both to the eighth.** ⚠ **"Every number in those tests is the number measured before the flip" was an over-claim: two of the four moved.** The two that the assertions turn on are preserved — `78.125in` with its `0.125in` middle (the in-band wall the old glue falsely refused) and `100.5in` with its `22.5in` middle (the mirror case, and the length the refusal sentence must quote). The two that moved are the *out-of-band companions*: the 14in-thickness run went `76.625in` → `75.125in`, and the length the sentence must NOT quote went `102in` → `103.5in`. Both moved because the notch is extended at **two** reflex corners rather than one, so the thickness difference tells twice — which the test asserts explicitly (`2 * (15.5 - 14)`). Neither is a number the refusal quotes or a boundary of the band; they exist to prove the run is thickness-dependent at all.
- `projectFile.test.ts`'s v24 fixtures: wall AB's run is 360in rather than 329in, so the off-grid fixture's widest slot grew by the 31in that frees up and the genuinely-tiled array gained its two corner slots. Without the second change that test would have passed through the load-time GUARD instead of the no-op branch it exists to exercise.

### What the harnesses had to change

All six are green from exit-0 runs of the final code. Three steps needed re-aiming, and in each case the app was behaving correctly:

- **`smearforn-stage-0-1` step 12b** took its "one unrelated retile" from any other wall. On this footprint that was an adjacent LONG wall, and a start stop on a wall that owns its corner orphans that corner, so the orphan rule grew the wall under test from 184⅛in to 199⅝in — whereupon its pinned set could no longer sum to it and every pin was correctly refused. The step now stops a wall sharing **no corner** with the wall under test, which is genuinely unrelated. `automaticPanelsLeft === 0` still holds, so the step is still non-vacuous.
- **`smearforn-stage-3` step 13** ("a stop that reaches a corner the wall OWNS") stopped the SHORT wall, which now owns no corner and so orphans nothing — it recorded `neighboursThatGrew: []`. It now stops the wall with the longest 3D extent, i.e. the one that owns its corners, and records `DA` growing by exactly 15.5in.
- **`smearforn-stage-3` step 11** discriminated "the plan gained an unbuilt-span boundary" by counting `#8a8a8a` pixels on the live Konva canvas. **That colour is both the dashed boundary AND the fill of every corner panel** (`panelColors.ts`), so the proxy only worked while the stopped wall owned no corner to lose: 1,404 with the stop against 1,308 without on `main`, and 1,169 against 1,403 after the flip, with the app correct throughout. The discriminator is now the printable plan sheet's **NO PANELS dimension read from the DOM**, which names the thing itself; the grey pair stays in the evidence, recorded and unasserted, because a number somebody once trusted should be visible rather than deleted.

### The review-fix pass (2026-10-01) — what the review found, and what it did NOT find

The review verdict was that **all three changes are right and the band widening is the correct fix**, with three must-fixes that were **all claim/documentation accuracy, not geometry**. Worth stating plainly what was NOT wrong, because it bounds everything above: **no wrong building number, no mis-flagged structural value, and no app defect papered over by a harness edit.** Independently re-confirmed by the review: the pinwheel tiebreak on a square (four walls, one corner each, 224.5in runs, where `main` gave AB two and DA none); octagons bit-identical in run length at 12/16/20/24/30ft with 62 of 65 legal on both trees and the same three pre-existing failures; the reflex fallback's three-way duplication at `retile.ts:248`, `wallBoxes3D.ts:87`, `perimeterRing.ts:98`; the census histogram with every wide bucket bit-identical; zero violations in the locked-width sweep on both sides; all three re-aimed harness steps non-vacuous; and the fixture rebuild sound.

**The eight things the pass changed, all of them a claim catching up with the code:**

1. **The Open Items pointers** — the spec's own named defect class, reintroduced for a fourth consecutive pass. Three items promoted to `## Open Items`; all four code pointers now name their item by title. Flags-check point 6 corrected in place. See point 6 above.
2. **This document's own `### The 51in–75½in two-corner dead band` section**, which contradicted the code in five places — including a named table row asserting "unchanged" for the one wall length the gap change deliberately moved. All five corrected, each with the old value kept beside the new one.
3. **"All 382 are pre-existing"**, false for 8 cases; and the replacement assertion described as stronger when it is weaker. Both corrected, and the assertion itself tightened from a wall-level `some()` to slot identity.
4. **The band step count** — 195, not 193.
5. **The Square Bale no-legal-tiling set grew 47 → 51 and was not disclosed.** Now a row on the "honestly WORSE" table.
6. **The octagon side spread** — ¼in (two eighths), measured, not "just under 1/5in", which is not a number the eighth grid can produce.
7. **Five smaller wording/code accuracy items**: `tiling.ts`'s "rather than 51in to 75.5in" (should be 75in), `tiling.test.ts`'s 37.6875in "worst case" (that is the pair's mean; the widest emitted is 37.75in), the re-baselined digest `describe` whose title was still false, a `safetyGapSheetThicknessIn` pointer naming the wrong file, and the notch fixture's "every number" over-claim.
8. **Two harness accuracy items**: a missing `\` in `/^Elevation:\s*/` that worked only by accident, plus a stated assumption on `sharesACorner`; and in stage 3, `shortWallId` renamed (it meant the opposite of its value after the flip) with `stoppedWallOwnsItsCorners: true` replaced by a derived, asserted field.

No version bump either: a bump buys an old deploy the ability to REFUSE the file, and there is nothing here for an old deploy to get wrong, since the file's contents are exactly as valid as they were.

It reads no version, date or flag — there is none to read — but compares each wall's stored slot total against the run the CURRENT rules give that wall, using `repairStateToEighths`' own `> slotCount` eighths tolerance, so a wall is named only when its stored tiling was genuinely kept rather than repaired on load. One entry for the whole project naming every affected wall with both lengths (a per-wall entry would be the same fact N times and would bury the rest of the log), it says plainly that nothing has been rewritten and nothing is lost but that each wall WILL re-tile on the next edit, and it is **self-clearing** — editing a wall removes it with no bookkeeping. ⚠ Two honest limits: it is measured with the **live run stops** (the unstopped run would report every stopped wall in the building, which is why it is a stricter test than the load-time guard it mirrors), and it is **not specific to this one change** — any stored-vs-current run mismatch lands there, so the sentence names corner ownership as the reason this is common right now rather than asserting it as the cause.

## Zoom, and the building you are allowed to draw (2026-10-05) — BUILT

**Tommy, 2026-10-04: _"The user should be able to zoom out and have access to a bigger footprint."_** He asked for it as a feature. It turned out to be a **bug**, and the same one-line confusion was also quietly corrupting measurement and wall-picking. Both are fixed together, because they are one fault.

### What was wrong

Konva has two pointer accessors and they are not interchangeable:

- `stage.getPointerPosition()` — the pointer in **screen px**, as an offset inside the stage's container.
- `stage.getRelativePointerPosition()` — the same pointer run through the stage's **inverse transform**, i.e. in the stage's own untransformed coordinate space.

Everything in `canvasGeometry.ts` is built as `ft * SCALE_PX_PER_FT + offsetPx` — the stage's untransformed space, which this spec and that module now call **plan px**. The pan/zoom view is applied to the Stage's own `x`/`y`/`scale`. So plan px and screen px coincide **only at 100% zoom with no pan**, and all eight pointer readings in `FootprintCanvas.tsx` used `getPointerPosition()`.

⚠ **A comment in that file asserted the opposite** — that `getPointerPosition()` "already returns coordinates in the stage's own local space, already compensated for this transform" — which is why the code had been read past more than once. That comment is now replaced by the measurement that disproves it.

**Measured in the running app**, one pointer, at 25% zoom: `getPointerPosition()` returned **599.3**, from which the app concluded **50ft**; `getRelativePointerPosition()` returned **2397.3**, the truth, **199.8ft**. A **4x error, exactly 1/scale.**

### What it cost

1. **The drawable building was capped at about 60ft x 40ft, roughly 60 panels, at every zoom.** Zooming out bought nothing: a drag across the whole plan at 25% committed a building a quarter the size of the box just dragged. ⚠ This directly blocked Tommy's stated target, *"300+ panels should be doable in this app"* (2026-10-02). **Measured before the fix: a full-canvas drag at 25% gave 62.8ft x 40.9ft, 66 panels.**
2. **The Measure tool under-reported by the same factor** — a quarter of the true distance at 25% zoom. A dimension tool that lies is the sharpest possible contradiction of *"this app needs to be perfectly tight with dimensions and wall lengths"*.
3. **Wall-picking compared a screen-space pointer against plan-space walls**, so clicking a wall while zoomed picked the wrong wall or none. Panning broke it too, since `getPointerPosition()` does not subtract the stage offset either.

### The fix

- All eight readings use `getRelativePointerPosition()`. **No tiling, geometry or model code changed** — only which number the mouse reports.
- **Thresholds are divided by the view scale** so they stay constant *under the user's cursor*: `WALL_PICK_TOLERANCE_PX` (20), `OCTAGON_SQUARE_SNAP_PX` (20), `DRAG_DISAMBIGUATION_DEADZONE_PX` (8) and the new named `MIN_DRAG_PX` (10, previously an inline `10`). Left unscaled, a 20 plan-px wall target is 2px of screen at the zoom floor and nothing is clickable. `findNearestWall`, `findNearestWallCandidates` and `snapOctagonBoxPx` take the scaled value as an argument, defaulting to the constant.
- **The zoom floor moves 0.25 → 0.1.** This is what sets the maximum drawable building, because one draw gesture cannot reach past the visible plan: at zoom z the canvas shows `(720/z)/12` ft by `(480/z)/12` ft.

| zoom | visible plan | approx. panels at a 40in standard |
|---|---|---|
| 100% | 60ft x 40ft | ~60 |
| 25% (the old floor) | 240ft x 160ft | ~240 |
| **10% (the new floor)** | **600ft x 400ft** | **~600** |

⚠ **This is a view limit, not a model limit.** Nothing downstream is bounded by it, and a building can still be grown past it by drawing, panning and dragging walls outward.

### Verified

- **In the browser, after the fix:** a full-canvas drag at 21% zoom produced **274'-2" x 178'-10"** against a predicted 274ft x 179ft, and the app reported **280 panels** — against 66 for the equivalent drag before. The app computed weight, price, carbon, materials and fasteners for it without complaint.
- **A new sweep in `retile.test.ts`** ("tiles legally at the sizes the zoom floor now allows") runs the real tiler over 120x80, 240x160, the 274'x178'10" shape actually drawn, 400x260, 600x400, and a 600x400 shifted off the foot grid so eighths have to settle. It asserts the same `fabricationViolations` the octagon cases use: every fabricated panel within [24in, 48in], and **every wall's slots summing to its run exactly in whole eighths**. It also asserts the sweep stayed non-vacuous (widest wall > 7000in, > 1500 panels total). ⚠ `fabricationViolations` previously hardcoded the octagons' `"0"` least-accessible corner and threw on a rectangle; it now takes one, defaulting to `"0"` so every existing caller is unchanged.
- Full suite **2751 tests green**; `tsc` clean; **lint unchanged at 174 problems (126 errors, 48 warnings)**, verified by linting the committed baseline and comparing, not by recollection.

⚠ **Still open, and Tommy has not been asked:** whether the **zoom control itself** should reach 10% in sensible steps. It is still `/1.25` per click, so the floor is now **11 clicks** from 100% rather than 7. Nobody has decided that 11 clicks is acceptable, and a "fit to building" or a wheel-zoom would both answer it. **Scroll-wheel zoom does not exist** — the wheel went with the view dial on 2026-09-29 and nothing replaced it.

## What an edit actually costs — measured 2026-10-06 — and the staged tile-once plan that follows from it

Tommy asked for the tile-once work to be planned. It is planned below, but **the measurement came first and it reordered the plan**, so the measurement is here too.

### The measurement

Production build (`next build` + `next start`), one wall-height change, main-thread blocking via `PerformanceObserver('longtask')`:

| edit | 40 panels | 232 panels |
|---|---|---|
| **wall height** (moves geometry) | **724 ms** | **5,335 ms** |
| — first edit after load | 1,574 ms | 15,761 ms |
| **target density** (moves only numbers) | — | **959 ms** |

Both the 40 and 232 figures are the SECOND edit, so they are steady state and not JIT warm-up.

⚠ **The "~22ms `page.tsx` render toll" that this work was scoped around was wrong by about two orders of magnitude.** It is seconds, not milliseconds. A typical 40–100 panel job pays roughly 0.7–1.5s per edit; the 300-panel buildings Tommy wants are unusable.

### Where the time goes — a CPU profile, two runs, same answer

V8 sampling profiler at 200µs, one wall-height edit on a **272-panel** building. Self time, idle removed (~4,920 ms of real work):

| | share | what |
|---|---|---|
| **2,526 ms** | **51%** | **`toDataURL` — the Project Summary PNG readback** |
| ~838 ms | 17% | JS in the main bundle (three.js + react-three-fiber + app, mixed) |
| 573 ms | 12% | WebGL scene upload (`uniformMatrix4fv`, `bufferData`, `drawElements`…) |
| 515 ms | 10% | V8 `(program)` |
| 331 ms | 7% | garbage collector |

**`toDataURL` ran twice per edit for 2,526 ms; one single call was 2,060 ms.** The warm-up edit was worse: 2 calls, **6,958 ms** (4,982 + 1,975).

⚠ **A WRONG MEASUREMENT WAS PUBLISHED FIRST, AND THE WAY IT WAS WRONG IS WORTH KEEPING.** `toDataURL` was first hand-timed five times in a row on an **idle** canvas and reported as **15.7 ms, "0.3% of the edit — frameloop exonerated"**. Every one of those five was cheap *because the GPU had nothing queued*. During an edit the scene has just been rebuilt and `toDataURL` forces a synchronous flush, so it absorbs all the pending render work. **The same call, in two different states, differs by more than 100x.** This is the October zoom note's mistake in a new costume: a measurement taken in a state that could not show the problem, then believed. Corroboration for the corrected figure: the one edit observed where the capture did not fire blocked **1,136 ms** against 5,335 ms with it.

### What that does to the plan

- **The biggest single lever is not tile-once.** It is a PNG nobody is looking at, regenerated on the critical path of every edit.
- **Tile-once is a smaller performance win than was claimed.** App + library JS is ~17% of an edit. Tile-once is still right — it deletes an entire class of reconciliation defects — but it must be justified on **correctness**, not on speed. Saying otherwise oversold it.
- ⚠ **`frameloop` was still the right merge.** Before it the summary image was frozen at page-load state and silently wrong on every project. It traded *cheap and wrong* for *correct and slow*. Stage 0 below is the third option.

---

## The staged plan

Each stage is separately mergeable, separately reviewable, and leaves the app working. Stage 0 is **not** tile-once and should land first.

### Stage 0 — Take the summary capture off the edit path (PREREQUISITE, not tile-once)

Measured at 51% of an edit. This is Tommy's own idea, 2026-10-02: *"We could maybe add a trigger somewhere - print and release shops for a particular edit... if it makes things easier we can compute shops upon a user initiated trigger?"*

Capture when the image is actually wanted — the Summary note opening, print, PDF export — not on every scene change.

⚠ **The trap, and it is why `BuildingSummaryRender` is mounted unconditionally today:** the print and PDF paths *read* `renderImageDataUrl` and have no way to ask for one. Stage 0 must give them a way to ask and must **never silently print a stale or blank image** — a visible "generating…" beats a wrong picture, which is the standing rule in this file.

**Done when:** the 272-panel edit is measured again and the capture no longer appears in the profile. Predicted ~1.1s from the accidental zero-capture observation — **predicted, so it must be measured, not assumed.**

### Stage 1 — Name the seam (no behaviour change)

Inventory every call site of `retile`, `retilePreservingOpenings` and `retilePreservingOpeningsWithRunStopMemory` in `page.tsx`, and classify each as either **(a) a re-derivation that is legitimate** — first draw, shape change, panelization-type change — or **(b) an edit that should not re-derive anything.**

Pure inventory plus a test that asserts the classification. Nothing moves. This is what makes every later stage reviewable instead of a 12,000-line judgement call.

### Stage 2 — Stop re-deriving on edits that do not change wall length

Panel width edit, panel type cycle, brace toggle, opening add/move. Each becomes a direct mutation of the slot array.

**Each removal deletes its own reconcile counterpart**, and each is its own commit with the regression net re-run — never a batch.

### Stage 3 — Drag a panel along the wall

The core of what Tommy asked for. The swap **preserves the multiset of widths**, so wall length is conserved by the operation rather than policed by an invariant.

- **Corner panels are pinned** (his decision, 2026-10-03: "Gap free, corners stuck") — a corner panel's position is not a rule about it, its position is what it is.
- The safety gap is movable and reports an unsatisfied rule rather than being refused.
- ⚠ **The drag must not go through `page.tsx` state.** The floor for a numbers-only change is **959 ms** at 232 panels against a 16 ms frame budget — **60x over**. Use the `CompassWidget` precedent: mutate the Konva nodes / refs per frame, commit to React once on release.

### Stage 4 — Wall length change: panels enter and grow at the dragged end

Tommy's verbatim spec of 2026-10-02. Live during the drag, not a recompute on release; panels shrink and disappear on the way back. Tiny panels mid-drag are acceptable **to him, explicitly**, because the elevation boundary-drag tool is the remedy.

After this stage, this is the **only** path that creates or destroys width.

### Stage 5 — Insert, delete, and undo/redo

Undo is cheap here precisely because **the panel array IS the document** — an undo restores a previous array rather than unpicking a derivation. ⚠ Open: per-gesture vs per-frame granularity; a drag that grows panels sixty times a second must not push sixty entries.

### Stage 6 — Retire the reconcile machinery

`lockedWidthIn` re-forcing, opening re-anchoring by ordinal, run-stop opening memory. **Only** once nothing re-tiles. Every deletion must show the test that covered it either still passing or deliberately removed with a reason.

### What stays re-derived, permanently

First draw, shape change (bump-out, octagon, ring), and panelization-type change. Those are re-derivations by definition and tile-once does not touch them.

### ⚠ The largest risk, named

**The regression net is built around re-tiling.** The six browser harnesses and much of `retile.test.ts` assert post-re-tile outcomes. They will need rewriting stage by stage, and a harness rewritten in the same commit as the behaviour it guards is not a guard. Rewrite the assertion first, watch it fail, then change the behaviour.

### Answered by Tommy, 2026-10-06

**1. Deleting a panel — a button, and a refusal with a reason.** His words: *"Maybe it's a button and you cannot delete a panel if the other panels cannot expand you meet that panels dissapeerence based on whatever each panels maximum widths are. Delete panel should be next to stop wall tool on elevation and plan editors."*

- **It is a button**, placed **next to the stop-wall tool, in BOTH the elevation and plan editors.**
- **The rule:** a panel of width `w` may be deleted only if the wall's other **adjustable** panels can absorb `w` without any of them exceeding its maximum. Concretely, delete is allowed iff `Σ(maxWidthIn − currentWidthIn)` over the adjustable slots `>= w`. Corner panels, safety gaps and opening slots are not adjustable and contribute nothing.
- **Otherwise refuse, and name what is in the way** — the same shape as the locked-width refusal (Stage 1x) and the run-stop refusal. This keeps the standing invariant: **a delete never changes the wall's length.**
- ⚠ **Distribution must follow `repairWallToEighths`' discipline** — whole eighths, round-robin over adjustable slots, never forcing residual into a fixed-width slot. That function is the one place in the codebase that already does this correctly; do not write a second one.
- ⚠ The 48in ceiling and the 24in floor interact here: absorbing `w` must not push a neighbour over 48in, and the delete must not be offered in a way that strands a sub-24in panel.

**2. Undo granularity — he delegated it with a number.** His words: *"whatever is a good balance of user friendly and computing power. 6 times a second?"*

⚠ **Recommendation, and it splits his number off the undo stack: 6/sec is right, but for a different thing.**

- **The undo stack gets ONE entry per gesture** (mousedown → mouseup). This is what CAD and design tools do and what a user means by "undo that drag". At 6 entries/sec a three-second drag would need **eighteen** undos to put back, which is the opposite of user-friendly.
- **~6/sec is the right rate for the LIVE COMMIT during a drag** — how often the dragged state is pushed into React and the derived numbers re-run, between the per-frame visual updates that bypass React entirely. That is the "computing power" half of his sentence, and it is a real budget: the floor for a numbers-only change is 959ms at 232 panels, so even 6/sec is unaffordable at that size and the live commit will have to be the cheap path only.
- Recorded as a recommendation, **not as his decision** — the gesture/frame split was not put to him in those terms.

**3. Projects drawn before tile-once — nothing to migrate.** His words: *"No one cares about any projects previously drawn in the app."* So the open question about pre-tile-once projects is **closed with no work**: they become documents as they are, and no migration, guard or version bump is owed. Consistent with [[no-real-users-until-november]].

**4. Fit to building — yes, build it.** His words: *"Add fit to building sounds good."* This answers the zoom-control question carried over from the 2026-10-05 zoom fix: the 0.1 floor is 11 clicks of the ÷1.25 button from 100%, and **a "fit to building" control removes the need to click there at all.** Scroll-wheel zoom still does not exist (it went with the view dial on 2026-09-29) and is not what he asked for.

⚠ **STILL UNANSWERED — he answered delete but not add:** which direction an **inserted** panel goes, and where its width comes from. Do not infer it from the delete rule; they are not symmetric (delete has width to give away, insert has to take it).

### Still open, and Tommy has not been asked

- ~~End-panel **delete** behaviour~~ — **ANSWERED 2026-10-06, see above.** Which direction **add** inserts is still open.
- **Undo depth** is still open. The per-gesture/per-frame question has a recommendation above, not a decision.
- ~~**Projects saved before tile-once**~~ — **CLOSED 2026-10-06: nothing to migrate.**
- ~~Whether the zoom control should reach its new 0.1 floor in fewer than **11 clicks**~~ — **ANSWERED 2026-10-06: build "fit to building".**

## The tile-once editing model — panelize on the first draw, then edit by hand (2026-09-30 / 2026-10-02) — SPEC'D, NOTHING BUILT

**This is the largest architectural decision in the project so far.** It does not add a feature; it removes a class of behaviour. Today every wall edit anywhere in the building re-runs the tiler over every wall (`retile.ts`), and every mechanism that preserves user intent does it by *anchor + reconcile* across that re-tile — `lockedWidthIn` re-forced by `reconcileBracedPlacement`, openings re-anchored by ordinal out of `oldSlots`, run-stop openings withheld and remembered. Tile-once says: **tile once, on the first draw, and after that the user moves panels rather than the tiler re-deriving them.**

**Interview provenance.** Taken across 2026-09-30 to 2026-10-02. Some of what follows is Tommy's own wording and is quoted with its date. The rest is **options written for him that he selected from**, and those are recorded as *"he chose X"*, with what he chose it **over** — the rejected option is often the most informative part of the record. ⚠ **Nothing in this section is attributed to him as a quotation unless it is one.** The staged build plan is deliberately **not** in this section; it is owned separately.

### His words, verbatim, because they are the provenance

**The origin, 2026-09-30:**

> *"For retiling.... I don't want to have to make a bunch of rules and such for what moves there with retiling. Would it make it simpler if we only panelized/tiled upon the first drawing of either a rectangle/square or octagon? Like once the shape is drawn and auto populated, I want the user to be able to drag a panel down the line, switching it's place with each panel it passes. I want that then to be able to cycle through to change each panel type. And also add beans and such and all the other tools. I think this retiling business doesn't need to happen after the first draw."*

**The drag, 2026-09-30:**

> *"when a user drags the east side of a square building making it bigger, it auto populates standard panels that enter and grow with the drag. When that side is dragged back, each of those latest panels shrinks and disappears. This will make some tiny panels as the drag is marked, and I think this is okay because there should be a drag tool on the elevation editor that allows one to drag the side of a panel and shrink/grow the one next to it and it only effects those two. You can't drag the last side on any run because thats the end of the wall. You can also delete panels and add panels — but yeah let's have a hefty interview sesh about that when that's up."*

**Part-width panels on release, 2026-10-01**, answering whether a leftover absorbs into its neighbour:

> *"2 but perhaps with thresholds. There might be some adding panels and divide by 2 if it wants to build a 4ft+ absorbion"*

**A window inside the part a shrink removes, 2026-10-02:**

> *"It shortens the width of the RO, header, and sill and those shrink with the drag. This happens until it's less than 1' in which case the RO, header, and sill all 3 get replaced by 1 standard panel. That continues down to zero (even though that would make an "impossible" panel - that's okay as long as the elevation edit tools can allow the user to fix it)."*

**On shop drawings following panel changes, 2026-10-02:**

> *"Shop drawings should adjust as the panel gets smaller for sure. There should be the case for any panel right? Say you're growing the wall and growing a standard panel - wouldn't those shops change?"*

### The model, stated

1. **A wall is tiled exactly once** — when its shape is first drawn (rectangle, square, octagon), by today's tiler, under today's rules: corner ownership, the two-tier safety gap, the gap-end rule, brace derivation, absorb-or-split.
2. **After that the wall's panel array is the document.** Panels are moved, cycled, inserted, deleted, resized and opened up by hand. The tiler is not re-run on that wall.
3. **Three kinds of change still reach a tiled wall**, and each has a named rule rather than a re-tile: a **length change** (panels enter and grow, or shrink and disappear, at one end), a **swap** (a dragged panel trades places with each panel it passes), and a **boundary drag** (one panel grows, the one next to it shrinks, nobody else moves).
4. **Two parts remain rule-placed and therefore keep moving by themselves:** the corner panels and the safety gap. Everything else is the user's.
5. **Where a rule can no longer be satisfied, the Review Log says so** instead of the tiler silently fixing it. That is the trade at the centre of this model: *rules become reports.*

### The property that makes it work, and why it is worth more than an invariant

The guarantee this whole app is built around is `Σ(slot.widthIn) === wallFabricationLengthIn(wall)`, exactly, in whole eighths (see "Dimensional Precision — the 1/8in grid"). Today that guarantee is **policed**: it is asserted across eight-plus functions, re-proved on every pass by a `bracedPlacement.test.ts` **790,440-case product sweep**, a `lockedWidthReforce.test.ts` **684,360-case** sweep, and two committed `tiling.test.ts` digests over 169,736 and 254,604 configurations.

**A swap does not need policing.** Exchanging two adjacent panels permutes the slot array and **preserves the multiset of widths**, so the sum is conserved *by the nature of the operation* — there is no arithmetic to get wrong, no residual to settle, nothing to distribute. The same is true of the type cycle (a type change at a fixed width) and of the boundary drag, which the grid section already specifies as conserving by construction: *"snap the boundary position, then `leftWidthIn = boundary − pairStart` and `rightWidthIn = pairEnd − boundary`. The pair total is untouched."*

**Honest about what this does NOT remove.** Three operations still do real arithmetic and still need the invariant and the sweeps: the **first draw**, the **length change** (a panel is born, grows, shrinks or dies — the only path where width is created or destroyed), and **insert/delete**. Tile-once shrinks the surface the invariant has to be defended across; it does not retire it.

### The evidence: every defect fought on 2026-09-29/30 lived in a re-tile path

Not an argument from taste. Six defects, measured and written up in this document, one address:

1. **Openings lost when a wall shortened.** Tommy's own report — *"whenever i stop wall over a certain amount, for one wall this boundary was 174\", it says that the panel wall doesnt add up"*. Cause: `retileWithOpenings` reserves every opening at full width because an `OpeningAnchor` carries an **ordinal** and nothing says where along the wall the opening sits. Fixed over four review rounds with a withheld-opening memory.
2. **Two openings permanently SWAPPED** by that fix's first version — a door where a window was. Cause: the remembered opening kept its long-run ordinal while the survivor was re-derived against the shortened run, so the two halves of one list were in different coordinate systems. **116 of 533 start stops came back swapped.**
3. **Hand-set widths silently reverted.** A `lockedWidthIn` pin is lost to a run stop and does **not** come back when the stop is cleared, because `reconcileBracedPlacement` maps old markers onto the new run by ordinal from index 0 and a start stop removes slots from the left. Measured on the 360in fixture with a 120in start stop.
4. **Hand-placed panels lost.** A wall went into a stop with **17** panels and came back from clearing it with **16** — length still exact to the eighth.
5. **Braces moving on walls nobody touched.** `planLockedWidthReforce` has to be a **fixpoint** precisely because `retile.ts` runs it over every wall on any edit anywhere, and *"a refused pin that became payable on a second pass would move a wall with no user action at all. That is the same defect the corner-brace combine was fixed for on 2026-09-29."*
6. **Slot indices sliding under spanning headers.** A header's stored coverage is a **base** slot-index range while the elevation, the sheets, the price, the 3D anchor and the Review Log all measure from `overlayWallSlots`, and `applyUniformPanelization` re-tiles each infill run so the two arrays do not share indices. Pre-existing, recorded, unfixed.
7. **A window from a deleted building reappeared on a new one.** `handleDraw` reset the run stops and the second story and did not reset `unbuiltOpeningsByStoryAndWallId`; wall ids are reused (`buildRectangleFootprint` always emits "AB".."DA"), and **no stop was needed to cash it in** — measured as 0 openings on AB after the draw and **1 after one re-tile**.

**What the list has in common is not "the tiler is buggy".** Every one of these is a *reconciliation* defect: the tiler's output was correct each time, and the loss happened in the machinery that tries to carry the user's intent across a re-derivation. Tile-once deletes the re-derivation, so there is nothing to carry intent across.

### The decisions — what he chose, and what he chose it over

#### 1. Bracing: derived once, never again

He chose **"Never — I place them."** New panels arrive as plain `standard`; he cycles them to braced himself; the Review Log flags a spacing gap for an engineer. **Chosen over** *"only new panels get braced by the rule"* and *"re-derive the whole wall."*

- **What it implies for the code:** brace **derivation** (the seismic spacing walk, two per corner, one per side of each window) becomes a first-draw-only operation. `applyBracedPlacement` stops running on edits. ⚠ **`reconcileBracedPlacement` is not the same thing and must not be deleted with it** — it also re-forces `lockedWidthIn` and serves the corner-brace combine, which are different customers.
- **It is the flags convention's own answer, which is worth stating because it is a coincidence worth keeping.** `seismicBracedPanelSpacingFt` and `bracedWallLineSpacingFt` are both `pending-BI-confirmation`. Under tile-once the app stops silently *applying* a provisional spacing rule to parts and starts *reporting* against it — strictly more honest, and exactly what the `status` convention exists for.
- ⚠ **Any new brace-spacing Review Log walk inherits a known under-count.** See `## Open Items`, **"Does a COMBINED safety-gap+brace slot count as bracing, and should `PanelInstance` carry `secondaryType`?"** — a combined slot is a real brace on the bench and arrives as a plain `safety-gap` with no `bracedPattern`, so a spacing walk counting `panelType === "braced"` will report gaps where braces physically exist.

#### 2. The end assembly: corner and gap follow the moving end, the brace does not

He chose **"Corner and gap, not the brace."** On an outward drag the corner panel and the safety gap travel with the moving end and new panels fill in behind them; the braced panel stays where it is. A corner left with no brace touching it is named in the Review Log. **Chosen over** *"all three follow"* and *"only the corner follows."*

- **Neither half of "follow" is new machinery.** The corner is positional by rule already (`cornerOwnership`, `retile.ts`), and so is the gap (`computeGapEnd`'s least-accessible rule, `computeSafetyEnd`'s left-seen-from-outside rule for mitered shapes, plus gap-second-to-last). What is new is that the brace **does not** follow, which is decision 1 restated at the wall end.
- **The corner-no-brace report has a precedent to copy rather than invent:** the corner-brace Review Log entry built 2026-09-30 and `cornerBraceCombineRefusals.ts`.

#### 3. Growth end: the end being dragged

He chose **"The end you're dragging."** **Chosen over** *"always the end furthest from the point of least accessibility"* — i.e. over reusing the safety gap's own placement rule.

- **Consequence, stated because the two rules now disagree on purpose:** growth end and gap end are decided by different rules, so new panels arrive beside the gap when the user grabs the gap end and at the far end otherwise. Combined with decision 2, dragging the gap end moves the gap outward and inserts the new panels behind it.

#### 4. Panel reordering: everything, including the gap

He chose **"Everything, including the gap."** A dragged panel can swap past windows, doors and the safety gap; only the wall ends stop it. A safety gap that ends up away from second-to-last is flagged in the Review Log. **Chosen over** *"only plain panels"* and *"anything except corners and gap."*

- **The rejected options are the record here:** he declined to exempt the safety gap from being pushed around by hand, which is the first decision in this project that lets a user override a positional rule rather than a width.
- **This is the decision the conservation property rests on.** His *"switching it's place with each panel it passes"* is an adjacent transposition, which is why the multiset of widths — and therefore the wall length — is conserved with no arithmetic at all.
- ⚠ **REFINED 2026-10-03, and this closes the ambiguity in the sentence above.** "Only the wall ends stop it" did not say what happens to a **corner panel**, which sits exactly at those ends. Put to him directly, he chose **"Gap free, corners stuck"** — **chosen over** *"corners movable, converting to a standard panel as they leave the corner"* and over his own floated instinct that *"maybe its best if the corner and safety gaps are stuck to the corner."* His framing going in was *"I want to say hand tooling/moving/dragging takes priority and you can move any panel around even the corners. I don't know if that's going to conflict with anything - like then dragging a wall around"* — **he was right that it conflicts, and the conflict is decision 2.**
- **The two parts are not the same kind of thing, and that is the whole answer.** A safety gap is a flat ¾ in (or ½ in) sheet of plywood, panel-depth and full height: its position is a **rule** (second-to-last, away from the least-accessible corner), so moving it leaves a perfectly real part with an unsatisfied rule — reportable, not impossible. A **corner panel turns the corner**: it carries a return leg onto the adjoining wall, which is why it prices with an extra edge (see "Corner panel edge pricing"). Its position is not a rule *about* it — **its position is what it is.** Dragged mid-run it would be an L-shape jutting into the room.
- **The conflict he sensed, named precisely:** decision 2 has the corner panel **follow the moving end** on a wall drag. A corner panel parked mid-run leaves that decision with no referent — nothing at the end to follow. So corners-stuck is not a restriction bolted on; it is what makes decision 2 coherent.
- **Hand tooling still takes priority everywhere it physically can**, which is what he asked for: the gap, every standard, every braced panel, every opening. The one exception is the one part whose geometry is its location.
- **It partially answers an existing Open Item.** See `## Open Items`, **"Corner and safety-gap are still not hand-placeable"**, whose stated blocker was *"a decision about what happens when the gap-end rule and a hand-placed gap disagree."* His answer: the hand placement stands and the disagreement is reported. That item is updated rather than closed — it also asks about hand-*placing* a gap, which is a different gesture from swapping the one that exists.

#### 5. Changing the standard panel width after drawing: leave existing walls alone

He chose **"Leave existing walls alone."** The setting affects only walls tiled from then on, and a project may legitimately hold mixed standard widths, noted in the Review Log. **Chosen over** *"re-tile everything with a warning"* and *"lock it after the first draw."*

- **Why this is consistent with decision 6 rather than in tension with it — the distinction is the sentence that matters:** the standard width is a **preference about how future tiling is done**. It changes no existing part. So nothing changes. Wall thickness changes **what a corner panel IS**. So the corner panels change. Both answers are the same model applied to two different kinds of setting.
- Unaffected and still required, and **it is not an Open Item** — it is the instruction under "Three neighbours in `data.ts`" in the minimum-panel-width section: *"⚠ The Standard width project setting must be floored at 24in too"*, since a 20in setting makes every plain panel it tiles unbuildable. Tile-once makes that stricter rather than looser: a wall tiled at a bad setting is now **kept**, not corrected by the next edit.

#### 6. Changing wall thickness or panelization type: treat it as a LENGTH change — **SETTLED 2026-10-02, and he changed his mind to get here**

⚠ **Record of how this answer was reached, because the first answer is on the record too.** Offered three options — re-tile the building with a warning, leave existing walls alone, lock it after the first draw — he first chose **re-tile**. The question was then re-opened on 2026-10-02 with a fourth option that had not been offered, and **he chose the fourth**: *treat a thickness or panelization-type change as a length change.* So the record is: chosen over all three of re-tile, leave-alone and lock, and chosen **after** reversing his own earlier "re-tile".

**What it means.** The corner panels resize, because they are rule-placed and a thicker wall's corner genuinely is a different part — a 14in wall's corner is not the same part as a 15¾in wall's. (⚠ The interview framed this as *"a 14in wall's corner is a different part from an 18in wall's"*; **18in is not one of this app's thickness options** — they are 14in, 15½in and 15¾in — so the illustration is restated against the real set. The point is unaffected.) Resizing the corners shortens the panelized **run** even though the footprint has not moved. From there **nothing new happens at all**: the already-specified length-change behaviour takes over. Panels disappear from the end as if the wall had been dragged in, and every other panel keeps its width, its type and its place.

- ⚠ **It is the only one of the four options that preserves hand work through a thickness change.** Re-tile discards it, lock forbids the change, leave-alone keeps a corner part that is physically wrong for the wall it sits in.
- **It removes an inconsistency this section would otherwise have had to defend.** Under "re-tile", the model would have said *standard width leaves walls alone but thickness re-tiles the building*, and that pairing needed an argument. It no longer needs one — see the distinction written out under decision 5. Both are ordinary consequences of one model: a setting that changes no part changes nothing, and a setting that changes a part changes that part.
- **Panelization type carries one consequence thickness does not, and it needs naming rather than deciding.** Switching to Square Bale moves the corner panel to **39in**, which shortens the run further *and* moves the refusal band — `findSquareBaleBandWalls` and the **78in–102½in** two-corner band, plus the merged-corner refusal over 48in. **So a wall that is legal today can become one the panelization control refuses.** That is a real outcome of this choice, it needs no decision from him, and it belongs in the Review Log rather than being discovered at the control. Listed in this section's Open Items as a surface, not a question.

#### 7. Second storey: length follows, layout does not

He chose **"Length follows, layout doesn't."** A storey above always spans the same length as the wall below — panels enter and disappear at its dragged end as the ground floor's do — but its panel types, widths and order stay independent. **Chosen over** *"tiled once, then fully independent"*, explicitly so that the two floors cannot disagree about how long a wall is.

- **Per-story slot arrays already exist** (per-story editing shipped 2026-07-21, and `wallSlotsForStory` / `secondStorySlotBoxes` are live), so "independent layout" is the state model the app already has. What the decision adds is a **coupling on length only**.
- **Implication:** a drag applies the enter/shrink rule **twice**, once per storey, each against that storey's own end panel — because the two layouts differ, the panel that grows upstairs is not the panel that grows downstairs.

#### 8. Bump-outs: the three new walls tile fresh, and both surviving stubs re-tile

He chose **"New walls and both stubs."** Each stub is now a different length with different corner ownership, so both re-tile. **He accepted that this discards hand-set panels on that wall.** **Chosen over** *"only the new walls"* and *"ask me at the time."*

- ⚠ **This is the only place in the whole model where he accepts a re-tile that destroys hand work.** Stated plainly so nobody generalises from it.
- **It is also the one decision where the model and the existing code already agree**, which is why it is cheap: `insertBumpOut` renumbers every wall id, and this document already records that *"a wall with no old counterpart loses its memory entirely… there is no basis left to measure a remembered opening's position against."* His answer converts a recorded, reluctant data loss into specified behaviour.
- **Not settled, and he was not asked:** whether the gesture announces the discard before taking it. The house precedent is the per-wall re-panelize confirm that names the count — *"This clears 9 hand-set widths on wall E."*

#### 9. Deleting a panel: split the width between both neighbours

He chose **"Split between both neighbours."** The deleted width is halved between the panels either side, each staying inside [24in, 48in]; adding a panel takes width back the same way. **Chosen over** *"spread across the whole run"* and *"one neighbour absorbs it."*

- ⚠ **This changes behaviour that is already built.** Smearforn Stage 2's `panelPlacement.ts` does exactly the rejected option: `redistributeFreeRun` re-tiles the whole free run flat with `distributeEighths`, *"so no two automatic panels differ by more than 1/8in."* His answer is a narrower, more local rule. **A correction to the brief this section was written from:** the whole-run option as built reuses `distributeEighths` via `redistributeFreeRun`, **not** `settleResidualEighths` — the latter is the residual-settling machinery used by the corner-brace combine and the locked-width re-force, and it walks a candidate list in order rather than levelling a run.
- **It bears directly on an existing Open Item.** See `## Open Items`, **"Should the free run re-tile flat after a hand edit?"** — which records that a hand-edited wall currently comes out flat where a tiler-laid wall has full-width panels plus one absorber. His answer removes the flattening from the delete and insert paths specifically. It does not speak to the other paths, so that item stays open and narrows.
- **The [24in, 48in] clamp implies a refusal path he was not asked about.** Two neighbours at 40in cannot absorb 24in between them without one passing 48in. The app has the pattern for it (`placementRefusalNotice`, and the Stage 2 notice that names what it gave up); what it does not have is his decision on whether such a delete is refused or falls back to reaching further along the run.

### What re-tiles, and what does not — the whole surface in one list

| gesture | under tile-once |
|---|---|
| First draw of a rectangle / square / octagon | **tiles** — the one and only tiling of that wall |
| Drag a wall end out or in | **length change** — panels enter/grow or shrink/disappear at the dragged end (decisions 2, 3) |
| Type a wall length | same length-change rule (**open:** which end, since nothing was dragged) |
| Drag a panel along the wall | **swap** with each panel it passes; wall ends stop it (decision 4) |
| Cycle a panel's type | type change at a fixed width; nothing else moves |
| Drag a panel boundary | the pair only, conserving by construction |
| Insert / delete a panel | halve from, or give back to, both neighbours (decision 9) |
| Change the standard panel width | **nothing on existing walls** (decision 5) |
| Change wall thickness or panelization type | corners resize → **run shortens → length-change rule** (decision 6) |
| Insert a bump-out | **three new walls tile fresh, both stubs re-tile** — the one destructive case (decision 8) |
| Second storey, any of the above | length follows the wall below; layout does not (decision 7) |
| Open a project saved before tile-once | **open — see this section's Open Items** |

### Reuse, not reinvention

**His part-width answer is the tiler's existing absorb-or-split rule.** *"2 but perhaps with thresholds. There might be some adding panels and divide by 2 if it wants to build a 4ft+ absorbion"* describes `computePlainSizing`'s decision of 2026-09-24 almost exactly: where a two-way split would put either part under 24in, do not split — emit one panel of `standard + remainder` instead; and where the absorb would exceed 48in, split. His "4ft+" is the 48in ceiling, by name.

⚠ **And it works with zero margin, for a reason worth keeping in front of whoever implements the drag.** Splitting is legal iff `S + r ≥ 2 × 24in = 48in`; absorbing is legal iff `S + r ≤ 48in`. **The two conditions are exactly complementary — they overlap only at 48in precisely — so every case has a legal answer, and only because `maxIn` is exactly twice `minIn`.** Move either number and a band of lengths becomes genuinely untileable. The coupling is asserted in two places so it fails loudly: `apps/web/app/tilerFabricationLimits.test.ts` (*"the coupling the absorb policy rests on still holds on the tiler's own copies"*, `expect(TILER_MAX_PANEL_WIDTH_IN).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(2 * TILER_MIN_PANEL_WIDTH_IN)`) and `data.test.ts` against the catalog pair.

**`settleResidualEighths` is the existing machinery for spreading a residual inside [24in, 48in]**, just extracted into its own module (`packages/geometry/src/settleResidualEighths.ts`, 2026-09-30, a verbatim move out of `bracedPlacement.ts`). It settles a signed residual over an ordered candidate list, returns `null` rather than approximating when it cannot reach exactly zero, and deliberately takes the **tiler's** bounds rather than a parameter. Two live customers (`planCornerBraceCombine`, `planLockedWidthReforce`) and the plan-then-commit shape both of them use is the precedent any new width-moving operation should copy rather than re-derive.

**Other machinery this model should consume rather than reinvent:** `OpeningAnchor`'s ordinal model (a swap is an ordinal exchange, which is what that model already represents); `lockedWidthIn` and its "absent = automatic, present = the user decided" convention, which `PanelSlot` already carries on `heightIn`, `sillHeightIn`, `bracedPattern`, `zones` and `secondaryType`; `distributeEighths` and `repairWallToEighths`; and `PLACEABLE_PANEL_TYPES` / `nextPanelCycleState` for the type cycle.

### The 1ft opening collapse — the one real-world number in this pass

From his own sentence of 2026-10-02, with a unit: as a shrink eats the part of the wall a window sits in, **the rough opening, header and sill shorten with the drag until the opening is under 1ft, at which point all three are replaced by one standard panel**, and that panel keeps shrinking to zero.

- **Status `confirmed`**, on the same grounds `fabricationMinPanelWidthIn` (24in) is: a first-hand Building Integrity statement with a number and a unit, recording rather than interpreting. **The note must quote his sentence**, including *"that's okay as long as the elevation edit tools can allow the user to fix it"*, because the tolerance for an impossible panel is part of the decision and not a side effect. **If an implementer finds themselves reasoning about what he meant, that is the signal to downgrade it** — flags-check point 2 exists for that moment.
- **Name it for what it is** — the width below which an opening collapses to a plain panel. **Do not name it anything that reads as a twin of `fabricationMinPanelWidthIn` or `panelWidthInRange.minIn`**; two similarly-named minimums are how the wrong one gets used.
- ⚠ **The derived consequence, which he accepted in the same sentence: 12in is BELOW the shop's confirmed 24in minimum, so the collapse deliberately produces a panel the shop cannot build**, and the drag continues down to a zero-width panel from there. **Nothing silently fixes it, and nothing needs to be invented to report it** — `findSubMinimumPanelWidths` already walks for panels under 24in and already has an entry in the Review Log. **This is a fourth customer for an existing Open Item:** see `## Open Items`, **"The app has no over-maximum panel reporter"** — the ceiling-side counterpart, since a boundary drag already produced a 56in panel that nothing reports.
- **No other number is introduced by this pass.** No tolerance, no snap increment, no minimum drag step, no frame budget, no new spacing and no new threshold.

### Shop drawings follow the panel — his own rule, answered with his own reasoning

> *"Shop drawings should adjust as the panel gets smaller for sure. There should be the case for any panel right? Say you're growing the wall and growing a standard panel - wouldn't those shops change?"*

Yes, and this is a statement about what already happens rather than a request: the shop fabrication sheets are grouped per unique panel and built from each instance's real dimensions, so a panel whose width changes is a different fabricated part and gets a different sheet. The relevant pre-existing consequence, already recorded, is the one he should know about: **a cut list already issued for a saved project can disagree with a fresh export of the same project**, and the answer on record is the sheet revision identity spec'd in Smearforn Stage 5 — not a change to how sheets are derived.

### Performance — the real risk, and it is an open design question, not a plan

A tile-once drag is a **per-frame** operation on a wall's panel rectangles, and the derivation chain hanging off wall slots is long: slots → panel instances → member geometry → cut lists → fabrication groups → plywood areas → board feet → weights → Review Log → 3D boxes.

**Measured on `main` @ `10fe6ea`, not estimated:**

- `apps/web/app/page.tsx` is **12,423 lines** and contains **100 `useMemo(`** calls.
- **`react-hooks/preserve-manual-memoization` stands at 68** — the React Compiler reporting memoization it **cannot** preserve — per the corner-ownership pass's own gate record (67 → 68 on its review-fix pass). ⚠ **Stated as that record states it: 68 is the count across `apps/web`, and `page.tsx` is where it is saturated** (that gate localised the +1 to `page.tsx` by linting the base and current versions side by side). Not re-measured by this pass; if the figure matters to a decision, re-run the gate rather than quoting this line.
- ESLint needs `--max-old-space-size=4096` on that file; it OOMs at 2GB (`apps/web/AGENTS.md`).
- **138 lines in `page.tsx` reference the wall-slot arrays** (`slotsByWallId` / `wallSlots` / `WallSlots`). ⚠ The interview brief gave 95 on a narrower pattern; both are the same finding — the slot arrays are read from everywhere in that file — and the number is recorded as measured rather than as handed over.

**The precedent for the shape of the fix already exists in this app.** `CompassWidget` forwards a ref to its rotating inner face and `Building3DView` sets `style.transform` on it imperatively — *"not React state, so it can track the orbit camera every frame without triggering a re-render"*. The analogous shape here is **update the panel rectangles live and defer the fabrication derivation to pointer release**.

⚠ **Recorded as the open question it is. This has NOT been profiled, and Tommy has been told so.** Nobody has measured one frame of that chain, so "defer to release" is a plausible shape rather than a decided design, and the honest position is that the cost is unknown. See this section's Open Items.

### Flags check — the 6-point check, run against this spec

1. **Does every real-world number carry a `status` and a `note`?** There is **one** real-world number in this pass — the **1ft** opening-collapse threshold — and it is specified with a `status`, a name rule and a verbatim note above. Every other figure in this section is either an **observation of the existing code** (12,423 lines, 100 memos, 138 slot references, the 68 memoization-rule errors quoted from the corner-ownership gate rather than re-measured, 790,440 / 684,360 / 169,736 / 254,604 sweep cases, 116 of 533, 17 → 16 panels) or a number **already in the catalog** that this pass only reads: 24in, 48in, 25.5in, 39in, 144in, 3/4in, 1/2in, 78in–102½in.
2. **Anything marked `confirmed` that is actually researched or interpreted?** The 1ft threshold is correctly `confirmed` — his own sentence, a number with a unit, no interpretation. **Nothing else in this section is marked anything, because this pass invents nothing else:** no tolerance, no snap increment, no minimum drag step, no frame budget. The brace-spacing figures stay `pending-BI-confirmation` and this model makes that *more* visible, not less (decision 1).
3. **Does the note trace to a real source?** Yes — his own dated sentences, quoted. **And the evidentiary distinction is carried throughout:** five verbatim quotations with dates, versus nine selected options recorded as *"he chose X over Y and Z"*, with decision 6 additionally recording that he reversed an earlier answer. No phrasing written for the interview is attributed to him.
4. **Structural figures using `PanelStructuralStatus` with no invented value?** Nothing structural moves in either direction. **The one place this pass could have slipped is decision 1**, and it goes the safe way: removing automatic brace derivation **lowers** the bracing the app models on an edited wall, and the answer is a Review Log report rather than a shear or spacing number. No shear, bearing, load or density figure is introduced, raised or lowered.
5. **Does the value surface in the Review Log where a reviewer expects it?** Yes, and that is the load-bearing half of this model — rules become reports. Four reports are specified (brace spacing gap, a corner with no brace touching it, a safety gap away from second-to-last, mixed standard widths in one project), and the collapse's sub-minimum and zero-width panels land in the **existing** sub-minimum walk with no new machinery.
6. **Where the spec marks something open, is it treated as provisional?** Yes. Twelve questions are listed below rather than answered, the performance shape is explicitly labelled unprofiled, and the two existing Open Items this model leans on are named by title so the claim can be checked: **"Does a COMBINED safety-gap+brace slot count as bracing, and should `PanelInstance` carry `secondaryType`?"** and **"The app has no over-maximum panel reporter."**

### Open Items — the tile-once editing model

⚠ **All twelve are recorded in the top-level `## Open Items` as well — in ONE umbrella entry titled "⚠ The tile-once editing model — twelve questions left for Tommy", which names every one of them inline rather than as twelve separate bullets** (the same shape the concentric-ring and top-bar workstreams use). Said precisely because a reader checking the claim should find what the pointer describes: one titled entry, twelve named questions inside it. This is the remedy written at *"a pointer is not finished when it tells the reader where to look. It is finished when the thing it points at exists at that address under the name the pointer uses"* — the defect class this project has reintroduced four passes running. They are kept here as well because this is the section that explains them.

**From the interview — his answers do not settle these:**

- **Deleting an END panel has only one neighbour.** The preview he saw said so. Does the single neighbour take the whole width, or is the delete refused? And since corner panels and the safety gap are rule-placed: can they absorb a deleted neighbour's width at all, and can they themselves be deleted?
- **Adding a panel — is halving from both neighbours what he means in the add direction, and what width is a new panel born at?** He answered the delete; the add was framed to him as "the same question backwards". `panelPlacement.ts`'s `PlacementPanel.widthIn` already has to be supplied by the caller for an insert, so the birth width is a live parameter with no answer.
- ~~**A window narrowed by a drag no longer fits the window unit he ordered.**~~ — **CLOSED 2026-10-03 by Tommy:** *"I don't think your going be to be dead on the wall if windows are already ordered. Changing RO is fine here."* So a rough opening narrowing under a drag is **accepted behaviour, not a hazard to guard**, and nothing needs to warn about it. Recorded because the question was raised and answered rather than dropped — and note it is specifically about the RO, not about the collapse-under-1ft rule, which stands as specified.
- ~~**⚠ There is no undo in this app.**~~ — **ANSWERED 2026-10-03: UNDO AND REDO ARE IN SCOPE.** Put to him as a consequence of this model rather than as a proposal; his answer was *"An undo and redo button seems like a great idea."* **Not built, and not yet specified beyond that** — what is undoable, how deep the stack goes, and whether it survives a save are all unanswered. Recorded as accepted, not as designed.
  - **Tile-once is what makes this cheap, and the reason is worth keeping.** Under the present architecture an undo would have to reverse a **derivation** — unpick a re-tile, a brace reconcile and a locked-width re-force, then hope the result matches what the user had. Under tile-once **the panel array IS the document**, so an undo restores a previous array. That is the difference between replaying a computation and remembering a value, and it is why this moved from a large piece of work to a small one without anybody optimising anything.
  - **It is also the safety net this model specifically wants.** Decision 9's *"that's okay as long as the elevation edit tools can allow the user to fix it"* accepts reachable illegal states; the three paths that still create or destroy width (first draw, length change, insert/delete) are exactly where a mis-drag loses work. Without undo, hand reconstruction is the only recovery.

- **A project saved before tile-once — what happens on open?** **The precedent is directly on point and is a warning:** the corner-ownership change of 2026-10-01 was deliberately **not** retroactive, with no version bump and a self-clearing Review Log line instead, *"because a re-tile migration would silently discard every pinned panel width and every locked-width plan in every stored file."* Tile-once has the same property and a larger blast radius.

The measurements and the `CompassWidget` precedent are above; the design question (what updates live, what defers to release, and whether the fabrication chain can be made to not run per frame at all) is genuinely open.

- **Does the safety gap's TIER change mid-drag, and who pays the 1/4in?** The two-tier rule keys the gap's thickness to the **run** length (3/4in over 144in, 1/2in at or under), so a drag that crosses 144in changes the gap's own width by 1/4in while decision 2 says every other panel keeps its width. Something has to absorb it, and nothing says what.

Whether a corner can be passed, and what the corner panel becomes if it is no longer at the end, is not settled by the option text.
