## Concentric Wall Ring Buildings — a courtyard, and the first topology change (2026-09-25) — PLANNED, NOTHING BUILT

Tommy, 2026-09-25:

> *"I would also like to add the ability to do Concentric wall ring buildings - an octagon ring or a square/rectangle ring with an interior no-foundation courtyard. Let's plan this out when appropriate and add the editor tools and code for this when possible this weekend."*

**Sequencing — CONFIRMED by Tommy 2026-09-25: Smearforn, then admin tooling, then rings.** His words: *"I like your plan here, building and reviewing the ring plan after Smearforn and admin tooling."* So this is planned now and built after Monday 2026-09-28, and it sits behind Stage 5 admin tooling as well.

The reasoning, kept because it is the reason and not just the outcome: Smearforn exists to get the Rogers-Sehorn ADU drawn on Monday evening. A courtyard is a change to what a footprint *is*, in the same model the ADU will be drawn in, days before he draws it. Landing a topology change and a live job in the same week risks the thing he actually needs for the thing he merely wants next. **His original ask was *"this weekend"*; he moved it himself once the size was laid out.** **And the one prerequisite is already scheduled: the 51–75in corner-geometry fix goes in WITH admin tooling this weekend** (his call, 2026-09-25, accepting the recommendation below). It needs no ring topology, it fixes a defect that exists today, and it is what makes an octagon courtyard tileable — so by the time this workstream starts it is expected to be done, and it is not one of the ring stages.

### Why this is a workstream and not a feature

Every polygon in this app is **one closed ring**. That is not an incidental fact; it is the invariant Smearforn Stage 3 was deliberately designed *around* rather than through — *"the footprint polygon stays CLOSED. 'Incomplete' is a property of the panel run, never of the shape."* A courtyard building is **a polygon with a hole: two rings, an outer and an inner.** That is the first genuine topology change this codebase has been asked for.

Read as: not "an extra shape tool". The shape tools are the cheap part.

#### What actually breaks, verified in the code rather than assumed

The single distinction that organises the whole audit:

- **Anything that walks the ring by wall SUCCESSION survives untouched** — `walls.find(w => w.startCorner === wall.endCorner)`. With two rings in one flat `walls` array and globally unique corner ids, each wall finds its own ring's successor and only its own, because a corner id belongs to exactly one ring. **`cornerOwnership` keeps working. So do `wallBoxes3D`, `computeInsetPerimeterRing`, `editWallLength`, `dragWall`, `wallAxis`, `panelSlotBoxes3D`, `tileWall`/`retile`/`wallGeometryFor` and `computeRoofBearingSegments`** (that last one never sees a footprint at all — it takes a slot array). This is the load-bearing finding of the whole plan and it is what makes a staged build possible.
- **Anything that treats `footprint.corners` in ARRAY ORDER as a polygon breaks, silently and badly.** Two rings concatenated into one array produce a self-intersecting figure with two spurious bridging edges. Enumerated: `computeFootprintAreaSqFt` (`footprintArea.ts:16`), `computeFloorMembranePolygons` (`floorMembranePolygons.ts:197`, whose own comment says it follows "the same convention `computeFootprintAreaSqFt` follows"), `computePierGrid` (`pierGrid.ts:34`), `computeJoistLayout` (`joistLayout.ts:39`), `floorPanelGrid.ts`'s in-polygon test, and `wallCompassDirection`'s centroid (`wallCompassDirection.ts:29`).
- **Two functions fail QUIET rather than wrong, which is worse to diagnose.** `orderedWallCycle` (`perimeterRing.ts:148`) walks from `walls[0]` and returns `null` the moment the chain closes before covering every wall — i.e. always, with two rings. Its consumer `computeInsetFootprintPolygon` then returns `[]`, and `computeFieldFramingLayout` emits **no floor framing at all**. Nothing throws. Nothing is drawn. Nobody is told.
- **One function contaminates one ring with the other's shape.** `isMiteredShape` → `footprintIsAllRightAngles` is an `every` over **all** walls. An octagon courtyard inside a rectangular outer ring makes the *whole footprint* mitered, which flips the outer ring's gap placement from the least-accessible-corner rule to the per-wall safety-corner rule and sets `allowBorrow = false` on every outer wall. **A rectangle's panel layout would change because of the shape of its courtyard.** `isMiteredShape` has to become per-ring, or mixed-shape rings have to be refused.

### 1. Data model — a ring index on the existing arrays, not a list of rings

**Recommendation: keep one `Footprint` with flat `corners` and `walls`, and add one additive optional field that says which corner ids form which ring, in ring order.** Shape, roughly: `rings?: CornerId[][]`, `rings[0]` = outer, `rings[1..]` = holes. Absent = today's single ring, which is every project that exists.

Why this and not `Footprint { rings: Ring[] }`:

- **It is the option that keeps `cornerOwnership` and the tiler at zero surgery**, for the succession reason above. A `Ring[]` refactor touches the `Footprint` type itself — **84 occurrences of `footprint.corners`/`footprint.walls` across 18 files in `packages/geometry`, plus 80 more across 9 files in `apps/web/app`** — and every one of those is a chance to introduce a bug in code that is currently correct and shipped.
- **The break list becomes enumerable.** With a ring index, the work is: add one accessor (`footprintRingPolygons(footprint): Point[][]`, returning outer first) and move the six array-order consumers onto it. Six call sites, each individually testable, versus 164.
- **It leaves the door open to N holes** without designing for them now.

**Rejected: an `innerRing` field holding its own separate `corners`/`walls`.** The inner ring's walls would then be invisible to `retile`, `wallGeometryFor`, `panelInstances`, the elevation viewer and the 3D pipeline — every one of which would need a second traversal path. That is a second copy of the wall pipeline, and this log has rejected second copies of the pipeline twice already (Smearforn's "a second copy of the tiler that drifts from the first").

#### `PROJECT_FILE_VERSION`: no bump needed, and that is a real saving

**Stage 0's as-built note settles this: "an additive optional key does not actually need a bump in this file"** — `wallReviewNotes`, `gableWindowAnchorsByWallId` and `maxPanelHeightIn` were all added without one. What made v25 real was the **asymmetry** (off for a new project, on for an existing file). `rings` has no asymmetry: absent means one ring for a new project and for a v25 file alike, which is the correct reading in both cases.

**This matters more than it looks, because a bump is no longer free.** The database redactor classifies money paths **by schema version** (`0009`'s `browse_schema_redaction` seed), so v25 needed `supabase/migrations/0010` — a migration that, per its own as-built note, **has not been applied to the live database and was never run against any PostgreSQL at all.** A v26 would need `0011` and would inherit that same unverified posture. Do not spend a bump on a key that does not need one.

**⚠ The one hazard of not bumping, stated so it is a decision and not an oversight:** a ringed project opened by an *older* deploy would read `rings` as unknown and draw the merged corner array as a single bridged polygon — a wrong building, quietly. A bump is the only thing that makes an old deploy *refuse*. If Tommy would rather pay `0011` for that guarantee, it is his call; the default is no bump. Note `supabase/` is out of scope for this workstream either way.

### 2. Corner ownership on the inner ring — the winding decision, and what it does to the rule

The inner ring's winding is the fork the whole data model turns on. Both options were worked through against the code; there is no free one.

**`isConvexCorner` (`cornerAngle.ts:44`) is a signed cross product against a GLOBAL winding assumption** — its own comment: *"for our clockwise winding with the interior always on the right of travel."* So:

| | Inner ring wound **CW** (same as outer) | Inner ring wound **CCW** (standard hole winding) |
|---|---|---|
| `isConvexCorner` at an inner 90° corner | reads **convex** — shorter-wall-wins applies unchanged | reads **reflex** — every inner corner takes the reflex branch |
| `computeFootprintAreaSqFt` (signed shoelace per ring) | rings **add**; hole must be subtracted by hand | outer − hole falls out, if `Math.abs` moves outside the per-ring sum |
| Inward normal (`+90°` rotation — `perimeterRing`, `wallBoxes3D`, `bumpOut`'s `outwardNormal`) | points **into the courtyard**, i.e. away from the wall material — wrong, needs a per-ring sign flip in three files | points toward the outer ring, i.e. **into the wall material — correct, unchanged** |
| `isPointInPolygon` even-odd, fed both rings' edges | correct either way (even-odd is winding-agnostic) | correct either way |

**Recommendation: CCW inner ring**, because it is right in three places and wrong in one, and the one is a single function with a known fix. **`isConvexCorner` gains the ring's winding sign** (or, equivalently, a `ringWindingSign` argument defaulting to today's value) so convexity is asked per ring instead of per app. Everything downstream of it — `cornerOwnership`'s convex/reflex fork, `footprintIsAllRightAngles`, `perimeterRing`'s and `wallBoxes3D`'s reflex extensions — then reads correctly on both rings with no further change.

**⚠ What happens if nobody makes that change is worth spelling out, because it is plausible-looking and wrong.** Every inner 90° corner falls into the reflex branch, which applies `extraLengthIn = thicknessIn` to one wall and `insetAmount = 0` to the other. On a four-wall rectangular courtyard that adds **four wall thicknesses** (4 × 15.5in = 62in at the default) of tiled length that does not exist, distributed one corner at a time. It produces a legal-looking panel schedule for a courtyard 5ft too long. That belongs on the over-count audit in §4 and it is the single most dangerous line in this plan.

**With the fix, the existing rule applies to the inner ring verbatim: shorter-wall-wins at convex 90° corners, ties by wall id; both walls own their corner at a mitered corner; the merged-corner rule when a wall is too short for both.** No new corner rule is invented here and none should be.

`primaryCornerIds` (the reflex tie-break, "the original wall wins") needs a stated convention for a ring created wholesale: **every corner of a newly created inner ring is primary**, same as a freshly built rectangle's are. It only matters once an inner ring can carry a bump-out, which is out of scope until R3.

#### ⚠ The 51–75in two-corner band is a PREREQUISITE here, not a background defect

The band, restated from the Smearforn log: a wall owning corners at **both** ends spends `2 × cornerPanelWidthIn` = **51in** on them, so its middle is `L − 51`, which is under the 24in fabrication minimum for every `L` below **75in (6'3")**. Below 51in the merged-corner rule already handles it. Between 51 and 75 there is **no legal tiling** and absorb cannot reach it.

> **⚠ Both the ceiling and the derived octagon range below are written against the PRE-2026-10-01 band and have NOT been re-derived here.** The two-tier safety gap moved the ceiling to **75½in** (the middle must now hold the gap before it can hold a panel), so the band is 51⅛in–75⅜in — **195 eighth-steps, not 191**. The corner-absorb fix shipped and covers the whole new band, so nothing in this plan's conclusions changes: a 10–15ft octagon courtyard is still the normal case and still tileable. What is *not* re-derived is the exact `10.26ft – 15.09ft` bracket, which moves out by a hair at the top; whoever builds R4 should take the band from "The 51in–75½in two-corner dead band — CORNER ABSORB" rather than from this paragraph, and not re-derive a building range from a number recorded for a different purpose. Tommy met this once and deferred it: *"I want to prioritize good building principles here with the panelizer. I like the corner geometry rule… Let's flag this and return to it after admin tooling."*

**An inner ring is exactly where short walls live, and for an octagon courtyard the band is not an edge case — it is the normal case.** `buildOctagonFootprint` gives every side length `0.41421 × boxDimension` (a regular octagon's side is `S(√2−1)` of its bounding box). So:

- **box under 10.26ft** → every wall under 51in → every wall is a single **merged corner panel**, eight of them, no middle panel anywhere. Legal, and a strange thing to hand a shop.
- **box 10.26ft – 15.09ft** → **every one of the eight walls lands in the dead band.** Not one wall: all eight.
- **box 15.09ft and up** → legal.

A courtyard between ten and fifteen feet across is an entirely ordinary courtyard. **So: the corner-geometry fix is a prerequisite for the octagon ring stage (R4), and a strong recommendation before the rectangle ring stage (R1).** It is also, separately, a live defect on small octagons *today*, with no ring topology involved — which makes it the one piece of this workstream worth building early on its own merits (see "What could be delivered early").

`cornerPanelWidthIn` (25.5in, `confirmed`) and `fabricationMinPanelWidthIn` (24in, `confirmed`) behave identically on an inner ring — they are per-wall constants and know nothing about rings. **Nothing about the inner ring changes either number, and neither should be touched by this workstream.**

Note `buildRectangleFootprint`'s `MIN_DIMENSION_FT = 8` clamp (96in) is what keeps a *rectangle* out of the band entirely today. An inner ring created by offset does not go through that builder and inherits no such protection — see §8.

### 3. Which face is exterior on the inner ring? — **DECIDED 2026-09-25 by Tommy: THE COURTYARD FACE IS EXTERIOR**

The courtyard side of the inner ring is weather-exposed, and Tommy has decided it carries the **exterior** assembly. **Independently confirmed by his roof answer** (§5): both roof forms he wants leave *"a totally exposed to the open sky courtyard"*, so there is no roofed-courtyard case that could have made the courtyard face a sheltered interior. The two questions were entangled and are now both closed in the same direction.

**⚠ The app would have reached this answer by accident, and that is still worth fixing.** `wallCompassDirection` picks a wall's exterior face using a **vertex-averaged centroid** of `footprint.corners` (`:29-34`) — the same heuristic this log already condemned and deleted in `bumpOut.ts`, `perimeterRing.ts` and `wallBoxes3D.ts`. With both rings in one corner array the centroid sits inside the courtyard, so every inner-ring wall's exterior face comes out pointing into the courtyard. **It happens to agree with Tommy. It is still not a defensible way to arrive there** — it agrees by an accident of vertex counts, it would disagree on an off-centre courtyard in a notched outer ring, and a correct answer produced by a broken mechanism is a bug that passes its own test. The per-ring fix in R0 stands: **direction naming is per-ring, and the inner ring's named face points into its own hole.**

#### ⚠ What this makes real: interior and exterior plaster areas stop being equal — a REQUIREMENT of R1

`plasterGrossWallAreaSqFt` today is `stories.reduce(... totalWallPerimeterIn / 12 * wallHeightFt)` (`page.tsx:3947`), and the single resulting `plasterNetAreaSqFt` is passed **twice** — once as the interior (clay) area and once as the exterior (lime) area (`page.tsx:3992-4004`). **That identity has held for the entire life of this app and is about to stop holding.** With the courtyard face exterior:

- **The inner ring contributes its courtyard face to the EXTERIOR area and its building-side face to the INTERIOR area** — so it contributes one of each, exactly like an outer-ring wall does. **The totals still come out equal for a plain ring.** Say that plainly, because it is the trap: the *arithmetic* happens to stay symmetric, so a naive implementation looks right and nobody notices the model is wrong.
- **They diverge the moment anything is asymmetric**, which on a ring building is routine, not exotic: a `WallRunStop` on an inner-ring wall (§7 — the courtyard opening, which is the *expected* case), different wall heights between rings, or a future assembly that differs by ring. Once the two figures can differ, computing one number and passing it twice is a silent error rather than a shortcut.
- **So the requirement is structural, not numeric: `plasterNetAreaSqFt` must become a per-face pair** — an interior area and an exterior area derived independently, each summing the faces that actually carry that assembly — **even where the two currently come out equal.** Building it as one number with a comment saying "these are equal today" is how it ships wrong later.
- **Where it lands:** `plasterSideResults`, `plasterLaborHoursPerSide`, `plasterActiveSideCount` and the Plaster Master's printed take-offs all read the single figure today. **This is a change to the Plaster Master's shape, not a coefficient**, and it is why this is an R1 requirement rather than a follow-up.
- **⚠ No price, ratio, coverage rate or labor figure changes.** Every dollar and every mix ratio in `plasterPriceDefaults` / `plasterMixPartsDefaults` stays exactly where it is, including the ones already flagged `pending-BI-confirmation` because the source spreadsheet carried no pricing. **This decision changes which area a confirmed formula is applied to. It introduces no new real-world value and must not be used as an occasion to touch one.**

**Two smaller consequences:**

- **Intello membrane** (`intelloWallRuns`, `page.tsx:3963`) runs on the interior face, so the inner ring's membrane run is on its **building side** — the opposite hand from the outer ring's, wrapping the annulus rather than the building. `computeMembraneCoverage` takes runs of `{lengthFt, heightFt}` with no side concept, so the **quantity is unaffected**; the *detailing* — which face, and how the inner ring's membrane ties into the outer ring's to close the air barrier around the annulus — **is not modelled by this app and is not invented here.** It is a real continuity detail, a close cousin of the floor-to-wall vapor continuity detail already sitting unbuilt in Open Items.
- **The elevation's interior-face drawings.** With a ring there are two interior faces looking at each other across the annulus, and an inner-ring wall drawn "from inside" is drawn from the room, not from the courtyard. The adjacent-wall filler resolves by wall succession and is ring-safe; the *label* is what gets ambiguous, and §7's UI-only ring label ("courtyard" / "exterior") is what fixes it.

#### The audit consequence

**Item 10 of §4 is now a live requirement rather than a note.** An inner ring whose two faces carry different assemblies is a different area calculation from anything the app has done, and the two-ring fixture must assert the interior and exterior areas **separately** — including a case where they genuinely differ (a `WallRunStop` on one inner wall), so that a single-number implementation fails the test instead of passing it by symmetry.

### 4. The no-foundation courtyard — the over-count audit

Tommy said the courtyard has **no foundation**. So the hole must be excluded from every plan-area and in-polygon computation. **Stage 3's audit of wall-length-derived totals found six real over-counts, one of which cut a real part wrong. This is the same audit, on the area axis, and it is an acceptance criterion of the topology stage — not a follow-up.**

Everything that would be wrong if the hole were ignored, with what it costs:

| # | Thing | What goes wrong | What it costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `computeFootprintAreaSqFt` | array-order shoelace over a bridged two-ring corner list — not merely over-counted, **garbage** | feeds 2 and 3 below |
| 2 | `intelloRoofAreaSqFt` (`page.tsx:3969`) | Intello roll quantity off the wrong plan area | material quantity, cost |
| 3 | `plasterFloorBottomAreaSqFt` (`page.tsx:3990`) | steel/clay bottom-skin area → `steelMeshCost` **and** `computePlasterCoatResult` for the floor bottom | **real dollars and real material volumes** |
| 4 | `computePierGrid` | piers placed inside the courtyard, where there is no foundation | pier count, cost, and a drawing showing piers under open ground |
| 5 | `computeJoistLayout` | joists spanning the courtyard (already known to over-run on L/U/octagon — the last bounding-box overhang in the Open Items) | board count, BOM |
| 6 | `floorPanelGrid` | floor panels generated over the hole | **panel count, area, weight, price, cut list** |
| 7 | `computeFloorMembranePolygons` | membrane/bottom-skin polygon covers the hole | area, and a visibly wrong 3D skin |
| 8 | `computeInsetFootprintPolygon` → `computeFieldFramingLayout` | `orderedWallCycle` returns `null` → **no floor framing emitted at all** | silent under-count; the only fail-quiet on this list |
| 9 | `cornerOwnership` at inner corners under the wrong winding (§2) | `extraLengthIn` at every inner corner | **panel widths and the cut list** — 4 × thickness on a rectangular courtyard |
| 10 | `totalWallPerimeterIn` → `plasterGrossWallAreaSqFt` → **one** `plasterNetAreaSqFt` passed as BOTH the interior and the exterior area (`page.tsx:3947`, `3992-4004`) | the *lengths* are right — inner-ring walls are real walls — but **one number can no longer stand for two faces** now that the courtyard face is exterior (§3) | **not an over-count: a model error that hides behind symmetry.** The two figures come out equal on a plain ring and diverge the moment an inner wall carries a run stop. **R1 requirement** |
| 11 | `computeInsetPerimeterRing` (bale foundation rim rings) | emits rim segments for inner-ring walls, which may be right or wrong depending on whether the inner ring bears on a foundation | **building question — Open Item, and §5's roof answer now constrains it** |
| 12 | `panelLoadOrder` | rotates `footprint.walls` to start at the least-accessible corner; with two rings the rotation spans both | load order is advisory — but §6's numbering now encodes an erection order, so the two orderings must agree or one must say it does not |

**⚠ Item 11 is the one most likely to be got wrong by reasoning too fast.** "The courtyard has no foundation" does **not** mean "the inner ring walls have no foundation" — an inner ring wall is a real wall and must bear on something, and under §5's form (a) it carries half a truss span. What has no foundation is the *floor of the courtyard*. **Do not infer the inner ring's bearing detail from Tommy's one sentence, and do not infer it from the roof answer either.** Still an Open Item.

**⚠ Item 10 is the one most likely to PASS a weak test.** An inner ring contributes one interior face and one exterior face, exactly as an outer wall does, so the two areas are equal on a plain ring and a single-number implementation looks correct. **The fixture must include an asymmetric case** — a `WallRunStop` on one inner wall — so the wrong implementation fails.

**How to do the audit so it is real and not a claim:** a synthetic two-ring fixture (rect outer, rect inner) whose correct answers are computable by hand — outer area minus hole area, pier count over the annulus only, zero floor panels whose centre lies in the hole, **interior and exterior plaster areas asserted separately and differing in at least one case** — plus a sweep over courtyard positions and sizes. Same shape as 1r's sweeps, which is the standard this workstream is held to.

### 5. The roof — **ANSWERED 2026-09-25, and the answer is TWO FORMS, not one**

Asked to pick between an open-courtyard two-plane roof, an inward-draining ring roof and an outward-draining ring roof, Tommy declined to pick:

> *"Can't decide between 1 and 3. I imagine most scenarios would be some kind of truss that spans from north inner to north outer and around the building giving it a two sloped roof all the way around. I can also see the benefit of having a 'shed roof' exclusively sloped towards the exterior that goes all the way around the building. Both options have a totally exposed to the open sky courtyard (although because it is a ring the courtyard is almost always shaded from the sun.)"*

**⚠ Do not collapse this into one choice. He asked for both, and R5 is therefore "support two forms and let the user choose", not "implement the roof".** That is a materially bigger stage than the one this plan originally sketched, and it is re-estimated below.

**Form (a) — the ring gable.** A truss spans **inner ring to outer ring**, north-inner to north-outer and around the building, giving a **two-sloped roof all the way around** — a ridge that runs the ring between the two walls, with one plane falling to the courtyard and one falling to the exterior.

**Form (b) — the ring shed.** A single plane sloped **exclusively toward the exterior**, all the way around. High at the inner ring, low at the outer.

**Settled for both, and it closes a question that was entangled with §3: the courtyard is ALWAYS open to the sky.** There is no roofed-courtyard case in either form. That is what independently confirms the courtyard face as exterior, rather than leaving the two answers propping each other up.

#### ⚠ Form (a) structurally couples the two rings — and it constrains an Open Item that is still open

A truss spanning inner-to-outer means **the inner ring is load-bearing for the roof.** It is not a freestanding courtyard wall; it is half the building's bearing line. **That bears directly on the still-open question of whether the inner ring wall sits on a foundation (§4 item 11), and in form (a) the answer looks forced rather than free** — a wall carrying half a truss span has to bear on something real.

**This plan does not answer that question, and deliberately does not treat "forced" as "answered."** Two reasons: form (b) does not force it in the same way (the shed's high edge still loads the inner ring, but the load path and magnitude differ), and the foundation *detail* — bale foundation rings, a different detail, or something else — is not derivable from "it must bear on something" no matter how obviously true that is. **What this section does is make the coupling visible**, so that when the foundation question goes back to Tommy he can see it is downstream of a roof decision he has already made, rather than answering it in isolation. That visibility is the whole point of writing it down.

**⚠ Structural capacity stays where it is.** Every panel's `shearValue` / `loadBearingCapacity` carries `STRUCTURAL_PENDING_NOTE` and `PanelStructuralStatus` deliberately holds **no value**, blocked on Building Integrity's own pre-engineering. A truss spanning the annulus is a real span with a real load on a real wall, and **this plan states no span, no load, no truss spacing and no bearing capacity.** Flags-check point 4: the gap stays visible.

#### His aside, recorded as his observation and nothing more

> *"because it is a ring the courtyard is almost always shaded from the sun"*

**Recorded verbatim and attributed, because it is his stated expectation about how these buildings behave and someone could easily design against it by accident** — a courtyard reads on a plan like an open sunny space, and he is saying it is not one. For a straw-core building, persistent shade is the kind of thing that matters to drying and to moisture.

**⚠ It is an observation, not a specification, and this plan turns it into no number of any kind** — no drying rate, no moisture target, no ventilation requirement, no orientation rule. It is written here so it is not lost and not embellished. If shading has a real design consequence for Building Integrity's assemblies, that is a separate question to put to him with an engineer in the room.

#### What the code already supports, and what it does not

- **`computeRoofBearingSegments` is per-wall and ring-agnostic** — it takes a slot array, not a footprint — so truss plates and box beams work on inner-ring walls unchanged. Both forms get their bearing line for free.
- **`ridgeLine.ts` and `areWallsOppositePair` pick gable-end walls out of `footprint.walls` with no ring filter**, so today an inner-ring wall could be chosen as a gable end of the whole building. **Form (a)'s ridge is not a gable ridge in the existing sense at all** — it runs *around* the ring, between an inner wall and the outer wall opposite it, rather than between two opposite outer walls. The existing gable model spans a building; this spans an annulus. That is the substance of R5 and it is why R5 is not small.
- **The generalized roofline profile** (peaked/flat-top multi-point, per-wall point positions, rise-above-eave heights) is the closest existing machinery and is the right thing to extend rather than replace. Form (b), the ring shed, is much the nearer of the two to what exists: one plane per wall pair, no ridge.
- **Until R5 lands, the ring stages ship with the roof treated as today and the roof editor's wall pickers filtered to the outer ring**, with a Review Log entry saying the ring roof is unmodelled. **That is a scope statement, not a design claim** — an unmodelled roof must not print as a flat roof.

**Re-estimate: R5 is now the largest single stage in this workstream**, larger than R1. Two roof forms, a ridge concept the app does not have, a user choice between them, and a structural coupling nobody has engineering numbers for. **Recommended: R5 goes last and is scoped as its own plan when it is reached, not built off this section.** This section is enough to stop anyone building a ring roof by accident; it is not enough to build one.

### 6. Nomenclature — the collision, and Tommy's answer: **SETTLED 2026-09-25, inner ring numbers first**

**The collision, stated first because the answer only makes sense against it.** The scheme, settled 2026-09-24: **cardinal-direction letter + number, hyphen dropped** — `N1`, `E4`, `S12` — *"I have spray paint stencils in the shop, and there is no huphen stencil."* Panels are counted per direction across the building, in wall order then slot order (`panelInstances.ts:280-282`). **On a ring building the inner ring has a north wall and so does the outer ring**, so both produce `N1` — and uniqueness is the exact reason Tommy chose the one-run-per-direction rule: *"every panel name in the building stays unique, which is what a shop needs when it stacks panels by label."* Two panels stencilled `N1` in the same yard is that decision failing in the open.

**His answer, 2026-09-25:**

> *"I presume the interior walls would be easiest to install first - naming an interior wall N1 to N6 and then the outer wall picks up at N7 for example makes sense to me. Any slight alterations of that would be fine too, nice and simple, just letter plus number."*

**DECIDED: one continuous number series per cardinal direction, spanning both rings, the INNER ring numbered first.** A courtyard's north-facing panels take `N1…N6`; the outer ring's north wall continues at `N7`. **No new letter, no prefix, no symbol** — the stencil rack is untouched and the scheme is character-for-character the one already shipped for the ADU. It is also the smallest possible change to `panelInstances.ts`: the per-direction counter already walks every wall in the building and already renumbers on every render; all that changes is the **order of the walk**, which must put inner-ring walls ahead of outer-ring walls within each direction.

**⚠ The reason he gave is a build-sequence fact, not a naming preference, and it changes what a panel number MEANS.** *"The interior walls would be easiest to install first."* Numbering now encodes an **erection order**. Before this, a panel number was a position on a wall and nothing more. **Anywhere the app currently treats panel order as arbitrary or as a display convenience is now a place that may be quietly asserting an install sequence.** The specific places to check when this is built:

- **`panelLoadOrder`** — already a real load-order model (it rotates the wall list to start at the least-accessible corner, so the last panel off the truck is the first one needed). It is now **downstream of a second ordering claim** and the two must agree, or one of them has to say plainly that it does not. It is also item 12 on the §4 audit for an unrelated reason.
- **The cut list, the shipping sequence and the truck load plan** — all of which order by panel instance today. If the numbering is an erection order, a load order that contradicts it puts the inner ring at the back of the truck.
- **The packing model is already flagged** as *"a deliberately simplified uniform-grid packer… illustrative, not a real optimized load plan."* That caveat now has to survive alongside a numbering scheme that looks like a sequencing instruction. **Do not let a number that happens to be an erection order be read as a validated one.**

**Making the scheme total, using the latitude he gave** (*"any slight alterations of that would be fine too"*). Three cases his sentence does not cover, resolved the simplest way rather than redesigned:

- **A ring with no wall facing a given direction** — the series simply starts at the outer ring. `N1` on a building whose courtyard has no north-facing wall is an outer-ring panel, and nothing special happens. No gap is reserved, no placeholder number is skipped: a reserved gap would be a number that names nothing, which is worse than a series that starts where the panels start.
- **Different wall counts on the same side** — already handled by the existing rule, since the counter counts *panels*, not walls. Two inner north-facing walls and one outer simply concatenate in that order.
- **Three or more rings**, if the `rings` model ever carries them — **innermost first, outward**. Follows his reason directly (install order), not his example.

**⚠ The real cost: the two rings' numbering is now COUPLED, so inserting a panel on the inner ring renumbers the outer ring too.** Tommy accepted always-renumber for the ADU (*"Everything downstream should get renumbered"*) and this log already records what that costs: *"the E-7 on the sheet in the shop's hand is the E-8 on the sheet in the office… Someone installs the wrong panel."* The mitigation is already a stated requirement — **sheet revision identity: project name, revision and date on every sheet, plus a line on the panel schedule saying names are positional and valid only for this revision.**

**Does a ring building make that staleness materially worse? Yes, on both axes, and it is worth saying plainly rather than assuming the existing mitigation simply carries over:**

- **More panels per series.** A ring building has two perimeters, so a given direction's run is roughly twice as long. A renumber moves twice as many labels.
- **The blast radius now crosses rings.** Before, a north-wall insert moved only north-wall numbers on one perimeter — and a builder could reasonably hold in their head that they had touched the north wall. Now an edit on the **courtyard's** north side shifts every outer-ring north panel as well, and the two walls are not adjacent, not visible from each other, and quite possibly being built by different people on different days. **That is the same failure mode as the building-wide `H` header series, whose own note warns of "a wider blast radius than the panels have."** The ring scheme gives the panels that wider radius too.
- **Consequence for the build order: the sheet-revision identity (Smearforn Stage 5) stops being a follow-up and becomes a companion requirement for ring buildings.** The **renumbering diff** — *"E-7 through E-12 shifted to E-8 through E-13"* — already recommended as the first follow-up after the editor stages, is the thing that actually makes this safe, and a ring building is the strongest argument yet for it.

**Consumers to re-check when this is built:** `combinedPanelLabel` and the jack-stud ref `${inst.name}-JS1`. The 1r audit confirmed those are the only two places a panel name is *formatted* rather than merely keyed, and neither is affected by the walk order — but both are affected by any future change to the format, and this decision deliberately makes no such change.

### 7. What the editor actually needs

Tommy asked for *"the editor tools and code"*. Concretely:

- **A courtyard tool, alongside `rectangle` / `octagon` / `bump-out` / `edit` / `drag-wall` in `shapeTool`.** It only exists when a footprint already exists — a courtyard is a hole in something.
- **How the user sets the courtyard size: by OFFSET, with the courtyard dimensions shown as a live readout.** The gesture is "how deep is the building between the rings", which is the number a builder actually thinks in and the one that has to stay legal. The courtyard's own width × depth is the same information and should be displayed (and typeable, through the existing `LengthInput`, which already parses `41 1/2` and snaps to the eighth) — but the offset is the primary because it is the quantity with a floor.
- **⚠ Offset-locked in the first ring stage; independently editable later, and the reason is a known missing guard.** `dragWallBounded` refuses any offset that self-intersects. **`editWallLength` has no validity guard at all** — it is already an Open Item in this log, with a worked example that inverts a footprint's winding from a value typed straight into the wall-length field. On a single ring that yields a coherently-broken polygon. On a ring building, an inner wall dragged or typed past the outer ring is **a building that cannot exist**, and every ring-aware consumer would be wrong together. **So: the `editWallLength` guard stops being a nice-to-have and becomes a prerequisite for independent inner-ring editing (R3).** Offset-locked editing (R1) needs no such guard, because the offset constructor can simply refuse an illegal offset — which is why it goes first.
- **Interaction with the Smearforn tools, which are all ring-agnostic:** typed panel widths (Stage 1, built), insert/replace/delete (Stage 2), and per-slot pins all operate on one wall's slot array and neither know nor care which ring the wall is in. **Nothing in Smearforn needs redoing for rings.** The elevation viewer's wall dial walks `footprint.walls` and would silently gain the inner ring's walls — it needs a ring label or a ring filter. **§6's answer does not cover this**, and deliberately should not: the panels themselves are one continuous series precisely so a shop never has to know which ring a panel came from, but a person *editing* on screen always needs to know which wall they are on. **Recommendation: an on-screen ring label ("courtyard" / "exterior") that is UI only and appears on no printed panel name.** Separating the two is the point.
- **A ring wall that STOPS is a legitimate combination, and it is probably the common case.** Smearforn Stage 3's `WallRunStop` on an inner-ring wall means **the courtyard has an opening** — a passage from the courtyard out through the building, or simply an unbuilt side. What it means precisely: the *polygon* is unchanged (the hole is still a hole), so area, floor, piers and framing still exclude the courtyard exactly as before; only the panel run stops. That is the same separation Stage 3 already established — *"incomplete is a property of the panel run, never of the shape"* — and rings do not weaken it. **One consequence to state rather than discover: a courtyard with an opening is still an excluded hole for the floor, so the passage floor is unfloored too.** If Tommy wants a floored passage through an unfloored courtyard, that is a second hole shape and is out of scope.
- **Not in the editor, deliberately:** bump-outs on the inner ring, more than one courtyard, a courtyard that touches the outer ring, and non-concentric holes. Each is expressible in the `rings` model and none is asked for.

### 8. Octagon specifically — what it inherits and what it does not

**Inherits:**

- **The equal-side geometry.** `buildOctagonFootprint` clips a box at `S(1 − 1/√2)`, giving eight sides of `0.41421 × boxDimension`. An offset octagon is still an all-45° octagon, so an inner octagon generated by offsetting an outer one is a valid octagon — the construction is closed under offset. That is what makes an octagon courtyard cheap *geometrically*.
- **Mitered corner ownership: both walls own their corner, every corner.** `cornerOwnership` skips non-right-angle corners and leaves the default `hasCorner: true` on both ends. So **every octagon wall spends 51in on corners** — which is what makes §2's dead band universal rather than occasional.
- **The 1/8in grid exception, and now twice over.** A 45° wall between two grid corners has an irrational length; the residual is ≤1/16in per diagonal wall, absorbed at the mitered joint by the safety/gap panel. That is settled and unchanged — but a ring building has **eight more diagonals**, so the count of walls carrying a rounding residual doubles. No new decision; worth saying once so nobody reports it as new.
- **The per-wall safety-corner rule** (`computeSafetyEnd` / `markSafetyCorner`) and the no-borrow rule, both of which are per-wall and ring-safe.

**Does NOT inherit:**

- **`MIN_DIMENSION_FT = 8`.** Both `buildRectangleFootprint` and `buildOctagonFootprint` clamp every side of their bounding box to 8ft. **An inner ring created by offsetting the outer ring does not go through either builder and inherits no floor at all**, so nothing stops a 2ft courtyard. It needs its own minimum — and a *useful* minimum courtyard size is a building question, not a geometry one. The geometric floor (the two rings must not collide, and a wall needs somewhere to be) is computable; the practical one is not. **Open Item; do not invent one.** Note also what the 8ft clamp has been quietly doing: 96in is comfortably above 75in, so **a rectangle built by that builder can never enter the dead band.** An offset inner rectangle can. (This is the clamp a builder recently rediscovered as "a rectangle can never merge its corners" — same constant, and the ring is where it stops protecting anything.)
- **`isMiteredShape` being a whole-footprint property.** See the contamination note above — this has to become per-ring before an octagon courtyard can sit inside a rectangular building, or that combination has to be refused outright.
- **`snapOctagonBoxPx`'s drag preview.** It snaps a dragged bounding box for a *new* octagon. A courtyard is created by offset, not by dragging a box, so the preview is a new (small) piece of canvas work, not a reuse.

**⚠ R2 has left this workstream.** The 51–75in corner-geometry fix was recommended here as a ring prerequisite. **Tommy approved slotting it in with admin tooling, this weekend, ahead of rings** — his reasoning the same as the recommendation's: it stands alone, needs no topology, and fixes a defect that exists in the app today. **So it is no longer a ring stage and no longer a ring dependency**; by the time R0 starts it is expected to be built, and R4 inherits it rather than waiting on it. Its own record stays with the Smearforn corner-band Open Item, where it belongs. **One thing for whoever builds it: it is a prerequisite for the octagon ring, so if it slips, R4 slips with it** — worth a line in its own as-built note so the coupling is not lost.

**R0 → R1 is the spine. R3 through R6 are each independently orderable, and none of them is now waiting on an answer from Tommy** — R5 waits on its own scoping pass rather than on a decision.

**⚠ R6 should land with R1, not after it.** A ring building that numbers two `N1`s is a ring building that cannot be sent to a shop, and R1 is the stage that first produces one. It is cheap enough to ride along.

### How big is this, honestly

**Bigger than all of Smearforn Stages 0–3 put together**, and that comparison is worth making precisely rather than as a gesture:

- **R0 alone is roughly Smearforn Stage 3.** Same shape of work — an exhaustive audit of derived totals against a model change, in code that is currently correct — and Stage 3's audit found six over-counts including one that cut a real part wrong. The §4 table already names twelve candidates *before* anybody has run the audit, which historically is when the count goes up, not down.
- **R0 + R1 ≈ all of Smearforn 0–3**, and R1 grew on 2026-09-25: the per-face plaster split (§3) is a change to the Plaster Master's shape rather than a coefficient, and it is an R1 requirement.
- **R5 alone is now larger than R1** — two roof forms, a ridge concept the app does not have, and a structural coupling nobody has numbers for (§5). **This is the single biggest movement in the estimate since the plan was written**, and it came from Tommy declining to pick one form rather than from anything found in the code.
- **The whole workstream is on the order of three times Smearforn** — revised up from two-to-three once the roof turned out to be two roofs. The caveat stands and matters more: **this estimate is less reliable than Smearforn's was.** Smearforn was four editor features on a model nobody was changing. This is the first topology change in the app, and the honest thing to say about a first is that the unknowns have not been found yet. R0 exists precisely to find them before anything depends on them. **The estimate has moved twice in one day, both times upward, both times because an answer arrived — which is itself the argument for R5 getting its own plan rather than an estimate.**

**Could anything useful be delivered early, without the topology change?**

- ~~**Yes, one thing: the 51–75in corner-geometry fix.**~~ **SCHEDULED 2026-09-25 — Tommy approved slotting it in with admin tooling, this weekend, ahead of rings.** The recommendation is accepted and the item has left this workstream (see the staging table). What made it the right answer is worth keeping: it needed no ring topology, it fixed a defect that existed in the app already, and it was on his own deferred list — so it was never a consolation prize standing in for rings, it was work that wanted doing anyway. **It is now also a prerequisite that is expected to be done before R0 starts; if it slips, R4 slips with it.**
- **No, "two separate buildings on one site" is not worth offering, and this plan declines to offer it.** It would not be a consolation prize, it would be a wrong answer with a friendly face. Two buildings do not share corners, do not share a roof, are not one perimeter, and number their panels independently — every single thing that makes a ring hard is the thing two buildings do not model. It would report a wrong area, a wrong perimeter and a wrong panel schedule for a ring job, and it would do so plausibly. The correct answer to "can I have some of it sooner" is **R0 and R1, in that order, after Monday.**

### Flags check — run against this plan

Per the 6-point discipline. **This plan introduces zero new `CatalogValue`s, and that is a deliberate outcome rather than an oversight.**

1. **Every real-world number in the diff carries a `status` and a `note`** — there are none. Everything R0 and R1 touch is pure geometry and topology: a ring index, a polygon accessor, a winding sign, a shoelace that subtracts instead of adds. Same argument `eighths.ts` makes for the 1/8in grid: *"a precision convention, not a building dimension — it is not a fastener spacing, a load, a density, or a cost, and it needs nobody's engineering sign-off."*
2. **Anything marked `confirmed` that is actually interpreted?** Nothing is being marked. `cornerPanelWidthIn` (25.5) and `fabricationMinPanelWidthIn` (24) are re-used unchanged and unmoved; **no catalog value is edited by this workstream.**
3. **Notes trace to a source?** Every number quoted above is either read out of the code (51in, 75in, 0.41421, 8ft, 15.5in) or derived from two of those by arithmetic shown in place.
4. **Structural figures using `PanelStructuralStatus` with no invented value?** The structural questions this workstream raises — what the inner ring bears on (§4 item 11), and how a truss spans the annulus (§5) — are left entirely unanswered. **No span, no load, no truss spacing, no bearing capacity, no placeholder.** The roof answer arriving on 2026-09-25 made form (a)'s structural coupling explicit, which is exactly the moment a plausible span figure would have been easiest to write down; none is.
   - **The same discipline applied to his shading aside** (*"the courtyard is almost always shaded from the sun"*). It is recorded verbatim and attributed, and it is turned into **no drying rate, no moisture target, no ventilation rule.** He made an observation; this log does not promote observations into values.
   - **And to the plaster decision.** The courtyard face being exterior changes **which area a confirmed formula is applied to**, and nothing else. No price, mix ratio, coverage rate or labor figure in `plasterPriceDefaults` / `plasterMixPartsDefaults` moves — including the ones already `pending-BI-confirmation` because the source spreadsheet carried no pricing. **A decision that opens a file is not a licence to edit the rest of it.**
5. **Do the gaps surface in the review log?** Required, and it is an acceptance criterion of R1: **one Review Log entry per unresolved building question that is live on the drawn project.** Two of the original three are now closed, so the list is: **the inner ring's bearing (§4.11)** and **the unmodelled ring roof (§5)**. The roof entry must say the roof is *unmodelled*, not that it is flat — an unmodelled roof printing as a flat roof would be a substituted value wearing a default's clothes. A ring building must not print looking complete.
6. **Is the code treating open decisions as provisional?** The original failure mode here was §3: `wallCompassDirection`'s centroid would have *answered* the exterior-face question by accident. **Tommy has now answered it the same way the centroid would have — and the fix stays in R0 anyway.** That is the point worth keeping: a correct answer produced by a mechanism that is wrong for the reason it is wrong is still a bug, it just stops being a visible one. It agrees by an accident of vertex counts and would disagree on an off-centre courtyard in a notched outer ring. **Do not close a point-6 item because the accident turned out lucky.**

### Open Items — Concentric Wall Rings

**Three open, three closed on 2026-09-25. The closed ones are kept in place rather than deleted, because two of them changed the shape of a stage and one of them constrains an item that is still open.**

- ~~**Nomenclature: what does a panel on the inner ring get called?**~~ **ANSWERED — one series per direction across both rings, inner ring numbered first (`N1…N6` inside, outer picks up at `N7`). See §6.** No format change, no new stencil. What it leaves behind is not a question but two pieces of work: **panel numbering now encodes an erection order**, so every consumer that treated panel order as arbitrary needs re-checking; and **the two rings' numbering is coupled**, so the sheet-revision identity and the renumbering diff become companion requirements rather than follow-ups.
- ~~**Which face of the inner ring is "exterior"?**~~ **ANSWERED — the courtyard face is EXTERIOR. See §3.** Independently confirmed by the roof answer below, since both roof forms leave the courtyard open to the sky. **Consequence, now an R1 requirement:** `plasterNetAreaSqFt` must become a per-face pair rather than one number passed twice — and it must be built that way **even though the two come out equal on a plain ring**, because they diverge the moment an inner wall carries a run stop. No price, ratio or rate changes.
- ~~**How does the roof work over a ring?**~~ **ANSWERED, and the answer is two forms rather than one. See §5.** A ring gable (truss spanning inner-to-outer, two slopes around) and a ring shed (one plane sloped outward, around), with a user choice. Courtyard always open to the sky in both. **This re-scoped R5 into the largest stage in the workstream and it should get its own plan when reached.** His aside — *"because it is a ring the courtyard is almost always shaded from the sun"* — is recorded as his observation and turned into no number.
- **⚠ Does the inner ring wall sit on a foundation? — STILL OPEN, and the roof answer now constrains it.** "The courtyard has no foundation" is about the courtyard *floor*. The inner ring wall is a real wall and bears on something — and under §5's form (a) it carries half a truss span, which makes the answer look forced. **It is not answered here on that basis.** "It must bear on something" does not yield a detail, and form (b) loads it differently. **When this goes to Tommy he should see it alongside the roof answer**, because he made that decision first and it narrows this one; answering it in isolation is how the two end up inconsistent.
- **What is the minimum courtyard size, and the minimum building depth between the two rings?** The geometric floor is computable; the useful floor is a building judgement. `MIN_DIMENSION_FT = 8` does not apply to an offset-generated ring, so without an answer there is nothing stopping a 2ft courtyard.
- **Is an octagon courtyard inside a rectangular building a real combination he wants?** It is expressible, and it forces `isMiteredShape` to become per-ring. If he only ever wants octagon-in-octagon and rectangle-in-rectangle, refusing mixed rings is cheaper and safer.
- ~~**Does the corner-geometry fix (the 51–75in band) get promoted ahead of admin tooling?**~~ **ANSWERED 2026-09-25: yes — it goes in WITH admin tooling, this weekend, ahead of rings.** Recommendation accepted on the stated grounds: it stands alone, needs no topology, and fixes a defect that exists in the app today. **It has left this workstream** (see the staging table) and its record belongs with the Smearforn corner-band item. **One coupling to carry into its as-built note: it is a prerequisite for R4, the octagon ring — if it slips, R4 slips with it.**
- **Is a `PROJECT_FILE_VERSION` bump wanted for `rings`, purely so an older deploy refuses rather than misdraws?** Not needed on additive grounds. It costs a Supabase redaction seed migration (`0011`), and `0010` is still unapplied and unverified against any PostgreSQL. **Recommended default: no bump.**

### Handoff to the coder — R0 only (nothing else is ready to build)

**⚠ Stages R1 through R6 are NOT handed off.** R1 is specced above but should not start until Monday's job is drawn and admin tooling is done, per Tommy's confirmed order; R3 waits on the `editWallLength` guard; R4 inherits the corner-geometry fix, which now lands with admin tooling ahead of this workstream; R5 is unblocked but **re-scoped to two roof forms and needs its own plan, not this section**. **R6 is unblocked and specced (§6) but belongs with R1**, since R1 is the first stage that can produce a building with two `N1`s.

**Not in scope for R0, explicitly:** creating an inner ring from the UI; any new `shapeTool`; any change to `PROJECT_FILE_VERSION`; anything in `supabase/`, auth or `apps/web/app/cloud/**`; any change to `cornerOwnership`'s rule (only to the convexity test it calls); any catalog value; the 51–75in band; **the roof, in either of its two forms**; panel naming; the `editWallLength` validity guard; **the per-face plaster split (that is R1's, and it is a change to the Plaster Master's shape — do not start it early because §3 is now decided)**; per-ring membrane handling.

**R0 — the ring index and the polygon accessor.**

*Scope:* make the geometry layer capable of describing a polygon with a hole, and move every array-order-as-polygon consumer onto a ring-aware accessor — **without any user-facing change and without any project being able to contain a second ring yet.**

*Files:* `packages/geometry/src/types.ts` (optional `rings?: CornerId[][]` on `Footprint`, outer first); a new `packages/geometry/src/footprintRings.ts` (+ test) exporting `footprintRingPolygons(footprint): Point[][]`, defaulting to `[corners in array order]` when `rings` is absent; `footprintArea.ts` (signed shoelace per ring, summed, `Math.abs` **outside** the sum); `cornerAngle.ts` (`isConvexCorner` gains a ring-winding sign; `footprintIsAllRightAngles` becomes per-ring); `perimeterRing.ts` (`orderedWallCycle` walks one ring at a time; `computeInsetFootprintPolygon` returns a polygon per ring); `pierGrid.ts`, `joistLayout.ts`, `floorPanelGrid.ts`, `floorMembranePolygons.ts` (ring-aware polygon + even-odd in/out across all rings); `wallCompassDirection.ts` (centroid from the wall's own ring); `retile.ts` (`isMiteredShape` per ring). `packages/geometry/src/index.ts` for the new export.

*Acceptance:*
- **Every existing single-ring project produces byte-identical output.** Every total, every panel width, every member, every price unchanged. This is the primary criterion and it should be asserted, not eyeballed.
- `npx vitest run` green and `tsc --noEmit` clean, per the gate rule.
- A **synthetic two-ring fixture** (rect outer, rect inner, inner wound CCW) where every answer is hand-computable: area = outer − hole exactly; `isPointInPolygon` false for a point in the hole and true for a point in the annulus; zero floor panels and zero piers with centres in the hole; `computeInsetFootprintPolygon` returns two polygons rather than `[]`; `isConvexCorner` true at all four inner corners; `isMiteredShape` false for a rectangle outer ring even when the inner ring is an octagon.
- **`cornerOwnership` on the two-ring fixture produces NO `extraLengthIn` anywhere** — the direct test for the §2 trap, the one that would otherwise add four wall thicknesses to a courtyard's cut list.

*Edge cases worth testing:* a hole whose edge is collinear with an outer edge; a hole with an odd vertex count; a point exactly on a hole boundary (`isPointInPolygon` is already documented as boundary-undefined — assert what it does, do not change it); `rings` present but listing exactly one ring (must equal the absent case exactly); `rings` referencing a corner id that does not exist (malformed input — leave it alone the way `quantizeFootprint` leaves a malformed wall alone, rather than silently zeroing); a footprint where `walls` array order differs from ring order, which is already explicitly not guaranteed.

*The one thing most likely to be got wrong:* **`Math.abs` inside the shoelace.** `computeFootprintAreaSqFt` currently wraps the whole sum in `Math.abs`, which is correct for one ring and silently turns hole-subtraction into hole-addition for two. It has to become: signed area per ring, summed, absolute value taken once at the very end. There is no test today that would catch the wrong version, because there is no two-ring fixture today — which is why the fixture is an acceptance criterion and not a nicety.
